HOMEWARD. Through shade and shine the journey lies Beneath the ever-changing skies. Our finite skill can ne'er divine If one dhy shall be dark or fine; God hides it from our anxious eyes. How well for him who daily tries By faith to pierce the clouds' disguise, And sees the Father's glad design Through shade and shine. 0 Thou, Who art the Only Wise, ,In mazes dark my way advise; Let bitter days with sweet combine To make my life more truly Thine; Thus led by Thee, my song shall rise Through shade and shine.
4-44 The Quiver" far Ma
THE NINE SUITORS.

. A British ship at anchor lay, In the harbour of New York; The stevedores were packing her With Yankee beef and pork. ' Nine slim young men went up the planks • And they were tall and good; But none of them had ever loveyl, They said they never would; But whether they wouldn't, Or whether they couldn't, Or their mothers said they shouldn't, The world will never know. The passengers were all on board, .The vessel got up steam, , And floated down the river, like The--ah—something of a dream. A pretty girl came up on the deck And near the railing stood. She never loved a fellow-man, And said she never would; But whether she couldn't, Or whether she wouldn't, Or her father said she shouldn't, The world will never know. - 'The nine young men stood in a row, Each trying not to stare, The lady looked embarrassed, and They offered her a chair. The nine young swells were very rich, And it was understood t 'That each of them could marry Whatever girl he would; t But whether he couldn't, Or whether he wouldn't, Or the lady said he shouldn't, The world will never know. • So things went on as usual, •The weather soon grew thick, = The nine young men were gallant, The pretty girl was sick; She certainly was charming. When they brought her dainty food,! " I'd eat it all now really, And truly if I could ; But whether she couldn't, ' Or whether she wouldn't, Or her stomach said she shouldn't, -171 , The world will never know. The nine young men came up on deck, Each in his Sunday clo'es, And went abaft the wheel-house, In order to propose; The lady had no preference, -. But said that, if she could, She'd marry every one of them, But it wasn't any good; But whether she couldn't, , •Or whether she wouldn't, _ Or that custom said she shouldn't, The world will never know, ' The lady asked the Captain how She ever should decide. Said he, "The love of those young men Should certainly be tried." So, when they all were present, She fell into the se-a, I . And eight of them jumped after her, The ninth—oh where where was he? Now whether he couldn't (swim), Or whether he wouldn't (jump), II Or the Captain said he shouldn't (try), • The world will never know. Once fairly out of the water, she Went up to him, and said, "Dear sir, you are a solid man, And have I level head; So, without further-parley, Or hint of a pretence, _ I agree to marry you, sir, For you have common sense." So her father said he couldn't, And her mother said she wouldn't; And the Captain said he shouldn't Refuse to give consent. • —roma "Over the Summer Sea."

Wtiat will hold all the Snuff in the world? No one knows (nose). Blessings are strewed 'lLke flowers in our pathway; it rests with us to gather Them up carefully or pass them I begin to suspect that the common transactions of life are the most sacred channels for the spread of the heavenly leaven.--Macdonalci. Wondrous state of man! never so happy as when he has lost all private interests and regards, and exists only in obedience and love of the Author.—Emerson. A friend declares that his wife is the most thrifty woman he ever knew. "Why, sir," he recently ex- claimed, "she has made ten patchwork quilts during the last ten years—made them herself, sir, out of the samples she collected in her shopping tours during tnat time I" Lorenzo Day having married. Miss Martha Week, a local paper comments : " A Day is made, a Week is lost; But time should not complain; There'll soon be little Days enough To make the Week again." The railroad restaurant on a certain line is kept by a veteran baker. A sprightly young traveller complained ef one of his pies the other day. The old man became angry. "Young man," he said, severely, "I made pies before you were bern."- "Yes," responded the traveller, "and I guess this must be one of those same pies." Little Amy, chidden for mischief, protested that Susan (the servant) had persuaded her. Said papa : "Tell me exactly what Susan said." "She said, 'You push that stand, miss, if you dare." " Them's my very words," interjected Susan. "And," pursued the little culprit, "I dared, so I pushed." This epitaph is very old and from some unknown locality:—

"Here lies old Jones, Who all his life collected bones, • Till Death, -that grim and bony spectre, That all-amassing bone collector, Boned old Jones, so neat and tidy, That here he lies, all bona fide." Lrkrt, Carasriens.—We may live to see men calling themselves Christians and differing in no single item from Mohammedans. in fact, even now there are re- ligionists among us who are not so near the truth as the followers of the false prophet. Oak has given place to willow; everybody has grown limp. Out of the gene- rality of limpness has come an admiration of it. A man cannot speak a plain word without being accused of bitterness, and if he denounces error he iS narrow- minded ; for all must join the Universal Admiration Company, or be placed under ban and be howled down. —Spurgeon. Efowever mean or inconsiderable the act, there is something in the well doing of it which has fellowship -with the noblest forms of manly virtue. Thus every action, down to the drawing of dline or utterance of a syllable, is capable of a peculiar dignity in the manner of it, and capable of a higher dignity in the motive of it. There is no action so slight nor so mean but it may be done to a great purpose, and ennobled, therefore; nor is any purpose so great but that slight actions may help it, and may be done so as to help it much, most especially that chief of all purposes, the pleasing of God. Hence Ceorge Herbert : " A servant with this clause Makes drudgery divine, Who sweeps a room as for Thy laws Makes that and the action fine." BEGIN WHERE You ARE.—The man who has really re- Solved to live the best life that he can, must begin right where he is—begin where his failures, his false educa- tion, his errors, and his sins have left him. By no single stroke of the pen can we erase whole pages in the his- tory of our lives. We have made or unmade ourselves as we are. If we could only begin at some lofty height which our moral dreams picture for us, it seems to us that there would be inspiration in going still further. But we cannot substitute in a moment the dream life for the real one. We are surrounded on every side by hard and tangible realities. We must begin where we are. i One who takes a practical and sagacious view of what is ' possible to him in life will not burden himself by dctempting the unattainable. He will begin when and where he is, and do that which lies in his power. Each day of life brings its own task; each task is an opportu- nity; each task accepted, each opportunity fulfilled, may be a step toward a higher life. Jacob's old dream was not an unreasonable one. His angels did not fly to heaven; they went patiently up each round of the lad- der, and they began at the bottom. —Christian Register. ESTABLISHED NEARLY 50 YEARS. When news came to England that he was,one of those poor prisoners in India who 'were tied back to back to fetter them; his mother exclaimed, fleaven pity the man that's tied to o,ur Davie." , Clackmannan a numberof youngsters were gathered: ' round a cart of coal which was about to be tipped up lbefore a door. When the boal went up with a burley gush the youngsters, of course, set up a "hurrah?" ef delight. But in the middle of the general jubilee a 'pugnacious youth rushed amongst them with doubled " *its and, aquarad arms, shouting, "Get oet „co' here? ellnolxkqrabatQOrOtl?" ; PLAIN TALK TO A GEILL.-.--YOIIT every-day toilet is a • part of your character. A girl who looks like a or s sloven in the meriting is not to be trusted, however e finely she may look in the evening. Nci Matter how • humble your room may be, there are eight things it should contain—viz., a mirror, washstand, Seep; towel, • comb, hair, nail, and tooth brushes. These am just as essential as your breakfast, before which you should • make good and free else of them. Parents -who fail to provide_ their children with such appliances not only make a great mistake', but commit a sin of omission. Look tidy in.the merning,and when dinneliwork is over improve erceer tolls. Make it a rule of your daiW life to "dress up" 'in the afternoon. Your dross mayor not be anything better than calico, but with a ribbon or flower, or some bit of ornament, you can have an air of self- respect and satisfaction that invariably comes with being well dressed. WHY GOOD STeCKINGS ARE MARKED WITH COLOURED Lie-rms.—Everyone has probably noticed that all good stockings are marked at the top with coloured lines, the threads of which the lines are formed being dyed either blue or red. The dyes are not what are called "fast" colours, but are 4' fugitive." The reason for the lines being placed there by the manufacturer was to show that the texture at the material of which the stockings were made was not injured when the articles were bleached, the bleaching being effected by the action of chlorine. Although this chlorine, when carefully used, and when proper care is taken that the goods are not ex- posed too long to its influence, is comparatively harm- less; still, ir employed in excess, it so destroys the tex- ture of the stockings that they quickly come into holes, hence the adoption of these coloured lines, as before the chlorine can injure the material to this extent the red or blue colour of these lines will be removed. For this cause, any stockings which do net show these colours are always sold at a lower price; but however low the prices at which they are sold, for the reason mentioned, they are not cheap, nor is it advisable to purchase them. —Cassell's "Household Guide." A TRAORD/AN'S Rese.—Cooke, the celebrated American tragedian of earlier times, once actually pawned himself for money in Philadelphia. Going along the street he discovered a pawnshop. He entered the door, and ad- dressed the man behind the counter thus :—" My name is Cooke. This is my benefit night. The manager can't do without me. lam no for Richard 111, 1 want some liquor: I have no money. Now, I propose to pledge my royal person for $lO, and you may lay me upon one Of your shelves." The pawnbroker paid the $lO, and Cooke was laid up. Meanwhile a largd audience had assembled at the theatre, and at seven o'clock the manager was obliged to apologise for the absence of Cooke, and asked permission to commence the performance with a farce. A boy awaited him as he left the stage, and presented a note written in cypher, evhich he translated thus :—" My' dear Jones,—l am pawned for $lO ; send and redeem me, or it will be impossible for Richard to bo himself to- night.—Yours, W. Cooke." The manager hurried off to the pawnshop, where he found Cooke with a piece of paper in his buttonhole marked, " N 0.1,473 ; pawned for $10." The amount was paid, a cab called, and Mr. Cooke and the manager returned to the theatre. Soon the eccentric tragedian was before the audience, and he never played better than on this occasion. Two BRAVE. Grrits.—On the sth December, 1879, two men had to cross the Ste Lawrence River, from La Rue Island to a wharf on the main shore. It was an intensely cold day, and a heavy gale was blowing strongly from the north-east up the river. a The men-loaded their punt with a sleigh, and had managed to wade' the middle of the channel, when a sudden and violent gust of wind swamped the punt and turned her over. The men clung to her while bottom upward, and tried to "tread" the water so as to get her to the shore, but in vain ; the cold was so intense that their legs were benumbed above the knees, and they gave themselves up for lost. They remained in this perilous position for a consideFable time, shouting loudly for help till their throats were sore. Making a final effort, they shouted again, and this time their cries were heard at the house of a Mr. Darling, who, with his family, resided close to the shore. That gentleman was ill ire,bed, but his wife and daugh- ters,-Maggie and Jessie, were at home, the men and boys being at work in the field at a distance. On bearing the last painful shout of the drowning nem, they quickly opened the door, to see them struggffng in the great river—a stream the width and -volume of which surpass anything in Europe: The first suggestion from the mother was to fetch the men from the fields, but before this could be done brave Maggie and Jessie—the latter a girl of sixteen years—had, without a word, launched the skiff, and were rowing with all their strength through the troubled waters and driving storm. They had the greatest difficulty in reaching the exhausted and helpless men, but at last their noble efforts were rewarded, and in ten minutes the poor fellows were being chafed and warmed by their father's fires--" The Sea: Its Stirring Story of Adventure, Peril, and Heroism" for May. TRICKING A BORILOWER.—An instance of vindictive

memory may sho;v 11;;W the horse remembers those who ill-treat him :—" I will relate a little circumstance which took place in Mexico a few years before I left there. One of my friends had a horse extremely gentle, and of such an easy agreeable gait, that he took the greatest I care of him, and held him at a great price. A well-fed, big and lusty friar was a friend to our neighbour—one wile liked the good things of this world, as 'well as he liked to ride out to the small towns bordering upon the city of Mexico, and take a dinner with the bonny lasses and countrymen inhabiting those villages. He used to ask my friend to loan him his horse to take these ex- cursions just around the capital; and, as his requests were granted with so good a grace, he, in a short time. went so far as to ask the loan of this favourite animal to go to Cuernavaca, a distance of eighteen leagues. As this happened pretty often, our friend complained to me one day of the indiscretion of the friar. I asked him if he could procure me a friar's dress ter a few days, and leave his horse with me for the same time. He did so. I dressed myself in the'friar's dress and went in where the horse was. I took' a good whip in my hand and made him do pennance for no other sin but that of too much gentleness. Going out I took off my friar's dress and went in again in my own dress, and handled him gently. I repeated the operation a few days, at the end of which I took the horse back to his master, :and told hini he might lend him to the friar whenever he pleased. A day or two after he came to my store. 'Your remedy,' said he, has had a marvellous effect. Our monk has just left my house, perfectly' persuaded that my horse is possessed with the devil. For when the holy person- age came up to take him by the bridle to get on him, he was so frightened, and wheeled round so quick, and flew away from him with so much terror, that one would have said he took him for the destroying angel." The friar 'crossed himself many times, hurried away in all haste to the convent to sprinkle himself with holy water, and never asked my friend for his horse again. ' —London Society.

CARDINAL NEWX6N AND GENERAL GORDON.—The Weekly Register says :—" The readers of Mr. Frank Power's letters from Khartoum, may be interested to know that a curious little relic linking the name of the late Times' correspondent with that of the hero of the Soudan, General Gordon, has reached Dublin, in the form of a tiny book, a duodecimo copy of Cardinal Newman's Dream of Geron- tins; with handwriting and marks inside. On the flyleaf is an Inscription: 'Frank Power, with kind regards of C. G. Gordon: 18 feb, and, lower, across the same page: Dearest Al—,—l send you this little book, which General Gordon has given me. The pencil-marking throughout the beck is his. Frank Power, Kbattoum.' The took has been forwarded to Mr. Power's sister, for whom his affectionate remembrance had destined the precious souvenir. The deep incisive pencil-marks drawn under certain lines, almost all of which name death, and cry for the prayer of friends, are touchingly interesting to see. 'Pray for me, 0 my friends!' 'Tis death-0 loving friende, your prayerS—'tis he!' 'So pray for me, my friends, who have not strength to pray!' 'Use well the interval 'Prepare to meet thy tied ! " Now that the hour has come, my fear is fled;' with many other longer passages all bearing on the supreme moment at band. The last words underlined before he gave the book to poor young Power are these : Farewell, but not for ever, brother dear; Be In ave and patient on thy bed of sorrow! The latest touch of interest is given to this memorable inci- dent by a letter written by Cardinal Newman to Mr Power's sister, who had sent the tiny, well-thumbed volume to the author of the 'Dream of Gerontius.' Cardinal Newman writes :--,Your letter and Its contents took away my breath. I was deeply moved to find that a book of mine bad been in General Gordon's hands, and that, the descrip- tion of a soul preparing for death. I send it back to you, with my heartfelt thanks, by this post, ins registered cover. It is additionally precious as having Mr. Power's writing in

At the public sales of pure-bred cattle in America last year, Shorthorns led in numbers, but Aberdeen Polled- Angus made the best average price, namely, £lO3 55., , 300 being sold. - An American pig breeder says There is no better feed for young pigs after they have learned to eat than good thrashed oats. If given dry and alone, tne pigs will chew at tfiem till they get all the kernels, but they will swallow little or none of the husks." At the April horse fair at Stewarton, 100 Clydesdale farm horses were offered. J. Clews, Barrhead, sold draught horses up_to £6B; John Crawford sold at from Z2O to £80; Hugh Crawford geld at £4O to £6O; Mr. Sim, Stewarton, sold a pony and draught horse at £l2O the pair. GROUND Gams.—"M. J. M. K." says :—"Having.talr a shooting_ of 740 acres on lease for 21 years, in which my landlord says, "I have the sale and exclusive right of sporting and taking and destroying-game and rabbits upon and over all his lands." lam now met by the farmers, who declare I have no right to the hares and rabbits in any way. The landlord himself on his farm was the, first to begin to ferret and snare rabbits en the farm over which I have the shooting. Havel any re- dress ?---We believe that you have not "the sole and ex- clusive right" of shooting. The Act gives the tenant an inalienable concurrent right to kill hares and rabbits. THE SMinL FARM AND LABOURERS' HOLDINGS COM- PANY.—Mr. Chamberlain is not very hopeful as to the sucress of the Small Farra and Labourers Holding Come. pany. In his speech before the members Of the Eighty Club on Tuesday, he said:—" The whole of the band of reactionary and impossible politicians have agreed in an experiment which, under such 'auspices, I venture to say is foredoomed to failure, but which at least has this to recommend it, that it recognises the wishes and the aspirations of those who have-been .for so long time entirely ignored." Would it not have been better to wait and see how the scheme is to be worked before talking of failure !--Hark-Lans Exprees. CHKESE AND BUTTER MAKING. Professor Sheldon, in an able lecture on cheese and butter making, just delivered at Sudbury, said: During the last fifteen to twenty years, we have seen or heard of many important changes in the practice el —dairy _farmers, and there has been an uncommon measure of activity displayed in various ways. We have seen the introduction of cheese and butter factories, and the growth of an enormous railroad milk traffic. What is technically known as 't winter dairying," viz., the pro- duction of milk in winter, has been developed to a de- gree our forefathers never dreamt of; and last of all, we have witnessed the advent of ensilage and of dairy I schools in the British Islands. But why not dairy schools as well as any other? The answer is: A new I generation is constantly springing; up, and must be trained. The need for education in dairy work, as in everything else, is perennial, and will remain so. It is certain that cheesemaking has declined in volume of late years, taking the county throughout; and that it has declined in quality too will hardly be disputed. There are Whole neighbourhoods to-day, in Derbyshire, in which scarcely any cheese at all is made, where a score years ago—nay, half-a-score—all the milk was turned into cheese or butter. Many farmers have de- voted their energies to the urban milk supply; others have gone into grazing; yet others have gone to the wall. The milk trade swamped cheesemaking in many places, and at last it has swamped itself.le Grazing, too, has gone to the dogs; and cheesemaking, low ae cheese' is to sell, is once more reviving a little in popular favour. Meanwhile, what has become of the dairymaids of a dozen years ago ? Disestablished and partia.ly dig. endowed by this self-same milk trade, note few of them were driven into matrimony in self-defence, and many have forgotten their cheesemaking. In some places there is a reaction in favour of cheese factories; for it is felt that the milk trade is not capable of unlimited expan- sion, that grazing will pay very small rents, and that a revival of home cheesemaking on the old lines is hope- less. For good or ill, universal hprne cheesemaking has, come to an end; •of tense it will survive in many places, but we, shall net again see it as gene- ral as it once was. I believe the finest cheese possible is made in some English farm-houses, as god as ever was made in the olden times, yet at the same time no farmer will begin cheesemaking in these days with a light heart. Even the old hands have a good deal of misgiving at times. Dairymaids of long experi- ence, famous for- the quality of their cheese, come sud- denly and unaccountably to grief, now and again, and there is lamentation.. The milk trade was once a means of escape from. the toil and uncertainty of cheesemAing, ' and everybody rushed-into it; but the thing new is to escape from thie Milk trade. The milk trade for the time being has been overdone, and is more-or less demoralised; uresently it will find its level again, and for s long time to come will remain the sheet anchor of a large propor- tion of our dairy farmers. Some persons attribute the decline in the average quality of farmhouse ch-ege to the ,high farming -which prevailed-in the third quarter of the current century, to the employment of purchased fer- tilisers and feeding 'stuffs; to the altered character of the herbage, the result of high farming. There is no doubt a good deal of truth in all this; but it-Is at the same time equally true that .a mond' system' fif cheese- making, intelligently carried 44t, will produce geed cheese on land fatined as intepsively_as,aey in _the.court- try, iave anreicCe-pt on sewage farms. Others attribute it to the lessened amount of care and . pains bestowed upon it, and to the want ofinterest taken by dairymaids in their special profession. 'Bale the cause be what it may, we lament the fact that theeheese of 'Old England is so uncertain, so variable, and frequently -so disap- pointing in quality, character, -and condition. I take it that ..the Cheddar system eheesernaking is more nearly scientifically correct than any Other in these islands; and, So far as is known at present, it is the only one that will answer well in any county or country. It Is pursued, to some extent, in various counties of Eng- land and Scotland; it is the basis en which nearly all the American and Canadian factory cheese is made; and it is practised in Russia, Australia, and other countries. The two features in Cheddir cheeseinakingwhich distinguish it are the regulation of temperature and the systematic development of acidity in the curd. Acidity, in fact, is the keystone of the arch,' and while it is intentionally and intelligently employed in the Cheddar system, to a degree which is not found in any other, it is really an 'important agent in many, other systems. Some twe or three, years ago, I spent a week among the dairy farmers of the Fylde of Lancashire, with a view to inquire into the mescal why there was so much disparity in the quality of the cheese produced in that excellent piece of country.. In each and every in- stance where I found good cheese, the salient feature was intentional employment of acidity; and wherever I find inferior cheese, this feature was conspicuous by its absence. But the method of its employment, differing in character from that of the Cheddar system, was more direct and international than in any other system I am acquainted with, and the result was an early ripening cheese, sound, full of mellow quality, and of excellent flavour. The modus operandi was simply this—One- fourth of each day's curd was kept, unsalted and loose in a pan, to be mixed with the fresh curd of the follow- ing day. The fresh curd for keeping over was taken from the rest, and became perceptibly acid by ten o'clock on the following morning, and communicated its acidity to the cheese with which it was subsequently mixed. The Rnest dairy of cheese I saw was made in the small kitchen of an old-fashioned farm house, and near to the fire. The weather was cold and damp at the time of my visit, and the curd which had been held over was placed in a warm place an hour or two before mix- ing, in order to mellow it and, promote acidity. The mixing of the sour curd, and the salting of the whole cheese, took place in the curd mill, after whieh the curd remained loose for an hour, exposed to the air, before it was put into the press vat. This exposure of an hour to the air had the effect of fixing the butter, of:ripening the curd, and of amalgamating the old with the new. In the particular dairy I am now describing, the milk was set for coagulation at 78deg. to 80deg. in warm weather, and 84deg. in cold. The souring of the curd was carefully regulated in reference to the weather ; and herein was exercised the judgment of the dairymaid, who was the farmer's wife. It must be understood that in the best Cheddar dairies groat care is taken in reference to the degree of acidity which is developed in the curd, and that it is best to develop it in the curd after the whey has been removed, the curd being kept warm and thoroughly exposed to- the air for the necessary time; and it must be borne in mind that while acidity is a very good servant, it is a very bad master, and must therefore be carefully controlled. A properly acidified cheese has already passed into the incipient stage of ripening, and this is why it ripens early; the whey is sufficiently got out, the curd is easily pressed into a compact cheese, and the ripening goes steadily on to the end, providing the cheese room is a good-one, and its temperature is main- tained at a fairly even point, say 68 deg. to 70 deg.; but an over-acidified cheese is dry, hard, crummy, and want- ing alike in quality and flavour, never ripening at all into a mellow end salvy article, and 'going to decay at last in a sort of dry rot. The "ripening," as it is termed, of the milk, particularly in cold weather, is an important matter in cheesemaking. It is well known that autumn cheese does not ripen so well as that of summer, and this is-because the evening's milk in the cold autumn .nights does not ripen as it ought, for warmth is neces- saryto ripening. The following are the important points to be attended to in cheesemaking :—Strict clean- liness everywhere; the temperature of the milk, the dairy, and the cheese-room; the judicious employment of acidity; the quality of the rennet and the salt ; and the condition of the weather. All this involves time, labour, and attention, but the result will be satisfactory in any country and on almost any kind of land. In this question of, temperature is the sphere in which the judg- ment of the dairymaid can be exercised to the greatest extent. It is in this particular sphere that we can lay down no special rules, which must depend upon her judgment to ,counteract any undue or evil influence which the weather might cause. Whether or not we fall beneath our possibilities in cheesemaking, we certainly do in buttermaking. The French butter excels in uni- formity of colour, grain, quality,-and flavour. It is specially prepared for the London market, and its uni- formity is the result of mixing together, by the aid of a rotating butter Worker, a number of different butters which are bought from the farmers. Wallffowers Of various colours have been diffneing their fragrance around our doors for some time. The same may be said of the Hyacinths, but With hues still more varied me brighter. The Tulips 'at present east all others into the shade, with their beautiful form and brilliant colours. There are pure whites, pinks, yellows, scarlets, crimsons, and purples. Others are striped with vermillion, rose, crimson, puce, and oerise. Polyanthus Narcissus are nearly at their best, and are .also very fragrant. Anemones, or the Wind-flower, witli their fern-like leaf, will be in flower for Some time to come. The Pelyanthus, Primrose, Double Daisies, Violas, Arabis (white rock), and Auriculas are familiar to %11 lovers of flowers, and are now at their best. The Forget-me-not, in its humble wee, is just-expanding its innocent-looking blue flowers. Other plants, less known, that are in flower are the Saxi- frages, Alyssum, AubretiaS, and the Grape Hyacinth. The grass plot should now be cut, and if there are any bare patches they should be made good by spreading fine 'sifted soil on the surface and sowing grass seeds, which are made up in smell parcels by seedsmen- to meet the wants of cottagers and others who have only a. small breadth to sow at most. If sifted soil is spread on the grass itself, it will impart vigour to it in a very short time. Of course there must be no brushing the ground over till the seeds are up and the grass fairly established. Even the grass, where cut, may 'remain on the ground to act as a mulching for the young roots. • RAILWAY GARDENING.—it is reported that the Midland Railway Company intend to offer prizes to the amount of £l.OO for the best platform flower gardem.to encour- age their servants- (who have already done some credit- able workin this direction), as well as beautifying the sta- tions and gratifying the public. It is said that on Tuesday the parties quarrelled. He knocked her down, and while lying on the floor, kicked her several times in the Rbdomen. She was severely injured, and was removed to Withington Workhouae. where she died on Friday. LIBERAL TEA PARTY AND BALL. SPEECH BY MR. W. CROSFIELD. i The annual tea party, concert, and ball in connection with the Warrington Liberal Club were held in the Public Hall on Monday evening, and were very largely attended. The hall as on previous occasions was elegantly and appro- priately decorated. In front of the organ in bold letters were inscribed the words " Crosfleld and victory," under- neath was a Russian shield reversed, the Warrington coat of arms, and the royal standard. There were also several flags and ornamental designs, which gave this part of the hall a somewhat striking appearance. Along the front of the gal- leries were the suitable political mottoes "Arbitration," , " Peace and honour,"" Health and happiness to our worthy member," and "Success to our club." The mottee " Health and happiness to our worthy member" was very prettily de- signed, consisting of green lettering with ornamental capi- tals effectively displayed on a maroon ground. At each of the windows and disposed at other parts of the hall were numerous flags and bannerettes, the various colours of which gave the room a bright and cheerful appearance. At the tea there were about 800 persene, and the manner in which this large number were attended to was very creditable to those who organised the arrangements, and to the ladies who served the tables. Trays were given by the following : Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P. (2) ; Mrs. W. Crostield (4) • Mr. John Crosfield (2) •, Mrs. G. Crosfield (2) ; Mrs. William Long (2); Miss Harvey (2) ; Mrs. W. Robinson (2) ; Mr, E. Milner (2) ; Mrs. C. S. Burgess (2) ; Mesdames F. A. Roberts, Fleming, Gomel!, Burgess, J. Greening, J. Platt, F. Meek' s J. Brown, Perry, Jenkins, Winser, E. Richard- son, Blackhurst, Strange, T. Carter, Broadbent, Barker, E. Twiss, T. Morris, W. Pierpeint, Briggs, P. Caldwell, Grime, R. Gamete, n If. Thornton, Guest, Armitage, J. Rylands, T. Birchall, J. S. Green, J. Haynes; Miss Jones, Messrs. J.Walker (Examiner), A. Browne, T. Miller, and G. Dakin. After tea a concert was given, at which the chair was occupied by Mr. W. Croefield,J.P. There were also on the platform the Rev. R. Pitcher, 8.A., Mr. Ben Brierley, and Mesere. C. Broad- bent, W. Pierpoint, J. H. Gorman, J. H. Fleming, C. S. Burgess, John Harrison, T. Birchall, W. Stirrup, W. Burn, T. Flood, H. Roberts, R. Biddall, J. W. Hall, T. Mather, J. P. Hudson, A. Browne, W. Crosskill, G. Belford, J. Garner, and W. Roberts. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with loud applause, said: Ladies and gentlemen, I have one apology to make before we begin, and that is to deliver a message from your worthy member Mr. McMinnies—(applauee)—who wishes Yoe to be informed that hi s Parliamentary duties keep him away from your gathering this evening, and that he wishes you a very pleasant evening notwithstanding his absence. I caanot begin to speak for myself on an occasion like this without expressing my own great thankfulness and con- gratulating you as a gathering of Englishmen and English- women, that this country has during the last few days been relieved from the heavy cloud which seemed to be hanging over us a few days ago, and that, instead of being hurled into war, as seemed not improbable a week ago, we are at any rate within arms' reach of peace. (Applause.) You must of course prepare to be told that this is a vain hope on our part, but we shall all of us remember that those who tell us this are practically the same body of persons who told us six months ago that what we supposed to be peace in our borders was not so. They are the people that told us that compromise was dishonour and that arrangement was only the prelude to war. We did not believe those statements I then, and I think you with myself will be unwilling to be- lieve it now. (Applause.) Wears now within a measurable distance of a eel= and quiet solution of the difficulties which undoubtedly exist between ourselves and another na- tion in the centre of the great continent of ! Asia. A few weeks ago there seemed to be , every probability of an outbreak which would be most disastrous in its effects—disestrous to us as well as to the l other great nation. Two gentlemen were sent into the middle of Asia to consider a very grave question concerning the frontier of a friendly power. It was an accident that they were military men, as they were sent there rather on account of their scientific ability. We mast all of us see the extreme danger we were in when questions of great in- ternational policy should be left to the arbitrament of men of purely scientific attainments, and we mast rejoice that the earnestness and determination of her Majesty's Govern- ment has withdrawn this very delicate question from the distant part of the world of which we certainly and even they themselves know so little. (Hear, bear.) Amid the boom of cannons and in the neighbourhood of batteries it is a very dangerous thing far military men to be discussing any great question, and we must all rejoice that this question of which we speak is to be discussed rather in the quiet of a room in the centre of London; that instead of the noise of war, where hot blood is apt to rise and bring about dieastrous re- } su'ts, it will be left to the quiet arbitrament of rulers and , compasses ; that the decisions which are foreshadowed in 1 lead pencil and can easily be rubbed out will have a prefer- ence over the more hasty decisions sod judgments which / might have hurled us into war if they had been carried on 1 ia the more distant part of the world, where the stains of I blood which would bs irreparable would be much more pro- ! bablethan those lighter decisions which can be reversed if i occasion requires. (Hear, hear.) I have spoken so far, perhaps, rather to the gentlemen who are present whom I assume to be to a very large extent members of the Liberal Club I i Cr if not that they are adherents and friends of the ; Liberal party in this town. (Hear, hear, and applause.) I I must therefore apologiee to the ladies for having seemed to reverse the ordinary course which politeneis dictates by putting gentlemen rather than ladies fimh And new may I say a word or two to the ladies, and say, how glad I am individually and the friends around me to see so many ladies hero to-night who if the are not immediately the friends of the Liberal cause they are attached friends of attached friends of the Liberal cause. (Applanee.) There are those who deprecate the interference of women in any political question, but I would desire to say from the outset Jam not one of those—(hear, hear)—and I rejoice that the day has arrrived when women without stepping from her natural position can take a part in the politics of the day. (Applause.) Those others to whom I allude who deprecate this position are rather those who live in Vie atmosphere of the past without regarding the circumstances in which we stand in the present day, and where they talking merely of the past I should be as willing as they to acknowledge that political agitation was not then a fit sphere for woman to appear in. (Hear, hear.) You no doubt are familiar with old electioneering stories ; they would some ef them remember that when a very heated contest was taking place in the county of Derby, when one of the noble house of Cavendish was seeking a seat in the unreformed Parliament, and when votes were exceedingly valuable, not valuable merely to the men ehe won, bat valuable to those who had the privilege of giving the notes that a beautiful Duchess of Devonshire was canvassing the county on behalf of one of her relatives, and she bought for that relative a vote, the price of which was a kiss, which she gave to a butcher. (L tugh- ter, and applause.) We may come nearer home. There was a story with which they in Liverpool were familiar of the late Lord Herrowby who when he was Lord Sandon canvassed the town of Liverpool. In this contest it was the freemen who had the votes to give and he c mvassed in St. John's market in Liverpool. In that market was one who in her day was a celebrated bearsty named Betty Taylor, and he is supposed to have carried on a conversation with Betty Taylor if not in these words to this purport "Oh, peerless market queen, fair Betty. , Deign to bestow on me a kiss; And if your charming daughter Betty Would da the earns, %would crown my bliss." (Laughter.) The answer was-- ~ Thank you, my Lord, with all my heart, You're kindry welcome to a buss; Betty and I will take your part. You may do whet you please with us." (Loud laughter and applause.) But those days, ladies and gentlemen, are gone. Ido not for myself see any very great advantage in allowing one's wife either to kiss or to be kissed for the sake of a vote. (Hear, hear.) Bat times were then not as they are now. In more recent day e we find that ladies still have been in the habit of interfering with politics in the higher ranks of political life, and wo know the great power our ladies have exerted. There is a little book which has appeared quibe recently, the Auto- biography of Lord Malinesbury, and nobody can read that book without being very much struck with the great useful- ness of politicians' wives. There were things which Cabinet Ministers and men of eminence in political life were unable to do themselves, but which they allowed their wives to do. If a coalition was to be made between one party and another, if the ranks were to coalesce, it wes unseemly that an ar- ent Liberal should enter into communication with an equally ardent Conservative, but it worrld be by no means unlikely that in the course of an afternoon's call the wife of the Liberal statesman would accidentally feel the politi- cal pulse of the wife of the Conservative statesman, and thereby find how he would like to join the other party. These things were considered quite comme if foot. Ido not know whether they take place at present, but at any rate, we find that in the higher ranks of political life ladies have their part, and we welcome the ladies here this evening as also having theit part. (Applause ) And I may Say further that in interesting yourselves in the welfare of your country you are taking a part which you can do without shame. (Hear, hear.) I would remind you how for nearly fifty years the highest political position in England has been in the hands of a woman. (Hear, hear.) I have been speaking to you of the position of politics fifty years ago, and I have pointed out how that position is improved in the preeent day, and I for one am ready to acknowledge my firm belief that it is the spirit in which Her Majesty the Queen has dealt with political questions that has made political life in England to-day so vastly better than it was fifty years ago. (Loud applause.) , The song, "Beloved star," was then sung by Mr. White, who was warmly applauded at its close. Mr. Joseph Mercer was recalled for his rendering of a comic song, and gave with equal success the laughable song, "More like your dad every day." Mrs. Dagnall was much applauded for her rendering of "Once again;" after which Mr. Ben Brierley, who met with a cordial reception, related" The adventures of a staffed monkey." This very amusing piece was in the Lancashire dialect, and being recited in Mr. Brierley's inimitable style, it was the cause of great merriment. Messrs. Mercer and Mr. F. J. DelLcontributed considerably to the enjoyment of the evening by the humorous trio, "Three young men who never went astray," and on being recalled they repeated a portion of the song. "The Pride of Kil- dare" was excellently sung by Mr. White, after which Mr. Brierley gave another recitation in the Lancashire dialect, entitled "Catching a weasel," and was again very loudly applauded. The Marquis of HARTINGTON said the Government be- lieved that the country would ratify and approve the con- duct of this Admistration as strongly as it condemned the conduct of their predecessors. He defended the expedition to Suakim, which was advised by Lord Weiseley, whether our troops remained in or withdrew from the Soudan. The fall of Khartoum had not been followed by an advance of the Mandi, who appeared to be in considerable difficulties, and that and many other considerations had weighed with the Government in reconsidering their determination. With regard to Afghanistan, the mover of the amendment had epoken with his usual accuracy of the Premier's demand for reparation—a word which the right hon. gentleman had never used, although he had spoken of preparation (Hear, hear, and laughter.) How could the Opposition form an opinion as to whether or not the Government had gained anything in these negotiations until they had read the papers? If the Government had succeeded in establishing a definite frentier to the dominions of the Ameer, and if the Ameer had invited our officers to visit Herat, something would have been gain-d. (Cheers.) Sir S. NORTHCOTE asserted that the object of the amend- ment was clear on the face of it—that before granting ex- traordinary supplies the House should have further info-- mation as to the present policy of the Government. Con- sidering how often the Government had changed its policy, this was not an unreasonable demand. He objected alto- gether to the manner in which the Geve nment managed its foreign affairs, attributing undue importance to small points, and urged that the motien would be pressed to a division, as the information at present forthcoming was ieadeqaate and entirely missed the points. Mr. GLADSTONE, rising at 1-30, referred at the outset of his speech to the contradictory views of the amendment expressed by the leader of the Opposition and his sup- porters. He then went on to remind the House that there were two questions before it. The first related to India, Afghanistan, and to Russia. The Government had told the House that they now saw their way to present papers on that subject at the end of the week. Under those circum- stances, the Opposition chose to bring forward a motion which, if carried, must displace the Government without those papers in their possession—(cheers)--and they sup- ported it by a series of assertions, every one of which, so far, was absolutely baseless. They heard that everything had been surrendered to Russia. Of that they knew no- thing whatever. (Ministerial cheers.) They said it was a base surrender to Russia to consent to carry on the negotia- tions in London instead of on the Afghan frontier. What if, when the papers were presented, they found that Sir P. Lumsden was averse to carrying them OR under the circum- stances ? (Cheers and counter cheers.) They spoke of the recall of Sir Peter Lumsden. Supposing they found he had not been recalled, but that his return to this country was in conformity with his own views. (Ministerial cheers.) They said everything had been surrendered in respect to the frontier. Supposing they found that, on the contrary, a frontier line had been drawn which had the thorough adhesion of the whole Indian Government, and which was as completely conformable with the views of the Ameer of Afghanistan. (Ministerial cheers.) As to the Soudan, the real question was Khartoum, and it was for not advancing to Khartoum the Government were now to be condemned. He was glad to see them abandon as desperate all attempts to defend the language of the noble lord the member for Woodstock, or, above all, that of Lord Salisbury. What did hon. members mean when they said they were not the friends of war, and at the same time indulged in this most unwise and most unjust language ? It was with grief and concern that he had noticed the change in the attitude of hon. members opposite since the heavens had cleared and signs of blessed peace had appeared. (Prolonged Ministe- rial cheers.) The House at two o'clock divided:— For the amendment 260 Against Majority for the Government 3O The Bill was then read a second time. THE SEATS BILL THHOUGH.—Sir C. MUSE moved the third reading of the Redistribution Bill.—Mr. EAMES moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. WAETON seconded the amendment.—After some discussion, the House divided :—For the third reading, 116; against, 33; majority, 83. _ .
~ The House was counted out at 3-20. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. - The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was read a third time and passed.—Lord Monson, on behalf of the Earl of Dalhousie, presented a bill for legalising marriage with a deceased's wife's sister, and fixed the second reading for the 11th of June. LORD SALISBURY AND MR. GLADSTONE —The Marquis of SALISBURY desired to make a statement of a personal char- acter in correction of a misrepresentation by some members of the Government of a speech delivered by him last week. The interpretation placed by Mr. Gladstone epon his speech was in direct defiance of the language he used. He was explaining to his audience that for the purpose of deciding whether it was wise to rely for the protection of our Indian Empire upen the promises of Russia, it did not matter whether Russia had intentionally broken her promises or whether she had broken them because she was unable to keep them, and in illustrating that position he used the commercial term in determining whether a man could be trusted as an analogy that it would make no differ- ence whether his inability to keep his promises had been due to misfortune or commercial dishonesty.— Earl Gnanyturn was glad the noble marquis had made the explanation, but the accusation made against his colleagues was not, in his opinion, well founded. The words " swind- lers" and " bankrupts " were so used as to give the impres- sion that they were applied to Hussia. In the same speech the noble marquis took the opportunity of assuring the electors of Hackney that it was impossible to impeach the historical accuracy of a speech of Lord Randolph Church- ill's, in which there were at least nine passages that were incorrect, and some of them were opposed to fact.—Lord Crtannnoorto failed to understand the ground on which the noble earl had used the opportunity afforded by the noble marquis's explanation to comment upon a speech made of Lord R. Chu-chill, who, if his statements were questioned in the House of Commons, was perfectly clpable of answer- ing for himself.—The Earl of KIEBBRLRY said it was impos- sible that such attacks as the noble marquis had made could be confined to one side of the House.

THE PROPOSED MARRIAGE OF THE PRINCESS BEATRICE. —The LORD CHANCELLOR read a message from the Crown announcing that her Majesty had agreed to a marriage be- tvveen the Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry of Battenberg, and stating that the numerous proofs the Queen had re- ceived from the House of Commons of their loyalty to the Throne and their attachment to her person and family, left her Majesty no donbt of their readiness to concur in making a suitable provision for her Royal Highnese.—On the motion of Eirl GRANVILLE it was ordered that the massage should be taken into consideration on Friday. The Industrial Schools (Ireland) Bill was read a third time and passed --The Submarine Telegraph Cable Bill was read a second time.—The Highways Bill passed through committee. BUSH!. AND INDIA.—The DIME Of ARGYLL resumed the debate (interrupted on Monday by the illness of Lord Dormer) on his motion that the circular despatch addressed by Prince Gortchakoff to the Russian representatives abroad, dated 21st November, 1364, should be reprinted. The policy described in that despatch was to absorb all un- civilised states and it was that policy which bad brought Russia from the Caspian to the frontier of Afghanistan.— Lord CRANBROOKE believed that Russia had been to a great extent compelled to make advances in Central Asia in dis- regard of her assurances, but that was the more reason why the statesmen of this country should have b•en more eager and more careful in the precautions taken.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY most cordially reciprocated the feeling that the subject should be treated independently of party. He hoped it would not be without effect when it was seen that, notwithstanding their strong party differences, there was an absolute agreement between all sections of the House as t 9 the necessity of defending India against all corners. (Cheers.)—The Marquis of SALtsrinny said he entirely agreed, but be regretted the limit which he placed upon the line of defence. The defence of India ought to be carried forward through Peskawur and the line of the Indus.—Earl GRANVILLE thought the tone of the discussion would, he believed, have a most important and almost vital influence in India, for it would convey to the people of India the knowledge that they might be sure of the united efforts of this country to defend them from any danger. . . -
The mot-ion was agreed to, and the Hon-se adjourned at 6.12.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. MISCELLANEOUS —The House was again crowded in an- ticipation of a division on Sir Massey Lopes' amendment to the Registration Rill. It was not until twenty minutes past five that public business was approached, the interval being occupied by discussion on the motion for the second reading of the Channel Tunnel Bill. This was opposed by Mr. Chamberlain, and on a division rejected by 281 votes against 99. Mr. Gladstone brought in the Queen's message asking for a marriage allowance for the Princess Beatrice, and it was arranged to take it into consideration to-morrow. With the exception of two or three of the Parnellites all the members uncovered whilst the message was being read. Mr. J. K. Cross, replying to Dr. Cameron, confirmed the ac- count published on the oth inst. of the blockade of Ma- kaiph. Answering Mi. Labouchere, Mr. Childers, said of the N ote of Credit for eleven millions the Government already stood committed to the expenditure of some eight millions. This included every liability incurred up to the present time. Mr. Gladstone, replying to Mr. Healy, said that nearly four years ago Lord Granville had given to Mr. Errington, then about to make a journey to Rome, a letter (If personal introduction ; but it was in no wise intended as a diplomatic credential. Mr. Gladstone, at the instanee of M. de Staal, corrected any impression that might have been created by his statement of the previous night that M. de Staal and M. Lesser had acted in their conference with Lord Granville and Lord Kimberley as Plenipotentiaries. M. de Siaal's own account of the matter was that the four gentle- men named had agreed to a draft arrangement for the setllement of the frontier, and that the proposal lead been submitted for the approval of the Russian Government, M. de Sisal aiving it his support, an account which only ver- bally differs from Mr. Gladstone's given on Monday night. ' In reply to Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, Mr. Childers said he would not take the Inland Revenue Bill till the first Mon- day after the holilays. TIER REGISTRATION BILLS.—On the motion to consider , the English Registration Bill on the report stage, Sir Nlzasnv LOPES moved on amendment, proposing that the \ Bill be re-committed, for the purpose of receiving a clause

providing for the repeal of so much of any Act or Acts re• hating to Parliamentaiy registrivion in cour.ties and lwrouhs as makes the expenses of overseers of the poor and cleiks of the peace or town clerks a legal charge upon the local rates. The House, which had remained crowded throughout question time, emptied when the hon, baronet rose, filling up again when the news went round that the Prime Minister was on his feet. The Premier, in a compara- tively brief epeech, declared that the Government could not compatibly with their arrangements and engagements I accept the motion. They were pledged to pass this session the Seats Bill, the Registration Bills, and a Bill making it possible to take the general election in the autumn. If they were to accept Sir Massey Lopes' ammd- ment, involving as it did the eetablishment of elaborate machinery, it would be simply impossible te carry these Bills. At the same time the Government were prepared to go farther on the path of concession upon which they had entered the other night. The basis upon which their pro position rested was to make an allowance to everseers to meet the access of labour imposed by the operation of the new Act. They had already promised to give twopence a name in England and Scotland, and were prepared to in- crease that sum by another twopence, making a contribu- tion from the national exchequer of £20,000 to Great Britain. With respect to Ireland it was proposed to contri- bute a sum of £15,000, being £5OOO over the sum already offered.—Sir M. HICKE.BEACH, on behalf of the Conserva- tive Opposition, declined to accept this proposal, as it did not include the boroughs ; and after a few words from Sir Charles Dilke, the House divided, Sir Mas- sey Lopes' motion being rej?cted by 280 votes against 258 a result bailed with rrolonged cheers from the Ministerial side. The Parnellites again voted with the Conservatives.—The House then re- sumed consideration of the Bill on the Report stage.—Mr. DAVEY proposed that medical and surgical assistance or the gratuitous bestowal of medicine should not be deemed to constitute parochial relief within the meaning of the Repre- sentation of the People Act.—After some discussion, this was carried by 87 votes against 50. The decision was re- ceived with loud cheers by the Irish members. The debate was continued till a late hour.—Mr. J. _...j•nwrirEla gave notice that on the third reading he would move the re- committal of the bill, with a view to invite the House to reconsider its decision on the previous arnenilment.--Some other amendments were agreed to. lhe ATTORNEY-GENERAL then moved the third reading of the bill, which was agreed to. The House adjourned at 2-10 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. _ _ .

The Speaker took the chair at 25 past 12 o'clock. A QUESTION OF PROCEDURE.—Mr. LOWTHER put a ques- tion to the Speaker on a point of procedure. In the die- cussion on the Registration Bill on Tuesday night an amendment disqualifyiag undergraduates in the Oxford and Cambridge Universities was carried by a very narrow ma- jority. The point was whether it was in accordance with the practice of the House to move the third reading of a bill immediately after report when a notice of motion to re- commit the bill had been publicly given.—Sir C. DILKE, before the Speaker decided the point, explained that when the report was finished, the Attorney-General proposed to take the third reading that day or next Thursday, and thereupon Mr. Stanhope, without rising, said " Why not ' now ?" and the Attorney-General expressed his willingnesss if he was assured that the right hon gentleman (Mr. Low- ther) did not press his motion. That assurance being given by Mr. Stanhope, the third reading was taken with general assent. Mr. SEXTON corroborated this:account. The SPEAKER Said ne point of order arose. The House had acted within its discretion, and on the understanding from the right hon gentleman's colleague that the motion was withdrawn. REGISTRATION OF VOTERS —On the consideration of the Registration of Voters (Ireland) Bill, a new clause was moved by Mr. SEXTON, requiring that copies of registers, notices, &c., under the bill, should be published by being affixed to the dem of places of worship and public build- ings for a period including two consecutive Sundays, and that, if any portion of a document so published were destroyed, mutilated, defaced, or removed, the person respon- sible for its publication was forthwith to place another document to the aame effect in its place.—Mr. CAMPBELL. BANNERMAN assented to the proposal.—On the clause being put it was carried by 116 against 36.—Mr. HEALY moved a new clause providing that nothing in the bill should entitle any person in siatit loupillari to be registered as a voter or to vote in respect of the occupation of premises in any col- lege.—Mr. PLUNKET objected to the clause as an attempt to disqualify a number of young men who were in every respect qualified to be put en the register.—The dinussion was continued by Lord E. Cavendish, Mr. Sexton, Mr. Bryce, and Mr. Harrington, and, on a division, the numbers were: For the clause, 87; against, 190; majority, 103. The clause was consequently rejecte&—The amendments on the report had not been completed at a quarter to six o'clock, when the debate stood adjourie I. MISCELLANEOUS—The order for the second reading of the Income Tax Administration Amendment Bill was dis- charged.--The Honorary Freedom of Boroughs Bill was read a second time.—The Consolidated Fund (NO. 3) Bill was read a third time. _ _
The House adjourned at 5 55. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QuEsrloNs &c.—Sir T. BRASSEY stated that an officer of the Admiralty had been instructed to organise a general scheme of coast defence by naval means, and it would be part of his task to say what duties should be assigned to the volunteer artillery, and how far assistance would be necessary in the form of a capitation grant.—Mr. Forster was informed that colonial government securities would, equally with foreign secutities, be liable to the new stamp duty.—Mr. MUNDELL/ described the recent account in an evening paper of a case of suicide at Adlington, near Chor- ley, resulting from harsh treatment at school, as of a highly sensational character. No blame whatever attached to the school managers in the case. The girl complained of harsh treatment at the factory, and she had much work to do at a farm before going to school as a half-timer. The child was living with her parents, and this sad case, said the right hon. gentleman, was another illustration of the fact that more labour was exacted from children of tender years in England than from almost any other child- ren in Europe.—Mr. ASHLEY' stated that the reports that a British protectorate was about to be established in Zululand, and that some representative of the Imperial Government would be employed in the work,were not based upon any action taken or decision arrived at by he- Majesty's Government. I—The Marquis of HABTINGTON informed Lord G. Hamil- ton that about £2,500,000 of the sum included in the Vote of Credit had been spent or absorbed by liabilities which would have to be met in consequence of the operations in the Soudan and Upper Egypt.—The PRIME Mierierme, referring to the negotiations with Russia, said they were proceeding, but he was not aware that they bad reaehed such a stage that the result could be announced. PROVISION FOR PRINCESS BEATRICE.

- Mr. GLABSTONE moved that a provision of £6,000 a year out of the Consolidated Fund be granted to the Princess Beatrice on the occasion of her marriage, and quoted the grants made to former Princesses to show that his proposal was a moderate, fair, sad certainly not an extravagant pro- vision. He mentioned that the life of the Princess would in all probability be spent in the future as it had been in the past, that her husband would be associated with her as a resident in this country, and that everything connected with the youthful Prince and the promise of his future life was what the country could wish. Referring to a topic ex- traneous to the proposal itself, the right hon. gentleman said it was the opinion of Ministers, after full consideration, that it would be decidedly to the public advantage and most consistent with the important considerations attaching to the subject if henceforth in regard to members of the Royal Family under the Crown the sys- tem upon which these proposals were founded should be submitted by the Government to a Parliamentary Com- mittee, and should receive the approval and sanction of that committee. He thought the establishment of such a method would tend to secure even more perfect unity of view in the House than that which heretofore bad been found to exist. It was therefore the intention of the Government to propose that a committee should be appointed to examine this sub- ject. Such a committee should only be appointed at the commencement of or very early in a session, and the Gov- ernment thought the early part of next year would probably form the best period for bringing this important and weighty iestrument to bear upon the settlement of this delicate question, so closely associated with the comfort both of the Queen and the Royal Family. Sir S. NORTHCOTE hoped the provision proposed would be made without any objection and with the unanimous assent of the House.—Mr. LABOUCHERE declared that it was a pure illusion to imagine that the Queen had ever given up a shilling in return for an engagement that the country should provide for her and her children. lie contended that the Sovereign had no more right to what was called the hereditary revenues ef the Crown than to the mountains in the moon, and before any demand was made it should be stated that the Queen was unable to sup- port her family. He argued that those who opposed the grant were greater friends of the Monarchy than those who supported it, the real danger to the Monarchy being that many persons might come to the conclusion that its great advantages were not equivalent to its cost if the latter were perpetually added to.—Upon a division the vote was agreed to by 337 to 38. -

THE limn REGISTRATION BILL.—The adjeurned debate on the consideration of the Registration of Voters (Ireland) Bill as amended being resumed, Mr. CAMPREIL-BANNERMAN moved a new clause applying to freemen the diequalidca- lions arising from receipt of pauper relief.—The clause was opposed on various grounds by Mr. Warton, Mr. Lewis, and Mr. Small, but was carried, on a division, by 145 to 25. Several ether amendments were deilt with, and at eleven o'clock, when the bill was still under discussion, Mr. Deasy moved the adjournment of the debate —This was opposed by Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, the latter say- ing that it was necessary to get the bill through that night in order that it might he pas2ed before the Whitsuntide recess.

ENGLAN D AND IiITSSII. NEGOTIATIONS IN LONDON. THE RETURN OF SIR P. LUNISDEN. The negotiations for the delimitation of the Russo-Afghan frontier have now assumed the form of a conference between Earl Granville and Earl Kimberley and M. de Stall and M. Lesser, as announced in Parliament. It is understood that the points in dispute between Russia and England arising out of the Peojdoh incident have been under the considera- tion of the King of Denmark, and that M. de Falbe the Danish Minister in London. has kept his Majesty well in- formed as to the various diplomalc outlets Irons the diffi- culties of the position. It is believed in official circles that it will be left to the honour of the Power adjudged in the wrong to make the amenJe suitable in the circumstances. Mr. Condi° Stephen arrived in Berlin early on Monday morning, and continued his journey to London without stopping, reaching the Metropolis on 'Tuesday. TutroL, MAY 'Dm (via Meshed, May lst).—Sir Peter Lumsden leaves here to-morrow with Colonel Stewart and Lioutenant Barrow for London, in accordance with instruc- tions from the Government. He will post to Astrabad. No ordera have been given respecting the' divosal of the Frontier Commission. The frontier, it seems, is to be mainly settled at home. Aitcheson's examination of the country has produced some important results in the way of botanical discovery. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—Orders have been issued stopping the further purchase of transport animals, and also further arresting the despatc,i of stores up the Bolan Pass to Quetta. The report of Lord Dufferin's resignation is abso- lutely unfounded. Mr. Garstin, a member of the Board of Revenue of the Madras Pre3idency, said, in a speech de- livered at the College there, that he has reason to believe that if well-conducted young native gentlemen applied to the Government for commissions in the native army the request would be favourably considesed. Stame, SUNDAY.—Two months' leave of absence has been granted to the Duke of Connaught. MESHED, SATIIRDAY.—GeneraI Sir P. Lumsden left Tir- pal for England this morning, after handing over the com- mand to Colonel Ridgway. The remaining members of the Commission regret the loss of a kind chief untainted by party bias, whose only object was to serve his country and save England's honour in a most trying position. The mem- bers of the mission are all well. No further Russian move- ments are reported.—Times. ENGLAND AND THE PORTE. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATUADAY.—The arrival here of Sir William A. White, as Envoy Extraordinary, is one of the reasons for HassaryFehmi Pasha's departure from London, as the negotiatiohs between the Porte and the British Government will henceforth be continued by Sir William. The statement that Hassan Fehmi Pasha's departure was caused by differences of opinion between Earl Granville and himself with respect to the Dardanelles question is un- founded. THE ENGLISH WAR PREPARATIONS. The Admiralty received instructions on Saturday to cancel engagements made for the conveyance of 2,000 British troops to India in the steamships Pelican, Duke of Devon- shire, and Kaiser-i-Hind. The vessels had their fittings for troops almost completed, and were to have left England on the 14th inst. Instructions to cease the work of preparing hired transports at Glasgow, Liverpool. and London are ex- pected. The replenishing of the coal supplies on the foreign stations is, however, to be continued, and the following col- liers, which are in foreign waters and able at short notice to land their cargoes at the points where coal is required, have been taken up by the Admiralty :—Energia, 3,177 tons; River Indies, 3,450 tone; Ghazee, 2,712 tons; Opah, 1,153 tons; and Moray, 2,185 tons. These ships can be utilised, if required, as armed cruisers. Captain Brownlow, R.N., with a staff of surveyors, paid a visit on Saturday to the steamers recently engaged by the Government for transports, and which are now lying at Liverpool. In the case of the National Company's steamer Egypt, it was decided to fit her up for the accommodation of 1,000 men and 50 horses, and the work of preparation was proceeded with during the day as rapidly as possible. It is understood that all the cruisers will be required to proceed to India. The arrival of urgent orders from the Admiralty received by the officials of Devonpott Dockyard show that, notwith- standing tha more peaceful character of the situation, there is no intention on the part of the Government te relax their efforts to have the ships of the navy in a thorough state of preparedness. Orders were received on Saturday at Daven- port that the Iron Duke (14), ironclad, Captain Robert H. Boyle, which was recently regarded as a probable flagship to the squadron proposed to he sent to the Baltic, was to proceed at once to Portland, and make her six hours' full speed trial on the passage round. Orders have also been I given that the Hotspur turret-ship and the Shannon iron- clad are to follow the Iron Duke to Portland with all despatch; and these ships, with others, will bs put under the command of Rear-Admiral W. H. Whyte, whose flag is now flying on board the Agincourt (17), ironclad, one of the ' ships of the Channel squadron. The transport department of the Admiralty are actively I engaged in making arrangements for the return of troops from Egypt, and four hired transports in London docks are com- pleting their fitting for that purpose. An order was received at Portsmouth on Wednesday em- powering naval pensioners who have been recently called up to claim their immediate discharge. THE RECENT FIGHT ON THE KUSHK RIVER. ST, PETERSBURG, TUESDAY.—The Official Messenger publishes a report from Gen. Komaroff, dated Dash Kepri, April 11th, containing details of the fight on the Kushk river, according to which the Russian force engaged consis- ted of one battalion of the line, four guns, three sotnias of Cossacks, one sotnia of Turkoman militia, and four com- panies of rifles. lb° Russians captured two Afghan flags, which were taken to St. Petersburg by Colonel Zakrejevski. Only 14 Afghans, including seven wounded, were made prisoners. The Russians did not pursue the Afghans in their flight. General Komaroff estimates the Afghan loss at over 500 killed, including four officers. Sail Salar, the Afghan commander, is said to have been wounded. Gen. Komaroff reiterates his assertion of the agressive attitude taken up by the Afghans and enumerates a series of suc- cessive provocations which he declared the Afghans offered to the Russians before the battle Cu the Kuslak. He says that on March 17th the left bank of the river WAS occupied by the Russian forces; the Afghans had only sentinels. It is not true that a detachment of Afghans was cut off. On March 18th the Afghans opened the first, for General Ko- maroff had himself forbidden Colonel Alikhanoff to make an attack, or even to reply toe fueilade unless he received special orders to do So. General Komaroff states that he received a letter from Captain Yate requesting him to afford protection to the English, but on Colonel Zahrzewski sub- sequently meeting Captain Yale behind Penjdeh the Eng- lish officer withdrew his request and declined to receive Russian protection for Englishmen. General Komaroff states he bad refused the request of the residents of Penj- doh and of the Turcomans and Erzariaes for Incorporation in the Russian empire. THE FORTIFICATIONS OF HERAT. SIMLA, TUESDAY.—OOI. Stewart and one other British officer will proceed to Hera'. to advise the Ameer concerning the fortifications of that city. Sr. PETERSBURG, WEDNESDAY.—Rear-Admiral Schmidt has been appointed commander of the Cronstadt squadron cruising in the Southern Baltic, and Rear-Admiral Golovat- scheff commander of the vessels now lying in Cronstadt roads and intended for service in the Northern Pacific; Rear-Admiral Novikoff to the command of the torpedo ' squadron. Mahomed Take Khan, assistant to the chief of the police at Sarakhs, has been promoted to the rank of captain-of militia. The war vessels which have been com- missioned for service were despatched yesterday to Cron- stadt Reads where they will receive their final orders. Tltunsiess.—lt is understood that the new fron- tier of Afghanistan will be as follows :—Starting from north of Zulficar, on the Hen i Rud, the frontier will tend in an easterly direction to Chaman-i-Baid on the Kushk, de- scending the river to Gaurtz-i-Khan. It will proceed from the latter place in a north-easterly direction to the south of Penjdeh along the margin of cultivation to Khoza Saleh on the Oxus. The line thus defined lies between the frontiers proposed by England and Russia respectively.

The Press Association is in a poeition to state that the negotiations now going forward in London between Eng- land and Russia regarding the delimitation of the Russo- Afghan frontier have progressed most satisfactorily within the past few days. Some further explanations upon the main agreement arrived at by Earl Granville, Lord Kimber- ley, M. de Steal, and R. Lessar will be required to be made before the agreement is ratified by both Powers, but these are not considered to be of a nature to cause any delay in the final adjustment of the difference. The Exchange Company's Berlin correspondent tele- graphs :—A despatch from the Russian Foreign Office has just been read to me, in which great irritation is displayed regarding Lord Salisbury's Hackney speech, which attrac- ted much notice both in Court and Diplomatic circles of St. Petersburg, and the despitch real to me describes it as insulting and offensive, and as unworthy of a great stateman at this or any other time.

THE QUEEN IN LONDON.—The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice, took a long drive on Thursday morning in the West end of London. Her Majesty left Buckingham Palace by the Garden entrance where a large number of I People had congregated, and drove through Hyde Park to the Albert Memorial, not returning to the palace for a con- siderable time.

FOREIGN NEWS. THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.
OFFICIAL INSPECTIONS.

Stream 9 SATURDAY.—Lord Wolseley, aceompanied by General Graham and staff, made an exhaustive inspection of the environs of Suakim to-day, in order to decide upon the strength of the garrison and the defences required to protect the place during the summer. General Graham afterwards inspected the newly-formed Camel Corps, under the command of Major James, Deputy-Assistant Adjutant and Quartermaster-General. The General expressed himself highly pleased with the appearance of the force, and said it would prove a most valuable adjunct in desert warfare. The Amaras are much impressed with the success of the British attack on Tahakool, and a large number of them are anxious to make their submission.

SIINDAY.—This morning Lord Wolseley visited McNiell's zarebas, and General Hudson explained to Lord Wolseley all the details of the attack of the 22.-id March. It is gratifying to find that the rebels have not disturbed any of the graves of the British dead. The New South Wales c3utingent have applied for leave to be employed as scouts, for which services they are eminently fitted, and there can be little doubt that the offer will at once be ac. cepted. There is a general feeling here that if the Austra• liana' services should be no longer required at Suakim, it would be a most popular and beneficial recognition of the bond between the colonial and imperial forces if they should be sent to England for a short time. Snextm, TIIESDAL—Lord Wolseley has inspected the Scots Guards at Tambonk. He was much pleased with the fine appearance of the battalion, which turned oat very clean and smart, fully maintaining its high reputation. Toe sth Lancers at Handoub have &any men and horses sick.

DONGOLA. SUNDAY.—It is reported that Osman Digna, with a few followers is at Berber. The Emir of Berber has gone to Khartoum to beg for troops to oppose the English from Suakin!.

Some members of the contingent will probably visit England as guests tithe home Government. THE SUEZ CANAL COMMISSION.
