THE CONVICTION OF A PRESCOT SURGEON. titTICIDI IN GAOL. A great deal of surprise and conversation were occasioned in the neighbourhood of Preecot on Friday and Saturday by a report that Daniel Murray O'Hara, alias Patrick O'Hara, alias William Murray, better known as Dr. O'Hara, had committed suicide in Walton Gaol. It will be remem- bered that on Seturday, the 2nd inst, the deceased was sen- tenced at the Liverpool Assizes to ten years' penal servi- tude for having endeavoured to obtain from a Preacot lady certain sums of money by threatening to spread a foul libel against her. An inquest on the body of the deceased I was held is Walton Gaol on Saturday before Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner.—Colonel Lennie, deputy-governor of ; her Majesty's prison, Liverpool, said that the deceased was 'a prisoner in Walton Gaol. He believed he was forty-six years of age. He was by profession a surgeon, and was sent to prison on remand on February 21st. He was sen- tenced to ten years' penal servitude on May 2nd, and was received at the gaol the same evening. He was placed in the cell in which he was found dead on the 7th inst, at about one p.m, by the chief warder. Witness had seen the deceased alive about a quarter-past ten that morning. He was not on the day of his death put to any kind of week. On account of his having made an attempt to commit sui- cide on the sth inst all rope was removed out of his cell. IWitness had him under his observation daily. He did not notice any mental peceliarity about him. Since his Sen- tence he had not complained of being unwell. He began Ipicking oakum after his sentence, but on account of his fingers being weak he did not nearly accomplish the required task of a convict. Witness went into the deceased's cell on the morning of his death and asked him if he wished to write to any of his friends. He said he had no friends to write to, and he only wished to write to his lawyer, Mr. Murphy.— Neil Ferguson, chief warder of the prison, said that he found the dace seed in his cell about 000 o'clock on the 7th Inst., apparently having strangled himeelf. He found round ' his neck the shreds of a sheet which belonged to his bed. They were attached to the iron handle that works the cell bellewhich is about five feet from the floor. He was press- ing very heavily against the wall in a stooping position, with his knees bent. His feet touched the ground. He ap- peared quite dead, but was not cold. He was instantly cut down. The assistant doctor saw him within four minutes,' and pronounced life to be extinct. The deceased was quite nude when found. He appeared to have turned the gas , bracket so as to point straight opposite him, and he had I fixed on the burner a picture of the crucifix, which he had ' tarn from a prayer-book. Witness saw him between ten and eleven o'clock that morning. He had never noticed any peculiarity of mind about him. There was a stool at his feet, which was upset. The prisoner, when found dead, had not touched his dinner, which was still on the table.— Griffith Williams, a warder in the prison, said he saw the de- ceased alive last at five minutes to one o'clock on Thursday. He knew that he was "on report." He did not go into the cell nor speak to him. He was standing at the table with his arms folded. Witness did not think deceased knew be I saw him. His dinner was then on his table.—John Hum- phreys, a warder, said be found the deceased in his cell en the sth inst., apparently attempting te strangle himself with a rope (produced) which was attached to the handle of the cell bell The deceased .would not say anything about it. Witness reported the fact, and all the rope was removed from the cell. When he found the deceased he was standing on a etml. He then slipped off it and the rope tightened and broke.—The Deputy-Governor, in answer to the ceroner, I said that since his first commitment to gaol the deceased had been reported four times for attempts on his life, and twice whilst he was in the hospital. He thought he had done thie in order to obtain sympathy.—George Thompson, 1 a warder, who had charge of the prisoner, said that the i latter took hie meals regularly till the sth inst. He did not take any food after breakfast on that date. He would not answer any questions respect'ng this. Witaess re- ported his refusal to eat food to the chief warder.— The Rev. Father Nugent, prison minister, said that the prisoner was a Roman Catholic. He saw him whilst he was in prison in February, and also several times whilst await- ing his trial. He had a long interview with him on Mon- day last, in his room. The chief object in that interview was to awaken the sympathy of the rev, gentleman, as he believed that he could laring some influence to bear upon Mr. Justice Smith. He told him that he had had an in- terview with the governor of the prison on the previous day, and that he had assured him that witness was the only per- son who could obtain a mitigation of his sentence The rev. gentleman said nothing, but the deceased must have known from his countenance that he did not believe that the governor had said this, as it was so unusual. He then went down on his knees and in a most solemn manner protested his innocence After which be looked at him and said, " Look at me straight between the two eyes, and tell me if you believe lam guilty." He replied that he had formed no opinion as yet upon his guilt or innocence. That would have to be a subsequent matter. The tale he had told about the governor proved to be false. As regarded his mind he found him a very complicated character to deal with. He had torn an article out of his library book, en- titled "Guilty or Not Guilty." This was found in a letter which he believed was addressed to the judge.— Christopher Concanon, governor of the prison, stated that what the prisoner had told Father Nugent regarding his de- sire to obtairi'a mitigation of *his sentence was absolutely false. The letter written by the prisoner was marked " private." He wanted it to be posted to the judge, but on being in- formed by witness that it would have to pass through the hands of the judge's clerk, he destroyed it. In reply to the coroner respecting the means by which convicts could com- mit suicide in their cells, witness said, a I consider any man who has any intention of destroying himself has every pos- sible opportunity to do it." He further added, in reply to another question respecting the hell handles in the cells," I think the bell handles unquestionably would be better re- moved."—Drs. Beamish and Hamilton both concurred in the opinion that death was the result of strangulation, and that all previous attempts made by the deceased to destroy himself were of a feigned character. They thought he was of sound mind, and that he had stripped himself in order to impress the officials that he was of unsound mind. Death must have resulted in about five minutes after the rope tightened.—The Cororvr then summed up the details of the case and the jury, after a short consultation, returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased met his death by strangulation, and that there was not sufficient evidence to show what was the mental condition of the deceased at the time of that occurrence. They also added that they con- sidered the prison officials had taken all necessary precut- (ions in the matter.

The Lord Lieutenant has offered the honour of knight- hood to Dr. Wycherley, High Sheriff of the city of Cork, in recognition of his services in the cause of loyalty on the oc- casion of the visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales. GENERAL NEWS.

The Daily IVesos hears that £6,0Q0 was offered far the copyright of General Gordon's diaries. The city of Glasgow has rejtcted the adoption of the Free Libraries Act by 29,946 votes against 22,755. It is Stated that bad trade is the cause of the adverse vote to the adop- tion of the Act.

THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF Drumm—lt is reported that the Pope has selected .for the Archbishopric of Dahlia Ma- e gnor Moran, Archbishop of Sydney since 1862. Thus the two Dish candidates have bath been passed over. Inuit Evicnoms.—Accordinr, to a return published on Saturday, in the quarter ending March there were 34,446 persons evicted in Ireland, embracing 720 familier. There were readmitted as tenants 228 persons, and as caretakers 1,642 persons. _

6 THE VICTORIA Caoss.—The Queen bag conferred the Victoria Cross upon Gunner Albert Smith, of the Royal Artillery, for conspicuous bravery at the battle of Abu Klea, when with only a gun handspike, ha protected Lieut. Guthrie from al attack of an infuriated Soudane. STRLIALAND.-Sir C. Warren has issued a proclamation to the inhabitants of Bechuanaland, in which he states his intention of withdrawing military rule from Stellaliind. Stellaland will henceforth be governed by the Baguet, under the advice of Captains Trotter and Vincent. THREE CHILDREN &REED Ti) DEATH —A fire broke out in a workhouse near Calais on Sunday night, and communicated with the house next door. A terrible scene ensued. The occupier and his wife and figs children were rescued, but three children were burned to death.

CHILD MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE -A married woman. named Roberts, living near Bangor, on Saturday, murdered her child by cutting its throat, and attempted to destroy her own life in like manner. The woman, who was for some time-an inmate of a lunatic aaylons, lies in a hope- less condition.

SETTING A WOMAN ON FIRE. —Joseph Tocker, shoe rive- ter, at Nottingham, went home on Saturday night in a drunken condition, beat a woman named Williamson, severely, poured some paraffin over her, and deliberately set fire to her by lighting it with a match. The woman wag fearfully burned, and was taken to the hospital, where her depositions were taken.

-ANOTHER CHILD MURDERED.—OR Sunday afternoon a murder was perpetrated at Alrewae, near Burton.on-Trent. The dead body of a child, aged about eight years, was found in a ditch near the main road leading to Burton. It is sup- posed) that the child belonged to tramps, and that they had killed it by suffocation. A woman bat been arrested in Birtninotarn on suspicion,_

DESPERATE LEAP AND MARVELLOUS ESCAPE.—A woman jtimivd off Clifton Suspenaion Bridge, Bristol, on Friday, and fell into the mud close by the water's edge, over 30() feet below. When taken out she was conscious, and ap- parently no bones were broken. She gave her name as Sarah Hamblin, Bristol. She was taken to the Infirmary. This is the first case of a leap from the bridge which has not been followed by immediate death.

OTERHEdD TELEPHONE WIRES.—Tbe committee on tele- graphs and telephones have concluded that overhead wires do not involve any serious danger. They are of opinion that tslephone companies should have the power of attach- ing wires to pr miss without the consent of the owners or occupiers. Alsi that the post office authorities should give facilities to the telet,hene companies for the use of their wires.

MURDER: THE REVOLVER AT WORE.—Soon after mid- night on'Saturday, a quarrel aross in a house in Hull, be- tween several men and women. An Irish-American sailor, named. John Kelley, accused others of robbing him. The lan,llord, James Ward, ordered Kelley to leave but the lat- ter refused, and threatened to shoot anyone who approached him. Ward advanced towards him, whereupon he drew a revolver and fired. Ward fell dead, the bullet having pas- sed through his forehead. Another man endeavoured to secure Kelley, who again fired, a bullet grazing the man's fingers. Kelley was afterwards arrested, and conveyed to the police station.

A PRISON WARDEE SHOT DEAD —A desperate encoun- ter between two prisoners and two warders is reported from Coonamble Prison, New South Wales, in which two pri- soners escaped after shooting one of the warders dead. Two prisoners were incarcerated in the one cell. One was named Angel ; the other was in irons. Oim morning the turnkey entered the cell for the purpose of cleaning it cut, when both prisoners instantly pounced on him. A desperate struggle ensued, but the turnkey was thrown down and his revolver taken from him. Hearing the struggle and the cries of the turnkey, one of the warders named Mitchell hastened to the spot. He saw his comrade on the ground, but was warned by Angel, who had then taken possession of the revolve-, not to approach. He, however, advanced, when Angel fired, the ball entering the left breast, just be- low the head, and corning out at his back. The two prisoners then made off. Mitchell died soon afterwards. RAIDS ON ALLEGED GAMBLERS.—EXCITING Smelts.— Shortly before one o'clock on Sunday morning raids were made on gamblers at the European Club, Percy-street. Tot- tenham Court-road, London, and at a Social Democratic I Club, Rathbone-place West. Over 40 prisoners were taken to Tottenham Ceurt-road Police Station. The members of the European Club escaped by the back door, and found refuge in the Club of the Social Democrats adjoining. Thither the police in great force proceeded, and, not finding the door open, smashed it in and over ran the premises. The Internationalists protested against the invasion of their I house, declared that no gamesters were there, and hindered the police in search. The latter drawing their staves, bore down the opposition, but only after serious disturbance, in which they were anathematised in all the languages of Europe, and retorted by epithets regarding "Nihilists." While this was going on, the mob cleared out the bar of cigars, liquor, and coats. Several persons were led te the station with their faces covered with blood and their heads in bandages. All except seven were discharged. These were charged on Moneay with obstructing the police in the execution of their duty. The magistrate adjourned the case for a week, and refused an application for permis- sion to apply for a summons against the police, observing that he would grant a summons later on if necessary. DEATH OF SIR WITUN WYNN, M.P.—Sir Watkin William Wynn, M.P., died at his Welsh seat, Wynnstay, Boehm. at an early hour on Saturday, after a long and painful illness. The death of the hon. gentleman has cast *deep gloom over the whole Principality, where he was known as " The Prince in Wales." Sir Watkin was born in London in 1820, and was educated at Westminster and at Christchurch, Oxford. He was afterwards gazetted to a cornetcy in the First Reeiment of Life Guards. At the death of his father, in 1843, he succeeded to the baronetcy and estates of Wynnstay and Rushton, Glanllyn and Bala, the largest estates in Wales. At the time of his death he was Deputy-Lieutenant for the counties of Denbighshire. Shropshire, Merionethshire and Montgomeryshire, Steward ref Her Majesty's Manorial Courts of Denbighshire, Provin- cial Grand Master of the North Wales and Shropshire Free- masons ; Aide-de-camp to her Majesty the Queen, master of the Wynestay Hunt, Colonel of the Montgomeryshire Yeomanry Cavalry, and Lieutenant-Colonel of the Royal Denbighshire Ride Volunteers. He had sat in the House of Commons for Denbighshire for forty-four year,. In 1832 the Queen, then Princess Victoria,was entertained at Wynn. stay. Mr. Herbert Lloyd Watkin Williams Wynn, who recently married Sir Watkin's eldest daughter, succeeds to the baronetcy and estates. Sir Watkin was the patron of seven living,. THE PEOPLE AND GOVERNMENT OF 'MM.—A lecture on the government and people of India was delivered at the Manchester Atheism= on Monday night by Mr. Lalmohun Crimea, an Indian gentleman, who is a candidate in the Liberal interest for the representation of Deptford.—Mr. Ghose said he believed irresponsible power was erremely demoralising to those who possessed it, and highly danger- ous to the country where it was allowed to exist. Speaking of India's taxation, he seid it was impossible to add to it without literally snatching away from the half-starved peasantry the handful of rice with which they had to keep body and soul together, and leave them to drag on an ex- istence than which the imagination of min could scarcely conceive one more miserable. No man who was at all con- versant with the condition of India, and who was not ut- terly callous to. human suffering and misery, could avoid praying with all his heart for peace. (Applause.) If it was desired that the people of India should be sincerely loyal to British rule, if it was desired to rivet the bonds of friendship between the two nations, the Indians must have given to them a share of the administration of their own country. They wanted some liberal measure of local self- gOverument, such as was intended to be given by Lord Mayo, and such as was proposed to be conferred upon the great cities and towns of India by the late Viceroy, Lord Ripon. The time had also come for a very thorough revision_ and reform of the criminal laws, so that there might no longer' be one law for the Indian and another for the Eng- lishman. (Applause.) MAY MEETINDS.—The Religious Tract Society: Held at Exeter Hall. London, on Tuesday night. The receipts for the year ending March 31st last had been £206,558, showing a decrease of £4,821, which was almost wholly accounted for by the decrease of £4 336 in the missionary funds of the society. The issues of the sonless from its formation made a total circulation of 2,368,277,880--Gorejregettio7ted Union of England and Wales : The annual meeting began on Monday night at the Memorial Hall, Loudon, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Theron, D.D., of Liverpool, re- cently elected chairman In the place of the Rev. Dr. Thomas Rees, of Swansea. The Rey. Dr. Hannay (secretary) read the report of the Executive Committee of the Union for the past year, which was adopted. The balloting for the chairman of the Union for MO resulted in the election of the Rev. Ed. White (London.) div.head: FRANCE AND CHINA.
div.p: FRANCE AND CHINA.

PARTS, SATURDAY.—At a Cabinet Council held to-day M. de Freycinet communicated the text of the instructions tele- graphed to M. Pstenotre at Tientsin, authorising him to enter into official negotiations with the Chinese Plenipten- tieries for the conclusion of a definite treaty between France and China.

SHANGHAI, MONDAY.—It is reported upon good Chinese authority that the protocol of the terms ef peace between France and China has been signed at TientE4n. PART, MONDAY.—The Viceroy of Yunnan promises that the Chinese evacuation will be completely effected by June 4th, and it is stated that Luh Vinh Phuoc, the cbief of the Black Flags, will obey his orders. The Viceroy of Yunnan has issued a proclamation calling upon the rebels to deliver up their arms and submit. PARIS, TIIRSDAY.—The Figaro states that negotiations have been opened between the French and Chinese Govern- ments for the cession of the Pescadores islands to Franca. THE FRANCO-CHINESE CONVENTION.

Rams, THURSDAY —The Minister of War has received the following telegram from General Briere de Lisle, dated Hanoi, yesterday:—" Our outposts beyond Than Moi have received official notification by a flap. of truce of the evacua- tion of Langson by the Chinese on the sth instant. The Chinese ask for a few days delay t) enable them to com- plete the evacuation of the Red River district. I have caused M. Patenotre to be informed that on account of material difficulties in the way I was prepared to grant a delay of ten days for the evacuation on condition that we were placed in possession of Daman Quan on the 25th inst. Since the evacuation commenced the re-appearance of piratical bands is reported in the direction of Than Moi and Dongson and between the River Clair and Longean. I have ordered them to be pursued without remission." GREAT FIRE AT CHICAGO.

Calms*, FRIDAY.—A fire occurred to-day in the lumber district of this city, causing the destruction of four timber yards. The loss is believed to be over a million dollars. —Saturday: The loss caused by the fire in the lumber district of the city is now estimated at 700,000 dollars.

div.head: CANADIAN REBELLION.
div.p: THE CANADIAN REBELLION.

OTTAWA., SUNDAY.—General Middleton, with a force of I one thousand men, left the camp at Gabriels Crossing yesterday morning, and marched a distance of seven miles, the gunboat dropping down the river at the same time. When near Batouche the gencoat was fired upon from both sides of the river. The scouts, with a Getting gun, there- 1 upon pushed forward, and came upon the advanced guards of the rebels. The Gatling then opened lire upon them, when they retreated behind a church and two houses. The artillery coming up, shelled the enemy, end dislodged them from the church, and also drove them from their rifle pile. While thus engaged, a large force of rebels suddenly emerged from the woods, with the object of seizing the guns; but the Gatling was pushed to the front, and when the enemy got within 20 yards, literally mowed them down. The rebels then broke their line and fled. The casualties among General Middleton's troops were unimportant. WINNIPEG, SUNDAY NlGHT.—Details of Sunday's fighting between the Canadian troops and the rebels have been re- ceived here. The rebels opened the attack by firing on the steamer Northcote, which was assisting the troops. The regulars at once returned the fire from their gene and small arms. Unfortunately, the steamer was disabled by the rebel fire and unable to render the assistance expected. The rebels made efforts to capture the cannon, but were beaten , off. Firing was kept up the whole day, and the fight, though stubbornly contested, was of an undecisive chaise. ter. By nightfall every house in Batouche was destroyed by the shells of the Canadians, but the rebels still held out among the ruins. OTTAWA, TUESDAY—The statements published represen- Mg the killed and wounded among the Government troops In the engagement at Batoche on Saturday are incorrect. IThe following are the casualties that have been reported : —Killed : Gunner Phillips. Wounded : Captain Mason, Gunners. Fairbairn, and Tooley, Thomas J. Stout and Chappatier.

div.head: SEVERE ENGAGEMENr.
div.p: SEVERE ENGAGEMENr.

()wawa, TUESDAY' 10 Ent.—A despatch from General Middleton, received by the Dominion Government this evening, states that the troops employed in strengthening the position surround the rebels in the ravine and in the rifle pits, and are starving them into submission. The rebels occasionally fire upon the troops, but without causing any casualties. OTTAWA, WEDNESDAY,—GeneraI Middleton reports this morning as follows: We had an engagement with the enemy on Monday. I received a message from Riel, saying," If you massacre our women and children we will massacre our prisoners." I answered, "Put your women in a safe place, point it out, and we will not fire at it." I then pushed on our advance guard, and, when I saw a chance, ordered a general charge. Our men responded nobly, and were splendidly led by their officers. Colonel Strauberzie drove the enemy out of their rifle pits at the point of the bayonet, and afterwards forced his way across the pliin and seized the houses, of which we are now masters. Our men bivouacked on Monday night on the field of battle. In the heat of the action Rid l sent another letter stating that if the General did not retreat or grant an interview the prisoners would be killed. The letter came too late, the advance being already ordered. The prisoners were rescued, and are safe in camp. The enemy had not time to kill them. Our loss is five killed and eleven woun- ded. The enema, sustained great loss. News received here from the Edmonton region states that Factor Young has arrived at Fort Saskatchewan, and re- ports that all danger of the Indians at White Fish Lake and Lac La Blanche joining Big Bar is past, as Chief Preen, of the former tribe, proves loyal and possesses influence to prevent an outbreak. CENTRAL AMERICA.

NEW You, ISIONDA.Y.—A telegram from Panama states that General Preslaw, the rebel commander, who set fire to Aspinwall, is now besieging Carthagena. DEATH OF QUEEN EMMA. SAN FRANCISCO, SATURDAY.—News has arrived of the death, on the 25th ult., of Emma, Queen Dowager of Hawaii. Queen Emma was the widow of Katnehameha IV., who died in 1863. She was the daeghter of an Englishwoman and a native chief, and was adopted by Dr. Rooke, an English physician in the island. Before her marriage with King Kamehameha, she was known as Miss Rooke.

- - - AN OLD MAID AND HER EATF.s.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, bliss Elizabeth Beesley, an old maid, residing at Prescot, was summoned for the non-pay- ment of .£2 7e. 61, amount of judgment summons and costs. Mr. Whitfield, one of the rate collectors for the Widnes Local Board, said that some time ago an order was made upon the defendant for the payment of £1 133. Od., amount due for rates upon her property in Widnes and the costs. As she did not pay a distress warrant was issued against her, but was returned marked 'No goads." The judgment summons was then issued, which, with the costs, brought the amount up to .£2 7s. tti. She had property in . . .
_ Widnes, and since January last had colkcted from it con- siderably more than £4. An order was now made for her committal to prison for a month, but it is not to if 13119 for 14 days.

He does not perceive that in Ve,i,rig such a statement he is exposing the tierVless and incompetency of the Oppost- t4-i, The latest move has been to obstruct ter; 'ate of Credit for Eleven Millions by a of fierce speeches based, absurdly, ter: Mild resolution asking for "adequate le.ttnation as to the present policy of Her "N.l4,ifie?4's Government." The Vote of 411(1-"It includes, it will be remembered, lour Okivi., half millions for the Eoudan CiAn- hen the understanding being that the lerip are, if need be, to be drafted off to 44;4 in case of a war with Russia. „ Lord tidij;ll!`iGTox took all the wind out of the -7,T0, the Opposition by explaining, early Wer'''onday evening, that the British troops or it to be withdrawn from the upper reaches lhar?. Nile, the proposal to go d to the 10"311fla having been abandoned; while the Riala MINISTER t stated that papers as .d o kief,tlegotiations with Russia would be lain thig-r`e Parliament in a few days. But a tee,- Which should have satisfied reasonable ibr,„ made the Opposition more unreason - they had tabled their Vote of Censure )441a1 t:heY went forward—to be defeated as tleir,„-"n argument and numbers, the motion I'VrA /ejected by a majority of 30. With k )0 the decision of the Government not QtrrlZ lorward to Khartoum, we cannot but Tetii it will be received by the country with ttpen,.P of satisfaction second only to those kce "enced on learning that, without sacri- th, tr. °I honour or any material 'advantage, Nal 18 every likelihood of war with Russia Itiihlkaverted. We have all along felt that, fall of Khartoum and the death of ll• e`al GORDON, there was an end, or ought the e.,40 end, to the Nile expedition. But 41441 Was raised that the death of GORDON kejat `4'e avenged, and, although the Govern- Vjere Ar4,ight not give much ear to the cry, they gafetv`uslaosed for a time to think that, for the tclwe'r. of Egypt, it was necessary that the akh of the MA,UDI should be broken at 4 4tton • 0,, -tn. Fortunately, the advent of the hot • " Put an end to operations on the Nile, 4f. for the rest, the stars in their courses Alse alight on our side, The power of the `4,troPhet is broken by internal dissen- 'l/4cl 141 ere is revolt amongst his followers ; ,111°4lr1stead of marching upon Egypt, he has I,'lt.e,t, than he can do to hold the few t Which he calls his own. Everything 9“1 ez.efore n • favour of withdrawing the .I,thel•ritish in who are encamped on 411 Ile in the neighbourhood of Dongola. eY wil 1 be brought, as soon as the river • kb, 40 rise on towards Egypt proper—to ,7 '4 • aua or Assouan--where a sufficient 4k • Vlll b ..41rist any attack stationod to secure the country "437 attack from insurrectionary tribes-

I men. It is notewothy that the Conservatives received Lord HARTINGTON'S statement as to the withdrawal of troops with derisive laugh- ter, and yet,iater on, during the debate on the Vote of Credit both Lord G. HAMILTON and Lord R. CHURCHILL gave the House to understand that it must not be inferred that they had ever been in favour, after the death of General GORDON, of advancing to Khar- toum.• Can it be that the Opposition, in view of the coming election, are disappointed at the Government being in a position to carry out thus speedily the policy they have all along announced—that of finally abandon- ing the Soudan? For our own part, the only regret we have is that they did not take this step earlier, and that there is some doubt as yet as to leaving Suakim. It is a relief, however, to know that there is no need now for the mili- tary railway from Suakim to Berber. If it be proceeded with, it will be continued in the interests of commerce, and with a view to the suppression of the slave trade. It is pleasing to hear of a railway as an agent of civilisation rather than an engine of destruction. Turning to the debate as it related to the dispute with Russia, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the Opposition are gre- viously disappointed that Mr. GLADSTONE has so managed matters that England has nothing to lose and everything to gain by the I proposed arbitration. There is a feeling amongst them that we must fight with Russia , soon or late, and the conclusion they have come to—honesty come to we do not doubt 1 —is that it would be better soon than late. But Englishmen, on the whole, take a different view of the situation. ! They rightly think that a war with Russia would be a terrible calamity ' to both countries; and they are "unfeignedly thankful" that the Government by fairness, and firmness, and preparedness for every , contingency, have won the civilised world to our side, ghd brought Russia to xefer the alleged breach of covenant to the lodgment of a friendly Sovereign It is preposterous to , talk in such a CQnnection of "cowardice," LI or " surrender," or " shanleful acts." The shameful thing would be to force any nation ' or any individual to fight when there was willingness to refer the cause of quarrel to a , disinterested tribunal. We are gaining all that we asked for in demanding an inquiry into.the origin of the fighting at Penjdeh. But we shall gain more, if, as seems probable, we delimit the frontier of Afghanistan in such a way as will be satisfactory not only to ourselves, but ,to the Czar and the Ameer. It is a small matter to this country whether Petildeh be defined as belonging to Russia or Afghanistan; the great point is to shave sonze demarcation of frontier; and as to this there is now every prospect of the work being done in London under circumstances which are favourable to the views of our own Govern- ment. Sir PETER -.LUMSDEN is now on his way to render his advice and assistance, and Mr. CONDIE STEPHEN has already reached England. Both gentlemen will apply them- selves to the task of delimitation fresh from recent surveys, so that the Cabinet will not be likely to err through lack of information. It is only fair to Russia to say that Mr. STEPHEN in his rapid journey across a large tract of Russian territory received every as- sistance from the authorities. We must be just even to our foes, and justice requires that we should acknowledge that Russia, since Mr. GLADSTONE'S great speech, has shown herself as amenable to reason as Eng- land, and as anxious, too, to avoid " the dread arbitrament of war."

THE Liberation Society held its annual meeting in London on Wednesday evening, when there was a large attendance, the Hon. E. L. STANLEY M.P., occupying the chair. At a meeting of the Council, in the afternoon, resolutions were passed in favour of disestab- lishment in Scotland and Wales, the amend- ment of the burial laws, and the abolition of oaths. Outsiders are too prone to think the Liberation Society concerns itself with nothing beyond Disestablishment ; but, although that is the great object of its exist- ence, kindred questions which tend in the direction of religious equality are not neg- lected. Great progress has been made in the way of reform of the laws regulating the man- agement ot parochial burial grounds, but much still remains to be accomplished. On the question of the abolition of oaths, the So- ciety has done good work, never hesitating to affirm and maintain its principles, notwith- standing the bitterness of feeling engendered by the BRADLAUGH controversy. It is not likely that any further action will be taken in the present Parliament; but it is hardly to be doubted that the new House of Commons will make short work of the obstructionists who may in the future seek to block the pas- ' sage of an Affirmation Bill. We cannot pre- tend to say that the Tories are greatly to blame for the course they have taken on this question. It is in harmony with their tradi- tions to oppose liberty of conscience; the blame rather falls upon those luke- warm Liberals who are but indiffer- ently acquainted with the foundations of their faith. An organisation such as the Liberation Society is needed to remind some people that there are such things as princi- ples, and that, at all cost, they are worthy to be upheld. A State Church is such an anomaly—such an excresence upon the body politic—that, if it did not already have its be- ing amongst us, it would not be permitted to come into existence. But it is in our midst; and it is the duty of all politicians who call themselves Liberal to do what in them lies to liberate the Church from State control. The assault has for a long time been almost entirely from without ; but such is the evil of the system as it stands—so notorious are its growing scandals—that good men within the Church ° are loudly demanding Disestablish- ment as the only remedy which can bb effec- tively applied. At Warrington, and at Earlestown, we have conspicuous instances of the dissatisfaction Of Churchmen with the existing state of thins, and of the need which is felt for the parishioners having a say in matters as well as the parson. Ireland has got rid of a State Church and is all the better for it—a fact which Irishmen would do well to bear in mind when they are consider- ing their grievances as compared with those of other parts of the United Kingdom. Scot- land and Wales are ripe for Disestablishment, and when the Church has been set free in these countries—as it will be before many years are over—it goes without saying that the reform of the English Church will speedily follow. Meantime the Liberation Society has plenty to do, and, as it has a lofty aim, and does difficult work with fairness and moderation, we trust it will continue to be well supported by the Liberals of this dis- trict.
THE Conservatives of St. Helens have found a candidate to contest the borough on their behalf in the person of Mr. SETON- KARR, a barrister with the special recora-

mend ition that he is a nephew of the late Sir THOMAS BIRCH, who formerly resided near Prescot. Mr. KARR professes to be alarmed at the new principles that are in the air, but we notice that he has nothing to say against the Caucus. Can this be because he was put through the ordeal of having to submit him- self to it on Monday night? Or is it that the Caucus is altogether wrong when it is Radical, and the pink of perfection when it is Tory? Mr. KARR s speech is a fair sample of Toryism. It promises great things in the way of a spirited foreign policy ; everything is to be done: for the British workman—that is if it can be accomplished by doing some- thing abroad; but we look in vain for even a promise of reform at home. Let the St. Helens elector, who for the first time will have it in his over to give a Parliamentary I vote, ask himself what he is likely to gain if such men as Mr. SETON-KARR are returned to St. Stephens. We more than suspect that he will be puzzled for an answer. There is nothing about improved dwellings for the poor, nothing about an amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, nothing about securing a fair share in county government, nothing about reform in the licensing laws, or such a change in the land laws as will make farming more pro- fitable, and, by finding employment for the rural population, relieve the labour market in our large towns. Reform is not in Mr. KAnit's line; he is for Church and State and no surrender. That is the sum and sub- stance of his home policy; while as to foreign affairs he would seek to mend matters by going to war with Russia, and trying to keep possession of the Soudan—a country as tur- bulent as Pandemonium,and as large as Eng- land, France, and Germany put together. Things may be bad, but the new electors must be as unfit for the Franchise as the Tories have always believed them to be, if they think they are to be improved by sending to Parliament such fossil-politicians as Mr. SETON-KARR. We have a higher opinion of them; they know better than he on which side their bread is buttered.

Mr. W. CRosrrEm, the Liberal candidate for Warrington, made an exceedingly ap- propriate and pleasant speech on Monday evening in presiding over the highly-success- ful meeting held in connection with the Liberal tea party and ball. He treated his audience to several stories of the way in which titled great ones had dispensed with their dignity, whilst canvassing, in order to make sure of a vote. But he omitted to mention the celebrated instance in which Sir GILBERT GREENALL took to turning a mangle as a means of getting into the good graces of an elector. Perhaps he wished to spare his op- ponent this reminiscence of the aching back which he got whilst giving a literal illustra- tion of the adage that one good "turn " de- serves another. Poor Sir GILBERT ! We are afraid that his days of turn and return are over. He was 79 the other day, and the chances are that if he enters into another election c ontest he will find next time that he has himself been mangled . It is too bad of his friends to force him into the arena again3t such a vigorous champion of Liberalism as Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD.
THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1885.

TILE SALE OF WORK in aid of the building fund of St. Paul's Church, Widnes, held on Friday alid Saturday last week, realised £65. WIDNES PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION.—Mr. E K. Muspratt has been elected president of the Widnes Division Liberal Association, and Mr. H. B. Shores, sacra cry. WIDNES Beaerssr CiIAPEL.—The Sunday school anniver- sary sermons were preached on Sunday by Mr. M. Roth- well, of Liverpool, and the collecdons amounted to about

_ VICTORIA ROAD IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WIDNES.—At the weekly meeting on Monday, Mr. Rawlineon read a paper on "The daty of the Church in re'atim to youthful amusements." Mr. Herbert Neild presided. MILTON LITERARY AND FRATERNAL SOCIETY, WIDNES. —Mr. W. Browne on Tuesday evening read a pap-r before the members of this society on "Petroleum." The Rev. R. G. Hughes occupied the chair, and there was an inter- esting discussion. BEACON Roca, RUNCORN —lt is stated that this historic landmark on Runcmn Hill is shortly to be blasted by gun- powder in order to quarry the stone underneath, and that the lessee of the land has offered to sell the rock to the Board of Commissioners if they wish to preserve it. Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Caulfield was charged with committing an indecent assault on a girl nine years of age, residing with her parents at 44, Dickson-street. The prisoner lodged in the house, and during the ptrents absence committed the assault complained of. The prisoner was remanded. Simms CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—Mr. G. R. Bell, of the Theological Institute, Manchester, on Sun- day preached two sermons in this chapel, Widnes. There were crowded congregations at each service. In the after- noon a children's service was held, dialogues and recitations being given. The collections resulted in over £l5 being added to the funds. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The anni- versary services took place in Greenway-road Caapel. on Suuday, when the Rev. F. Jeffs preac'..ed in the morning and evening to large congregations. In the afternoon the Rev E. J. Robinson occupied the pulpit. Under the con- ductorship of Mr. Poole the children sang special hymns in a praiseworthy manner. The collections amounted to £2l. WORKMEN AND THE MAGISTRACY.—It is stated that Mr. Henry R. Stetter, secretary of the Provincial Typographi- cal Association, his been appointed a magistrate for the county of Lancaster. Similar offers of appo:ntment to the magistracy have, it is understood, been made to Mr. T. Birtwistle, of Accrington, secretary to the Operative Weavers' Association of N )rth and North-east Lancashire ; and Mr. Fielding, of Bolton, who holds the post of secretary to tho local branch of the Operative Cotton Spinners' Asso- ciation.

CLIIM BY A RUNCORN BOATMAN.--It the Hyde County Court on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Hughes, Q.C., Henry Goode, boatman, of Runcorn, brought an action against the Hyde and Houghton Colliery Company, to recover damages caused through the boat of the defend- ant coining into collision with a boat of the plaintiff's on the 12th Much last.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, of Runcorn, was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Smith, of Hyde, represented the defendants.—A verdict was given for the plaintiff for £6 14s. 101 and costs. HOLY TRINITY Y.M.C.A. Gs:4gAsneet.—ln connection wilts this organisation an assault at arms was given in Holy Trinity Schools, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance to witness the performances of the members, and the Rev. W. Preston presided. Dumb and bar bell exercises, club work, and parallel and horizontal bar performances were gone through in very creditable style, the proceedings being interspersed with a recitation by Mr. H. Fletcher, a song by Mr. Jones, and a performance on stringed instruments by Messrs. L. and J. Kilcross. The exercises were gone through to music performed by Miss B. liankinson and Mr. H. Hankinson. I.acnNsEn VICrnALLEas AND THE BUDGET.—A meeting of the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers' Asso- ciation was held at the Uaicorn Inn, Winwick.road, on Tuesday afternoon, when the chair was occupied by Mr. Joseph Taylor' the president. IP." These charges are the same as have been ad:pled in Manchester and Liverpool and other large towns.

THE DIVISION ON THE AMENDMENT TJ THE VOTE OF CREDIT—The division on this vote of censure was of a more strictly party character than any which has been taken for some years on the foreign policy of the Government, not a single Liberal voting in the minority or a single Conservative in the in tj irity. Twelve ra ulerate Home Rulers supported, and thirty-eight Parnellites opposed the Governmen,. but Mi. Parnell himself abstained. The GJvernment were supported by Messrs. Agnew, Armitage, Arnold, Jacob Bright, Cheetham, J. K. Cross, Fort, and Grafton. Lord Hartingtm, Me•isrs. Hibbert, Hop vogd, Leaks, McMinnies, Mason, Poilips, Penn ngton, Potter, 'Viands, and Slagg, the Hon. E. L Stanley, Messrs. Sum• mere and Thomasson. The minority included Mr. Codding- ton, Sir R A. Cross, Messrs. EAersley and Ecroyd, the Ron. A. Egerton, Major-General Feilden, Mr. Houldsworth, Col. Stanley, Messrs. Tomlinson and Warburton.

SINGULAR THEFT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. .T. Brundrit, William Butterworth, a labourer, was brought up on remand charged with steeling half-a-sovereign, the pro- perty of George Bushell. Bushell is the captain of a steamer which arrived in the Runcorn Docks on Monday, and Mr. Richard Abel, boat owner, Trentham-strest, engaged the prisoner and a man named Hampsan to aid in coaling the vessel. Their services were not, however. re- quired, and Mr. Abel asked Bushell for sixpence to give the men "lowance." Bushell handed him what he thought was a sixpence, and Mr. Abel :rave it to the prisoner. Sat). sequently Bushell discovered that instead of sixyence he had given half-a-sovereign, and inquiries made showed that the prisoner had attempted to change half-a-sovereign at Hayward's tobacconist's shop, Top Llcke, and had succeeded in doing so at Miss Mack's, High-street. On Thursday morning P.C. Bryan went into the cells, and the prisoner admitted that he had received the half- sovereign, and took him to a place near Savage's Bridge where he had hidden the change. The money had, how- ever, disappeared. The Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's hard labour.

DEDICATION OF A PULPIT AT WIDNES.—A gool congre- gation assembled at St. Paul's Church on Thursday after- noon to witness the dedication of a Pulpit by the Rev. Canon Lefroy, rural dean of South Liverpool. The pulpit, which is the ofLring of Mrs. Deacon, Mr. H. W. Deacon, and Mr. Alan Deacon, is built of terracotta, embellished with an alabaster top, pillars of the same stone, ornament- ing the five panels that ornament ths scructure. In the centre panel is the fi,pire of Christ, the other panels being occupied by the four Evangelists, all cut in stone of a c3loar that harmonises well with the terra cot'a. The in- terior of the structure is lined With stained and polished oak, and the floor is so fixed that it can be raised or lowered ac- cording to the height of the preacher. The pulpit is a beautiful piece of workmanship, and is from the designs of Mr. H. Shelmerdine, of Liverpool, the builders being Messrs. Norbury, of the same city. The Psalms proper to Ascension Day were chanted, the Rev. G. Bond road the lessons, and the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar, said the prayers. The choirs of St. Mary's and St. Paul's were united for the occasion, and under the leadership of Mr. Crawford, sang special hymns. Mr. J. B. Imison was at the harmonium. The Rev. Canon Lefroy preached a ser- mon on the Ascension. He referred with gratification to the prominent part the manufacturers had taken in the erection of St. Paul's Church, thus showing that they re- cognised that their workpeople had souls as well as bodies to be taken care of. A collection was made in aid of the building fund

SINGULAR DEATH AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Crown lan, Ann- street West, on the body of James Yarwood, a lihmrer, who died under somewhat peculiar circumstances on Thurs- day, May 7th.—Catherine Burns, widow, 9, Caroline-street, said the deceased was her son, and was 23 years of age. He worked at Messrs. Muspratt and Sons' works, Live pool, in January last, under Mr. Scrymgeur. On th 3 12th January he came home ill, and told her that a man named Barrow had thrown a rope upon his head. He complained of pains in his head, and in consequence of losing his eyesight was taken to the Eye and Ear Institution. Afterwards he was taken to the Royal Infirmary, where he remained nine weeks. He was then brought home, but he never recovered his sight. He died on Thursday.—Thomas Barrow, mason, Sutton, near St. Helens, deposed that he was engaged in putting up a condenser at the time in question. He never threw a rope upon the deceased. The deceased complained 1 that he had got a drop of chemicd liquor in his eye, and he thought he should have logo to the Hospital —Mrs. Burns, recalled, said she never told Barrow that her son had been struck with a rope.—Peter Scrymgeour, mason, St. Helens. said the deceased and Borrow were in his employ. Tar- wood complained that he had got a drop of acid in his eye. He never said anything about a rope striking hie n on the head. He had seen the mother several times on the station at Widnes, and at Liverpool. Her language was vary bad, and she was under the influence of drink. She had asked him to go and see her son, but he hardly thought it safe to go to her house.—The Coroner said the evidence was very unsatisfactory, but it was the best they could get at present, anal be did not think an adjournment would be of any use, The deceased did not impute a wilful act to Barrow, even if that person did let a rope fall.—Aft¢r some deliberation the jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death," but whether it was the result of a rope falling upon the head of the de- ceased or the injury to the eye with acid, they contol not

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

NEW WORKS FOR RUNCORN.—It is rumoured that the works on the Sprinch, Runcorn. recently used for the manufacture of glycerine, have been taken by a soap manu- facturer who formerly relided in the town. HOLY TRINirY D.S.Y SCHOOLS, RUNCORN.—The annual sermons on behalf of these schools were preached in Holy Trinity Church on Sunday by Dr. Shone, the Lord Bishop of Kilmore. Large congregations attended each service, and the collections realised a good sum. CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.— The following officers have been appointed by this society : —President, Mr. H. Randle ; vice-presidents, Messrs. G. S. Hazlehurst. S. C. Beckett, W. J. Shore, Rev. T. Hackett ; committee, Messrs. J. Dutton, W. Yates, W. Massey, and J. D. Jones ; secretary, Mr J. Nancollis. UNITED FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—In aid of the circuit funds of this church the Rev. G. W. Chisholm on Sunday preached two sermons to good congregations. On Monday evening a large audience gathered in the same building to listen to a lecture by the rev, gentleman, entitled "Pen and ink sketches of funny folk." The lecturer frequently elicited applause by his sketches of human nature, and his humour- ous sallies were provocative of mach laughter. Mr. W. Bray presided. • RUNCORN RECRE&TION FOOR&LL CLUB.—This club has concluded a most successful season. Out of 20 matches played 15 had been won, and 5 drawn, the club having scored 17 goals, 28 trier, and 85 minor points, against their opponents 2 goals. 4 tries, and 21 minor points. The total receipts were £l5 63 611, and after paying all expenses there is a balance in hand of £3. Mr. J. Green has been re-elected captain for the next season, and Mr. J. Faulkner sub•captain. Mr. H. Pendlebury is secretary, and Mr. R. Col I Inge, treasurer. ENTERING THE LION'S DEN AT RUNCORN. Colonel Boone, the lion tamer, last week exhibited his collection of lions at the Theatre Royal, and put them through a start- ling performance. A local volunteer had promised to enter the "den" on Friday night, but he failed to put in an ap- pearance, and Mr. John Ellis, captain of a Runcorn schoo- ner, cooly stepped forward and without the slightest hesita- tion stepped amongst the savage beasts with Colonel Boone. He remained there for sveral minutes, and had the hardi- hood to stroke the head of one of the lionesses and to kiss it. He was greeted with a perfect ovation en descend- ing to the platform. &nicotine VOLUNTEER COMPETITION.—.The three compe- titions to select two Volunteers to represent the F and G Companies of the above regiment at the Wimbledon meet- ing in July were completed on Saturday, with the result that Colour-Sergeant J. Mort (F Company) and Sergeant W. H. Harvey (G Company) will represent the Runcorn detachment this year. Stormy weather prevailed on two occasions, which accounts for the lowness of the scores. ,mpetitions. TJ. let 2nd 3rd tat. Colour-Sergeant J. Mort 64 84 80 228 Sergeant W. H. Harvey Sergeant D.
