GOO-D TEMPLAR ,T WIDNES. The weekly session of the Samaritan Lodge 1.0.G.T. took place no Tuesday even- ing, when the imprisonment of detective Williams came up for discussion. This racer is new undergoing seven years' penal servitude for perjury alleged to have been committed at Poole in connection with a raid made upon public-houses by Alderman Norton, a member of the Poole Town Coun- cil. The Horne Secretary, Sir William Harcourt has been petitioned to allow a new inquiry to be made into the case, but he has declined to do to, and the Good Templars throughout the country are taking the matter up. The Samaritan Lodge decided to summon a meeting of represen- tatives from all the lodges in Widnes for the purpose of drawing up and presenting a memorial to the South-West Lancashire District Lodge, urging the necessity of petition- ing Parliament in favour ef Williams's release through the county members. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—THE FINANCIAL CONDITION. —The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Cemetery on Wednesday. Mr. James Handley, J.P., pre- slded, and there were present Messrs. Moss, Coleburn, Whittaker, Rogerson, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary.)—The report of the Finance Committee showed a balance on the month's cash account of £34 2e 21,—Mr. Moss moved the confirmation of the report, and in doing so said he thought it well to draw attention ta a statement made at a rate- payers' meeting to the effect that the cemetery ought now be considered as self•supporting. That would be very satisfactory if it were so, but in his opinion it was not ad- visable that the ratepayers should remain under that impression when it was not so. The expenses of the ceme- tery for the last year amounted to £530, and the revenue from all sources was £420, thus showing a deficiency of £llO. If they added to this the £l2O which was drawn from the rates as repayment of debt, which might fait ly be charged to revenue, they would be £230 short of meeting the pay- ment. Another statement at the same meeting was that the debt on the cemetery would remain in its present form until the year 1931, whereas it would only remain so until 1910 or 1911.—The Chairman observed that it was quite right to draw attention to these matters.—Mr. Rogersou secended the motion, which was carried.—The Secretary reported that the interments for the month eeding the 25th April were 43 ; corresponding period last year, 24 ; increase, 24. The fees received during the same period amounted to £42 se; last year, £33 913; increase £8 16.3.—This concluded the busittees.

WIDNES POLICE COURT.—Yesterday, before Mr. T. S. Timmins, Richard Taylor, a gipsy, who goes about the country with a van, was charged with haying been drunk and disorderly in Liverpool-road, Crouton, and also with acting in an indecent fashion to Hannah Harrison, a domestic servant. The prisoner was remanded until Mon day. SWINE FEVER IN iVIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday James Douglas was charged with a breach of the Infectious Diseases (Animals) Act.—P.C. Bruce stated that on Wednesday night, the 29th April, he saw the de- fendant driving three store pigs along Warrington-road. The defendant admitted that he bad brought the animals from Warrington without a licence.—lnspector Wood said it was well known Widnes was an infected area.—The de- fendant was fined 10s and costs. THEFT OF A WATCII AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Wednesday Henry Richards WAS charged with haying, on the 29th April, stolen a watch valued at £4, and a purse containing 275, the property of Emmanuel Simpson It appeared that the prisoner lodged with the prosecutor at 29, Milton-street. On the 29th April the prosecutor's watch was hanging in the bedroom, and the same day he missed the watch And a purse containing 275. On Tuesday P.C. Steele received the p-isoner into custody in London. He ackowledged taking the watch, and stated he pawned it for El 15s at Birkenhead. The prisoner was remanded.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK —At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following persons were each fined 5s for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—Joseph Woods, Wellington-street; William Shaw, Granville-street ; Matthew Edwards, Alcock-street ; John Hughes, Holloway ; William Taylor, Gilbert-street ; Bridget Frame, Mersey-street ; John Cshaw, C,)oper-street ; John Antrobus, Wilson's-row; William Price, Cooper- street ; Joseph Bushell, Stone-street ; Richard Hone, Shaw-street; John Doyle. Mersey-street ; Elizibeth Webb, Ashworth-row ; and Henry Skelding, Talkeld's-square.— The cases were proved by Mr. T. Bowyer, visitor to the School Board.

BREACHES OF THE CANAL BOATS ACT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, The British Salt Company, Anderton, were summoned for contravening the Canal Boats Acts by allowing two boats to be used on the Trent and Mersey Canal, which were not marked, lettered, and numbered on both sides of the cabin.—Mr. J. Farring- ton, inspector to Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, proved the case.—A representative of the firm produced documents showing that the boats had been registered, but owing to the delay of the builders the boats were not marked.—The Bench said there was clearly no attempt to evade the law, and imposed a nominal fine of Is and costs us 6,1 in each case.—Messrs. V. and J. Adams, carriers, Tunstall, for a similar offence, were mulcted in a like penalty. ENTRAPPING A SAILOR AT RUNCORN. Ellen Newton, a woman of loose character, was brought before Mr. W. Banks and Mr. J. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with stealing £1 33 2,1 from the person of a sailor named George Fiest. Fiest arrived in the town on Monday afternoon on board the schooner Nellie Baynes, and in the evening he was in the street, when he net the prisoner who said she would take him where be could get a good glass of beer. Afterwards he purchased some baked potatoes, and a quantity of tripe and roast pork, and went home with the prisoner. During the night he discovered that his pockets had been rifled, and he seized the prisoner by the neck and nose and about seven shillings dropped from her mouth. He thereupon gave her into custody to P.C. Bryan. He had been unable to recover .£1 33 3d of the money taken. The prisoner was committed to gaol for a month. ASSAULT ON TEE POLICE AT RUNCORN —Before Mr, H. Reynolds and Mr. J. Brundritt, at Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, Thomas Janni no, described as a "loafer," was charged with being drunk in Cooper-street. On the previ- ous afternoon P.C.'s Wallace and Bryan entered Hart's beerhouse and found the prisoner there drunk with a glass full of beer before him. The landlord's attention was called to the prisoner, who was then turned out. In the street he created a disturbance, and was locked up. He Was fined 101, and costs 53. Si., or 14 days. The money was paid.—Fanny Jannion, his sister, wee charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with assaulting and resisting P.C. Wallace whilst is the execution of his duty. The prisoner attempted to rescue her brother, but finding her efforts unavaiiing she struck Constable Wallace iu the face. For being drunk and disorderly the prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, or a month ' • and on the other charge she was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

POACHING NEAR RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Robert Moores, a young man, was charged with having on the 3rd May at Clifton unlawfully tres- passed upon land in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Stokes in search of game. On the Sunday morning in question Peter Jones, a labourer for Mr. 13 ankles; of Peewit Hall, saw the defendant and several others coming along the road and he concealed himself behind a hedge. Two hares were playing upon one of Mr. Stoke's fields, and he heard the rnea shout to a dog they had " N>w, now," and the dog chased the game a long distance. Moores went along a private road across a field, for about five hundred yards, and Jules met him on his return. Moores said "You won't do anything Ito me for fetching the dog back."—The defendant Vated he called the dog back, and walked along a cindered footpath to fetch it beck. lie knew there was a long list against him, but he was innocent this time.—Mr. Bankes said there were 18 convic ions against him, many for trespass, end he I would be fined 40r and costs or a month.—Defendant said they always put it on the poor workingman.

THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF A RUNCORN SCHOOLMASTER. —Before Mr. W. Bankes and 'ir. John Brun lrit, at Runcarn Police Court, on Tuesday, James Craig, principal of the Runcorn Collegiate School, was charged with having no the 16th February unlawfully stabbed, cut, and wounded himself with intent thereby feloniously and with malice aforethought to kill and murder himself.—Dr. Robinson said he was called in to see Mr. Craig on the morning of the day in question. He found the prisoner at his house with his throat veri badly rut. The prisoner had I.st a great deal of blood. Ile could not judge of the prisoner's state of mind at the lime, bathe afterwards discovered when he had recovered sufficiently that he had been completely out of health. Hr was emaciated and completely out of health bodily and his mind was not rational. A razor was pointed out to him, and he had no doubt from what he sag that the wound was icflicttcl by the pris mer's own hand.-- Superintendent Leah : How long did his mind remain in that deranged state P—Witness : I cannot say that he s properly recovered yet. It is only lately that his skin hem done peeling after w' at is called nervous faver and brain inilammation.—Mr. Stokes : As a matter of fact I suppose he was labouring order temporary insanity. 7—The witness replied in the affirmative. His core was that of delirium of fever and inflammatisn of the brain. Mr. Craig (the pri- soner) went away to Blackpool lately without his sanction, and le was not responsible for his going.—Superiniendent Leah : He went away to recoup his health 7—Witness Yes.—The Ben.ffi asked if there was any feather evidenc?.— Superintendent Leah said the doctor was the first man who had seen the prisoner—Dr. Robinson sail Mr. Craig's con- dition was sir critical that ha got another Surgeon to see him. He was pulseless.—Tbe prisoner : I could tell you a great deal mysel,.—The Chairman : Tat won't do.—After a brief consultation the Bench discharged the prisoner, and Mr. Craig at once left the court.

IMPORTANT TO RUNCORN FUSTIAN CUTTERS.-Before Mr W Betakes and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Eden Gallagher, of Widnes, was summoned by Mary and F. 0. Mostyn, fustian cutters, Lymm And Run- corn, to answer a claim of Is compensation for having ab- sented herself from work without just cause or lawful ex- cuse, and to show cause why an order should not be made upon her to fulfil the terms of her apprenticeship deed.— Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the complain- ants, and Mr. J. Barton for the defendant—Mr. Browne said the Actual toss to ths complainants in the case was ' about £lO, but they only claimed nominal damages of Is.— Joseph Walker, foreman, proved the indenture, and said he told the girl that she would only have to pay 61 per week to cross the Bridge as Mr. Mostyn had made an arrange- ment with the Railway C ampeny. The defendant could earn 7s per week.—Mr. Mostyn said an apprentice ought to be able to earn 7s per week after six or eight weeks' experi- ence. The trade had now, however, gone down 50 per cent. The defendant had never been to her work since August. He failed to make an arrangement with the Rail- way Company for the apprentices to cress the Bridge at half fare. but in February he agreed to pay the d efendant half the Bridge fare, and she promised to return to her work.—ln reply to M. Burton witness said he did not know what he should do if there were no pieces of velvet to cut. Ile had never been placed face to face with such a possibility.—Mr. Burton contended that an indenture must be for the benefit of the apprentice, and as there was no un- dertaking on the part of Messrs. Mostyn to find any work for these apprentices, the present indenture was invalid. One clause gave the firm power to impose penalties, and this clause made the whole apprenticeship indenture void, for how could these penaliies act but to the prejudice of the apprentice. He quoted neve and clauses in support of his argument. The foreman had also represented that half the Bridge fare would be paid by the complainants, but after the tepee of two or three weeks she had te pay full fare,—The defendant called stated that she had once 31 I stopped for holes made in a piece of cloth although she had not made them. She could not earn the wages stated by the plaintiffs.—Mr Browne, replying to Mr. Burton, said the very terms of the deed implied that work would be found for the defendant to allow her to earn proper wages, and if Mr. Burton's contention was correct it would be utterly impossible to bind an apprentice. He held that the dedoction for wilful damage and damage caused throueb neglect could not be regarded as penalties, and the clause referred to if rigidly carried out would tucks the girls good cutters, and therefore it was beneficent in its effect. If there was any doubt as to how the damage was done the foremen were instructed to give the apprentices the benefit of that doubt. The girls, in particular the defendant, were most generously treated by the complainants—The Chair- man said the case was a very important one, and the Bench wovld adjourn it for a week so that they could fully con- eider their decision.—Mr. Browne said he could not be pre- sent then, but if the decision was against him he wished it to be understood that he should ask for a case to be stated. The fustian cutters in Warrington were greatly interested in it and would no doubt take the question up.

On Thursday morning, at Leek, a gay bachelor, named Lovett, aged 78, was joined in matrimony with a blushing widow., named Johnson, three years his junior, who lost her former spouse only five weeks ago. The Earl of Dalhousie has issued an urgent appeal to members of the House of Lords to support the second read- ing of the Bill for Legalising Marriage with a Devased Wife's Sister, which he intends to move on the 11th June.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Tuesday afternoon the fortnightly meeting of this body was held at Dutton Workhouse, when the chair was occupied by Mr. John Ashton, their being also present Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, and Messrs. Ilandley, Norman, Stokes, Aaron, Mclntyre, Wilkinson, Campkin, Hadfield, Lewis, Arrow- smith, Hall, R. Ashton, Baguley, Fisher, W. Linaker (clerk), and H. W. Linaker (deputy clerk). CORRESPONDENCE.-A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the payment of £35 for the past year's services of the clerk to the School Attendance Committee of the Union. The Local Government Board also wrote under date the 8.11 inst. sanctioning the appoint- ment of Mr. George Ward to the office of retiQving officer for Runcorn district at a yearly salary ef £lOO per annum. —The letters were received without c)nament.

THE SUPERANNUATION OF MR. WRIGHT.— Mr. Handley proposed that the Board grant a superannuation of £65 a year to Mr. Wright, who had served as relieving officer for Runcorn district for over 30 years. That sum was fixed upon a months ago, but it was found out that a month's notice had to be given to every Guardian to m lice it strictly legal. He took it, therefore, that his motion now was merely formal.—Mr. Aaron seconded, and Mr. Norman supported, the resolution.—Mr. Campkin objected to the amount proposed. 'Mr. Wright might be an old servant, and have faithfully fulfilled his duties, but why should they give him such a large amount, if anything at all. Be was a large ratepayer, and represented a township with a large ratable value, and he protested against such an increase of expenditure. He moved that the sum be fixed at M.— Mr. Wilkinson seconded the proposition.—Mr. Handley said that the committee had found that Mr. Wright's salary had been nothing like commensurate with the salaries of the other relieving officers of the Union. Mr. Wright had always been faithful and honest in his duties, ant had given the Board valuable assistance for many years. A large amount of credit must be given to Mr. Wright for his careful investigations, and keeping himself posted in all inattere relating to relief. He thought that he wasspeaking the opinion of the peop:e of Runcorn in saying that they were quite willing that Mr. Wright should have a year.—Mr. Norman supported the original resolution, and Mr. Hadfield also spoke in its favour.—Mr. Mclntyre ob- jected, on principle, te the giving of pensions, but at the same time, in this case, would have liked to have seen the resolution rectived unanimously. He proposed, for the sake of securing a unanimous vote, that the amount allowed be £s2.—Mr. Weir thought that per week would be sufficient.—The Chairman said that the committee ap- pointed for the purpose had recommended the payment of £65 per year, and he thought when they .deferred a ques• tion to a committee they should to some extent be guided by the recommendation of the committee.—Finally. the first amendment was withdrawn, and the second one, that the superannuation be fixed at £53 a year, was carried. This was all the business:

div.head: RURAL SANIIARY AU iLlOaltY.
div.p: RURAL SANIIARY AU iLlOaltY.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr John Ashton presiding, and there being also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. L3ckwood, and Messrs. Weir (vice-chairman), Stokes, Aaron, Mclntyre, Arrowsmith, R. Ashton, I'. Hall, W. Wilkinson, Joseph Knowles, W. H. Ltnaker (clerk), and H. Linaker (deputy clerk)

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Adams reported a case of typhoid fever at Stockton Beath, Appleton. The patient was employed at the Walton Arms, Walton Sup- erior, when she was attacked, and was afterwards removed ho.ne. The cause of the outbreak was in his opinion the very impure drinking water in use at the Walton Arms. This water was analysed in 1884, and was then reported to be "a very bad water, not fit for domestic use," and in spite of such report no steps have haen taken to provide a better supply. The use of the weer should at once be discon- tinued and the well closed. He had visited the patient and given the usual directions as to isolation, disinfection, etc He had also to report a death from typhoid fever at Crow- mere Lake, Frodsham Lordship. The premises were inspected and disinfected, but the source of the disease was not ascer- tained. During April the following deaths from measles oc- curred in the district of the Authority :—llalton 4, Kingsley 4, Five Crosses (Frodsham Lordship) 3, Overton 1, total 12. These, added to the deaths given in the qnarterly re- port, brought the death roll from measles up to 26 for the first four months of the year. He was glad to be able to state that it was his impression, from personal inspection, that the epidemic now appeared to be on the decline. Four cases had occurred in Dutton.—The Deputy Clerk remarked that the report offered a suggestion that the people should drink Wilderspool beer, and Mr. R. Ashton said that he would rather drink the water.—The report Was simply received. TIIE NCISANCE OFF HALTON-ROAD.—The minutes of the Parochial Committee appointed to consider this question were read, and stated that Mr. Aaron bad had an interview with Mr. Smith, wile stated that Major Orred would have no objection to the sewage going in its present course if the Authority would keep the ditch elem. The Rev. J. Lockwood reported that the tenant of land through which the ditch in ques'ion passed had stated to him that he would clean out the ditch on receiving instructions from Major Orred. It was then resolved that a letter be written to Mr. Smith. c.mt doing the information furnished by the Rev. J. Lockwood, and requesting that the necessary in- structions be.given to Mr. Knowles. It was further resolved that the Authority be reco 'linen led to write to the Runcarn die Company and point out that the field that has been recently acquired by the csmp toy for extension of their works is the natural outfall for the sewers from the town- ship of Halton, and the course in which the sewage has , hitherto ti k wed, and that the Authority will require such I initiall to be retained.—The minutes were adopted without discussion.

MiscELLANISOIIS.--It was decided that the seal of the Board he affizod to the contraci for drainage at Overton.— la consequ-nce of some pl ins hiving been sent in too late, it was resolved that in future all plans should be deposited with the inspector not less than seven days before the meet- ing of the Board.—Mr. Farrington, inspector, presented a report upon the pollution of a pond and stream in the town- ship of Whitley Superior, and, after discussion, it was decided that he endeavour to confer with the parties in- terested, with a view of an imp‘ovetnent in its present con- dition being made. This was all the business.
PRESENTAIION TO A WIDNES MANUFACTURER.
UALLA NT CONDUCT.

An interesting presentation took place at the works of Messrs. N. Mathieson ar.d Sons in the presence of the work- men on Saturday. It will be remembered that on the 14th of February Mr. Thomas T. Mathieson leaped into a cistern containig acid liqeor and highly poisonous gas, and res. cued a workman name,' George Roberts,. The man died a day subsequently, but Hr. Mathieson, who was unconscious for upwards of an hour, and for a considerable period was confined to his bed, gradually recovered, and is now fully I reetorad to health. He has been presented with the medal ' of the Humane Society, and the workmen of the firm decided to show their appreciation of his courage and bravery. The testimonial took the form of a beautiful illuminated address, the work of Mr. James Orr Marples, of Liverpool, and this was presented on Saturday by Mr. E. Marston • Mr. L. Ki'cross, in commencing the proceedings, said In this Englandof Ours we had a custom of recording acts of bravery and self-denial no matter by whom such acts were done. Be he peer or peasant, master or man, it was pretty much the same to them so long as the deed was brave and noble, and the end to be otaimil right and true. It did one good even to read of such things whether done in our own 1 time or in the brave old days gone by. but when they were done in their very midst, when a deed of such unselfish heroism was enacted almost before their eyes, there was little wonder that they were met there that day to give ex- pression to their admiration and regard for the man who, at the risk of his own life, so pluckily rushed to the rescue of the poor fellow who had passed away from atnongst- them. That he failed in his generous effort would be proof, if it were needed, of the great danger he himself escaped. He hoped that Mr. Tom would accept the address as the united tribute of the workmen to his manliness and pluck, and that it would come none the less agreeably to him be- cause it had its origin amongst his own wo-kmen, who bad the best opportunity of judging of the gallant conduct that called it forth. (Applause.) Mr. E. Marston then read the address as follows : •• Thos. Train Mathieson, Req., Beechtield, Princess Park, Liverpool. We, the employes of the firm of Messrs. N. Mathieson and Co., of which you are a respected member, desire to express oar admiration of the fearless courage which prompted you on the 14th February last to risk your own life by leaping into a cistern containing dangerous gaseous liquors to rescue George Roberts, one of our fellow- workmen, who had fallen therein, and was already over- come by noxious gases, and whose death we deeply regret resulted the following day, thereby preventing you from experiencing the satisfaction of having saved his life. We congratulate you upen your recovery from the illness con- sequent upon your noble self-sacrificing act, and respect- fully request your acceptance of this address in commem- oration of your heroic conduct. We also take this opportu- nity to thank you for the uninform courtesy and kindness we have invariably received at your bands, and heartily wish you may be spared to live a long and happy life. Wid- nes, A.D. 1885." Mr. Marston accompanied the presentation of the address with a few appropriate remarks. Mr. Mathieson said ha had often declared that nothing would ever induce him to make an attempt at speaking, but he felt he should be wanting in respect if he did not in some way try to thank them for the very kind manner in which they had spoken of his act, and for that handsome testimanial. He assured them he appreciated it very much, and should always look with pleasure upon it as a mark of their respect and esteem. The only thing he had to regret was the d ,ath of one who, in endeavouring to do Ms duty, lost his life. He felt that on that occasion he only did what one man might deserve at the hands of another. He had much pleasure in accepting the testimonial. Mr. Marston said he was sure he was only exprif37l,L; the feeling of all present when he said that under similar cir- cumstances be (Mr. Mathieson) would again go to the rescue of a working-mm who was in danger. (Applause.) 111.0 act was fully appreciated, and would always be held in , grateful remembrance by all of them. (Appleuee ) Mr. Whitley moved a vote of thinks to Mr. Marston for the able manner in which he had presented the address. Mr. J. Calrow seconded the motion, remarking that Mr.l Marston was one of the oldest servants of the firm, and was the confidential officer to Mr. Mathieson. The motion was carried by acclamation, and the pro- ceedings terminated.

fWOMEN'S SUFFRAGE MEETING AT RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the National Society for Womer.4 Suffrage a public meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Memby night. The body of the hall 7719 crowded, and there was a fair number of persons in the gallery. Dr. MacDougall presided, and he was supported on the platform. by Miss Lydia Becker, Miss C. A. Biggs, Mrs. McCormick, the Revs. J. D. ThOM:I9, R. Edwards, Messrs. W. H. Ye/din, J.P. (Conservative candidate for the Northwich Division), Thomas Norman, F. A. Lake, H. Coleburn, J. N. Lello, and J. W. Eightburn. The greatest unanimity prevailed throughout the proceedings, and the addresses of the ladite on "Taxation as it affects women," and " The right of womea ratepayers to vote for mernbas of Parliament," were listened_to with appreciative interest.

The Chairman read letters of apology for absence from the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., and Mr. Rebel t Shaw •, and ob- served that this was the ti St meeting of its kind that had been held in Runcorn, and alteough it was essentially a politica meeting, it was Equally true that it was a non- party one, and he should have the honour of introducing to them two ladies who were closely and hencrarably identified I with objects of philartbropy as well as education. The political question which would be discussed was assuming an acute character, and it must be apeereat to everyone who waiinclined to be a lover of fairulay and freedom that it was rather a curious anomaly that ladies should have been so long deprived of the privilege of voting there sums of money which were so necessary tor the maintenance of the State machinery without at the same time having a voice in its distribution. (Applause.) Miss Beeker, who had a cordial reception, said they had been explaining the question of the admission of women to the Perliarnentary suffrage over the country for many years, and still they found in many mee's minds some doubt as to the precise claim they made. se She wished, therefore, distinctly to state that they were not asking for the franchise for all women, or for any woman, merely be- cause she was a woman. All they asked was that when a woman was a householder, a ratepayer, and a taxpayer, in- dependently, and on her own account, she should not be de- prived of the privilege of the franchise because she was a wom tn. (Applause.) Within the last twenty years the country had been nuking advanc-s towards the cendition of things by which every householder was to be represented in Parliament. The first step to tbat was made in 1867 by the Reform Bill passed by Lord Derby's Government. That established the principle of household suffrage, bat its prac- tical application was by no means uraiversed. Even in boroughs, where it was supposed to prevail, there were, as a matter of fact, households unrepresented. Perhaps if Mr. Disraeli had been in power when the County Franchise ; Bill, last session, was passed, he might have thought that was the right opportunity—of which he had recently spoken—to take for making the principle universal. The present Government brought in a bill to extend the prin- ciple of the household suffrage to the counties. They asked them to make the bill complete by including every tax- payer, and the head of every household, whether that head was a man or a woman. (Heir, hear.) But the Govern- ment were afraid that the men might lose their votes if there was a little delay, so they said it would endanger the votes of the men if they allowed the women to have their votes too ; and under thit excuses they said to the women, " Stand aside; let the men householdere have their votes before we begin to think of you." They were puebed aside last session, and the men were now in possession of their votes. As a woman householder, she said she was in the same pose, tion as these men were before the last Reform Bill. She wanted the vote for the same reason as they wanted the vote. She objected as much as they objected to be taxed without being represented. She objected as much as they objected to seeing her neighbours on either hind in pos- session of a privilege for which they paid no more than she did, and to be denied that privilege. (Applause.) The in- justice of the exclusion of women householders from the franchise had been greatly intensified by the service fran- chise of the last Reform Bill, by which a lady owning an estate and paying taxes was forbidden to vote, while her stable boy, eh° slept in a loft, maybe, was to have a vote because he slept in a tenement that belonged to a lady owning the very estate. The anomaly was so great that she thought it had simply to be placed before the common sense of Englishmen for them te say that it was unjust and injurious (Applause.) It was not only the want of direct represtntation, but the anomaly cast a kind of slight on the intelligence and public spirittof women. Minors, idiots, , criminalsawnodmefA er Criminal eai w disfranchised,hen e et at t liberty r nt ye nNev was allowed o m l e t teol ye as ercise the franchise. A minor when be came of age was en- franchised; and if, in a lucid interval, a lunatic WAS cap- able of knowine what he wag doing, be could have his vote; bat the law never allowed a women to have a lucid interval in which she was sufficiently ColitpOs MC /Iti3 to vote. (Laughter and applause.) Alluding to the heaviness of the iajustice, Miss Becker pointed out that the number of I women-farmers within the decade 1861 to 18S1 bad diminished from 22,00 to 2.0,000. That was easily tic- counted for. It was the habit of most landlords that when a nun died and the widow ctuld have car tied on the farm they turned out the widow because they would have their farms represented by votes. She thought that was a very natural wish on the part of the landlord, and one which he might reasonably entertain without expecting to exercise any undue influence on the minds ef his tenants, because it did give his property and his estate a certain measure of importance to have it represented by as many votes as there were farms, the woman was, theerefo7e, turned eat, net because she could not !am, but because she could not vote. She, therefore, lost her borne; and any capital which her husband might have put in the land in his lifetime was last, and the woman and her children reduced to comparative penury. (Applause.) That fact alone ought to be suffi- cient to remove the injurious disability. The speaker alluded to the Married Woman's Property Act as a great boon, because by it a married women had been raised from a chattel to a person. (Applause.) Women, she argued, had just as much right as men to say whether the Church of England shculd be disestablished. She knew some Liberals who bad been earnestly in favour of disestablish- ment, including the late Professor Fawcett; and he said he would rather never see disestahlishment at all should the law be enacted without consulting the wishes of the women as well as of the men. She held that women were of suffi- cient intellectual capacity to exercise the franchise, while their admissim to the full rights of ceizenshie she believed would amalgamate beth parties. The Liberal party had pretty nearly accomplished all that they had been strug- gling for, and both sides, she thought, might now unite at Conservatives to conserve the liberties of the people which bad been so widely extended. She appealed to the men recently admitted to the franchise not to rest until they' bad given the boon of enfranchisement to their asters, and to the women householders all over the country. (tee- plause.)—Mr. Verdin, who Was received with applause, moved "that in the opinion of this meeting women who Possess the qualification for the parliamentary suffrage should no longer be denied the right to vote." He felt, he said, that the wotnen of ttes country bad not had full jus- tice done to them, and he thought they ought to ltel very much indebted to Miss Becker for advocating, the rights of her fellow women. It was hit pleasure to know many ladies who were qualified to take part in pirliamentary elections, and wherever the greateet civilieation existed there they would had the greatest honour paid to women. Personally, he was sorry that during the last session it was not considered desirable to introduce a clause in the Fran- chise Bill which would enable women to take part in par- liamentary elections. He was all the more suprisel be- cause they had evideece in the result of the voting that then took place that not only many Liberals but also a great number of Conservatives were willing to grant this privilege. Mr. J. N. Lello seconded the resolution, observing that anyone who had studied the question must be impressed with the thought that for a long time a very great injus- tice had been done to women. (Applause.) Mist Riggs supported the resolution. She pointed Out that the power to vote was only taken away from woman by asked to return to the time when women, the Court of Common Pleas about 16 years ago, and that householders, only had the power to exercise the fran- wthheoy were were chise. She contended that women who paid taxes were fully entitled to the franchise. (Applause.) She asked these who had recently been ad- mitted to the franclaite to say that they would no longer enjoy a privilege which was not theirs unjustly, but which was as equally justly the privilece of women; and with the force which the newly-acquired vote had given them, get Parliament to piss a measure which should meet the just claims of women householders. (Applause.) The resolution WAS then put to the meeting, and unani- mously carried. Mr. F. A. Like then moved a reset utien ha the effect that petitions to both Houses of Patilament, in support of the former reeolution, be adopted and signed by the Chairman i on behalf of that meeting, and theta memorial be forwarded to the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton and Piers Egerton Ware burton, Esq.. members for Mid-Cheshire, recteesting them to support a bill entitled " A Bill to extend the Paaliementary Franchise to Women." The speaker thought it was a groes mistake to suppose that women were to some extent inferior to men. If men were stronger than women in body, had it never struck them that women were superior to men in many other matters? As Miss Biggs had pained out, it was the combined work of the two sexes which would make the natein what it should be. Ho thought that Teneyson itt "The Prinbess " had beautifully described what should be the aim of the two when he said:— Toe man be more of woman, she of man ; He gain tn sweetness and in moral hei,,kt. Nor lose the wrestling thews that throw ths world ; She mental breadth, nor fait in chili:tweed cue, Nor lose the childlike in the larger mind Till at the lest she set herself to man. Llke perfect music unto nabie wordy. (Applause.) • ee, Rev. J. D. Thomas supported the resolution. The resolution was also supported by tee Rev. 13. Edwards and the Rev. Wm. Prestos. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mica Becker moved that a vets of thanke tre Parsed to tee chairman, at the same time expressing her Creeks to the audience for be kind reception which they had given to herself and Miss Biggs. William Hulmes, Earlestown, was summoned for being drunk on the 4th inst., and was fined 5s and costs.—Wil- Ham Green, of Earlestown. for beng drusk and disorderly at Havelock os the 26 h nit., was fined 5a and costs.—James Littler was summoned 40-r being drunk and disorderly at Golborne on the 2nd inst. Two persons, a roan and a boy, were killed at Leeds on Wednesday by the accidental discharge of firearms. Mr. Isaac Hoyle, who has been chosen as the Liberal can- didate for the Heywood Parliamentary division, attended a Public meeting on Thursday night at Heywood Reform Club. He had an enthusiastic reception. BOILER EXPLOSION IN t'COTIAND.-011 Tuesday one of the four egg-ended boilers at Auldton Colliery, eight miles from Hamilton, exploded, killing one man and injuring five others. The miners were being wound up the shaft at the time, and the pithead erections were completely wrecked. A passenger train on the Caledonian Railway passed just be- fore the explosion. THE DISPUTE IN THE YORKSHIRE COAL TIRADE. At Barnsley, on Monday, a lara:ely attended conference of miners was held to couside, the present state cl affairs in the Yorkshire coal trade. The delegates expressed theit determination to resist the reduction of 10 per cent. in waged, but stated their willingness to submit the question to arbitration, and the secretary to the conference was I instructed to write to this effect to the Employers' As !octagon. At a meeting at Barnsley, on Tuesday, attended by 15,000 miners, a resolution in favour of continuing the resistance to the reduction in wages was carried unani- -11201151Y. Ths Barnsley to ,gistrates on Wednesday issue' warrants of ejectment against over 30 miners occupy ing cottages at Carlton Main Colliery. The Yorkshire Miners' Association and the Central Strike Committee will provide houses for those evicted. At Carlton Main, near Barnsley on Thursday, the oecuparss of 27 houses owned by the col- liery company were ejected by the police, acting under war- rants recently obtained In connection with the strike of South Yorkshire miners it is confidently believed that a set tlernent of the dispute will not long be delayed. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at th Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Brown, Appleton, Ratcliffe, William Houghton, Mackie, Hunt, Jolley, Darbyshire, Greenall, John Houghton, Balharry, Harrison, Blackhurst, Broadbent, Greening, Jeans, Borman, Grange, Gibson, and J. C. Button (clerk). Mr. Henley, Local Government Board Inspector, was also present.

div.head: MB H01:19i COMMITTBH.
div.p: MB H01:19i COMMITTBH.
The minutes of this committee stated that Mr. Brown had been re-electsd chairman of the committee, and that their meetings should be held as heretofore, on the Friday.of each week.

THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee mentioned that the Rev. G. F. Roberts had been appointed chairman and Mr. Green- ing vice-chairman. The gentlemen, in accepting their re- spective posts, expressed regret at the retirement of Mr. Darbyshire tram the chairmanship of the committee The committee had decided that in any case of infectious disease, however slight the infection might be, the linen and clothing.of the children infected should be thoroughly cleansed and disinfected, and not used or brought into con- tact with other apparel until so cleansed and disinfected.— Mr. DABBYSHIRE asked if there had been some case of infec- tion which had led to these precautions being ordered?— The CLERK said the subject would be brought up subse- quently by Mr. Henley, and any discussion on that matter had batter be left over.—Mr. BROADBENT wished to know if it was a usual thing for the chairman of the Beard to be appointed chairman of any committee. At the same time he did not think the committee could have a better chair- man than Mr. Roberts.—The CHAIRMAN said he put forward that objection at the meeting, but the clerk considered it was quite a proper arrangement.—The CLERK pointed out that the Mayor of Warrington was chairman of the Watch I Committee, and that there were certain committees over I which it was a convenience for the chairman to preside.— Mr GREENING mentioned that the present Mayor of War- rington was chairman of three committees.—Mr. BROAD- ! Birarr 'hoped the chairman of the Board would not be too I lenient in regard to the chairman of the Schools Com- mittee. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—The minutes were then confirmed.

SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. This committee reported that Mr. Blackhurst had been re-elected chairman of this committee. Seventy-three oases of relief had been dealt with, 11 of which were new and 62 old.—Confirmed.

div.p: RAISING TRH SPIRITS.

_ A letter was read from Messrs. G. and J. Greenall, spirit merchants, stating that the Chancellor of the Exchequer in his budget having increased the duty on British and foreign spirits 2a. per gallon, they begged to announce that they had consequently been compelled to advance the price of duty-paid spirits.—Tbe CHAIRMAN: That does not affect. us.—Mr. HARRISON: It affects us individually. (Laugh- ter.)—Dr. MACKIE thought from what appeared in that morning'slSapers that the tax of spirits nould not be en- forced. Rethought Messrs. Greenall had better wait for a week before they gave them any decided answer. If there was to be no war there would be no necessity for putting on that tax, and the general opinion was that neither the beer nor spirit tax would be imposed.—Mr. Joust pointed out that the Board were supplied under a contract. —The _dia- -1 cussion then dropped. THE WORKHOUSE Dm &c. - -

The CLERK reiTa.r-eiu—rn which 13;c1 been prepared at the request o Mr. Henley, in which particulars were given as to the consumption of spirits, Jo.' and the dietary ar- rangements.—Mr. HENLEY explained that his object in having that report was that they might have some informa- tion as to what was going on in the workhouse with refer- ence to the use of spirits and extra diets. He was glad to see that no extra allowances were made to the inmates who did such work as they were able to do. He thought it was also of importance that they should know what the cost of the officers rations were in the workhouse, and it was of more importance now that superannuation grants were not only based on the officers' salariea but also on the allow- ances, including attendants, rations, ctc. (Hear, hear.) It was also desirable to know the cost of the wines and spirits, and other such-like things that were consumed in the work- house, and the price of beer per gallon, which he found to vary very much at different workhouses. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: FAVOURABLE REPORT.
div.p: A FAVOURABLE REPORT.

It was stated that the result of the recent examinations of the echools by the Government inspector, Mr. Moseley, had been that he bad reported a very considerable progress upen last year's work. In the girls' department 49 were presented for examination, all of whom passed successfully, 34 of them passing in all subjects. Religions knowledge and singing were very fair, and needlework good. In the boys' schmol 90 were presented for examination, and of these 73 passed successfully, 37 having passed in all subjects. Religious knowledge was fair ; singing, band performance, and drill being good. The inspector considered the intel- ligence in the upper standards in both schools to be very fair.
THE PADGATE SCHOOLS.-SERIOUS STRICTURES BY THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INSPECTOR.

Mr. HENLEY (the Local Government Board Inspector) said that the last time he met the Guardians be promised that if he found anything wrong in any of their establish- ments he would as soon as possible let them know. In con- sequence of a report he had bad from his friend and col- league, Mr. Stephens, he visited the schools at Padgate, and he thought the state of the schools merited the very serious attention of the Guardians. There was no doubt that the Guardians acted most wisely in building that excellent es- tablishment upon a most splendid site ; and in endeavour- ing to remove the children from contact with adult pauper- ism. According to all modern Ideas they had acted wisely, but there were two things he should like to mention. The I first was that the children were not removed from contact with pauperism, and the second was that there was a considerable amount of eruption in the school which had existed for a vary considerable time. They first of all must understand what WAS the meaning of the eruption he was speaking of. The Medical Officer re- ported at the beginning of this year that the children were suffering from itch, and from that time up to the time he (the inspector) visited the schools they had been suffering from itch. Bat first of all with regard to the quasi-paupers in the school, he found that they bad four persons in that school wholly occupied with matters in the school who had cattail:4y been paupers, and were still to all intents and purposes quasi-paupers, although they got a small amount per week to make them coverable servants. First of all they kept a carpenter there, and he asked if it was neces- I sary that they should keep an estate carpenter which they I all knew was a very expensive thing even when there was plenty ot work to do' and as a general rule it Was far more economical to employ a proper tradesman to do the work. At any rate he was really displacing the labour of another who worked for his own thine' and paid rates. (Hear, hear.) He then referred to each of the other paupers engaged in the schools, and advised the committee to carefully consider the question, and if necessary to engage properly paid persons to do the work. Coming to the mast important part of the question, that was the question of itch, he found that from the beginning of the year up to the time he was at the schools the children had been sufferiug more or less from this disease, and he found in the Medical Officer's book an astounding entry made in February, to the effect that the children were suffering from chilblains, and that "as usual in the spring season itch had made its appearance amongst the girls." He (air. Henley) did not think there was anyone of the Guardians prepared to have the schools stamped with such a descrip- tion as that—that itch was to make its appearance every year among the girls. They all knew that itch was a thing that if properly attended to could be eradicated at once. Surely the Guardians, after having gone to all the expense they had done to establish those beautiful schools, were not prepared to let such a thing stand as that year after year itch was to be the experience of the children. Such a thing had never occurred to him in his experience, and he was quite sure that if in other parts of his district such an entry bad been made the Guardians would have been perfectly horrified at seeing it. It was an entry which could not stand any scrutiny. He asked what means were taken to blot out the disease ? He said no moans were taken. And what steps were taken to prevent the spread of the disease ? Were the clothes properly cleansed, and the blankets and beds turned out and every means 'taken to get rid of the insect? Nothing of the sort. The girls seemed to be washing in the ordinary course, and the boys were wearing the same jackets and trousers they had on during the whole time they had the itch. It was a won- der to him that every child and every officer in the school had not got the disease. Mr. Ilonley then proceeded to crit- icise the arrangements of the hospital at the schools, and pointed out that it was not being used for the purpose for which it was built. They had provided, he said, all the means of isolation, and all that was wanted, if he might be permitted to say so, was the exercise of common sense. What would any of them think if in their own families the children who were suffering from infections disease were permitted to herd among the healthy. (Hear, hear.) lie could only find in the Medical Officer's book one recoin- mendation to do anything, and that was to USP a little lime. If the medical officer thought he was going to get rid of that disease by the ule of a little lime be was certainly a more sanguine man than he (Mr. Henley) was himself. At the same time a very little care would get rid very rapidly of the disease, and be knew perfectly well that itch ought not for one moment be allowed to enter their schools. They had special facilities for the prevention of infectious cases getting into the schools ; they had no conflict of opinions between medical officers, as all their arrangements were in the hands of one officer, and it was entirely in his hands whether or not he removed persons to the schools or kept them at the workhouse in probation. He then called the attention of the Board to directions sent out by the Local Government Board as to the methods of dealing with such cases as he bad referred to, and again impressed upon them the necessity of isolating children when searing aed the same should be done even if there was any doubt as to infection. Referring to the doctor's visits to the schools, he said he did not think that while the children were suffAring from itch one visit in the week was anything like sufficient. lie considered that a medical officer of a school Should have I his whole heart interested in keeping that school a model for ether schools in the neighbourhood. If he knew that a child was suffering from disease he should not be there once a week, but once a day. He did not think a visit once a aveek was anything like sufficient, and he asked the medical officer until that disease of itch was eradicated to attend the school daily. In conclusion he called the attention of the committee to the defective state of the yard at the schools,—ThoCumnuarr said they were obliged to Mr

Henley for triaging these matters before them in the man- ner be had done. Some of the charges were very serious, and be thought they had perhaps better ask their medical officer what he had to say.—Mr. BROADBENT said they had been painfully intereeted in what Mr. Henley had told them. He had thrown a flood of light on many points which be (Mr. Broadbent) was stare would not be lost on the Board or the committee. But the question he wished to ask was with regard to the clothing of the children. They had suffered very seriously from chilblains, and they would remember he had suggested in the winter that the children should have some woollen clothing instead of being entirely confined to cotton and fustian. What he wished to ask Mr. Henley was what in his large experience he had found to be the best clothing for preventing that very pain- ful disease of chilblains.—Dr. SPINES (the medical officer) said with regard to the itch mentioned in his report book, he made that entry when there were three or four cases.

It was their experience there, as it was the experience of medical merrall over the world, that itch was more preva- lent in the spring of the year that at any other time. And with regard to his treatment of the disease, when Dr. Monet visited the sckools he found that he (Dr. Spinks) had used the very thing he himself approved of—that was a lotion that was used in the army. One or two applications of that lotion destroyed all the insects, and he ventured to say that there was not a single insect in the whole schools that morning. The druggist who at present eupplied the schools had not known how to make that lotion, and be sent for it to London. When it was used, however, it was found to do no good, and he (Dr. Spinks) asked to see it. He found it was of no earthly use and in fact was not the same thing at all. He then went to the druggist and give him a description of how it was made, and since then the lotion had been all right.—ln answer to a question, Dr. SPINES said they had been using a useless lotion for two months. He had, however, been at the schools the previous day, and found that the proper lotion had completely killed the insects. This lotion never required more than one or two applications. The reason why he did not use the hospital was that there was not a proper atten- dant, and there had been several narrow escapes through the children's clothes catching fire. Unless there was a proper nurse to look after the children, it was dangerous to let them go to ,the hospital. As to the other arrangements of the hospital which Mr. Henley had complained of, he did not know they had been made.—Mr. HARRISON: I sup- pose you were in the habit of walking through the hospital? —Dr. SPINES: About once a month I went through the various rooms. And as to hit attendances when he was ap- pointed it was agreed that be should visit once a week..... Mr. HENLEY: You stand upon that; that ills only your duty to go there once a week?—Dr. SPINES: Yes, unless there is something required.—Mr. HENLEY said he should like to aek the doctor why he bad not called the attention of the committee to the want of a proper nurse at the hospital.—Dr. SPINES said he had several times ; but he had not put anything in his report book about it.—Mr. HENLEY said that book had by the Local Government Board been specially ordered that the medical officer might enter in it what he considered necessary' and thus prevent disputes as to what he had recommended, and if the matter was not mentioned in that book be warenot to come there and say he had reported the matter azain and again to the committee. He (Mr. Henley) asked where was it in that book ? If it was not entered in that book the blame rested with the medical officer.—Dr. Senors : I know that very well.—Mr. HENLEY said it was a remarkable fact that not until Mr, Stephens and himself had ascertained what was going OD had those children been so speedily cured. But if they had been so speedily cured last week why were they not speedily cured last January? It was the doctor's boun- den duty to see that they were cured, and it only made the matter ten times worse to say that they had not had the proper material to care them with. Then with regard to the clothes, the medi- cal officer did not mean to say that when a person had been suffering from itch it was not necessary to disin- fect their clothes ?—Dr. SPINES : Ido not.—Mr. HENLEY said that if be did, and. if he was like every other medical man in England, he should certainly say he was wren. With regard to Vie question as to the chilblains, he cer- tainly never saw children in a more sad state with regard to chilblains. They were so bad that it made him almost doubt whether they were chilblains or not. They appeared more of the nature of a scabby disease. There was no doubt that the two hest remedies to prevent chilblains were woollen clothing and plenty of exercise. The children eaght to be encouraged to take as much ex- ercise as they Properly could, to be In the sun, and to take part in gymnastics. There was a certain class of children, those of torpid circulation, Who were more apt to suffer from them than ethers, but he had never seen children in any school suffer so much from chilblains as the children in these schools.— Dr. SPINES said that instead of playing the children stood shivering about.—Dr. lalecnre said he had listened to Mr. Henley's common-sense remarks with deep pain, and the consternation that would be felt outside when they got into print would be greater than they could well conceive. They had spent £lO,OOO or £15,000 on these schools, and they had had meetings without end during the last two or three years on purpose to make them as comfortable as possible, and he had no doubt that all those things which were for the embel- .. .

lishment of the schools had been thoroughly well attended to. He was of opinion that unless they put a proper gov- ernor over that ineitution, or made the governor of the workhouse governor of the schools, they should constantly be open to derelictions of duty and oversights, to use no stronger terms, and they should never have that comfort they expected from those schools. He wanted to ask their opinion whether it would not be well for them at once to arrange that the governor of the workhouse should take such supervision of the schools as be took of that house.— The CHAIRMAN said that matter was scarcely before them.— Mr. BLACKHURST considered that it was a question entirely for the Guardians to deal with.—Dr. Mame said he wanted Mr. Henley's opinion as to the working of such an arrange- ment. If it were necessary they could connect the two places by telephone.—Mr. Menne said he should advise the Guardians not under any circumstances to put the mas- ter of the werkhouse in connection with the schools. There was first of all what might, perhaps, be called a sentimental reasoa, that it was best to entirely sever the children from adult pauperism; and there was atother practical consi- deration of greater weight, that the master of the workhouse should have no excuse for being absent from the work- /house. The less he was absent from the workhouse the better, and he thought under no circumstances should the Guardians allow the master of the workhouse to undertake duties outside the workhouse. (Hear, heir.) At the same time NI did think that there was required a stronger management by the superintendent and the matron of the schools. but he did not see that that was any mason why the echoelmaster should not be able to exercise control over an establishment of such limited extent, and there was no reason whatever why the matron should not have ample time to look after the_establishment. Whether they had performed their duties sufficiently he was hardly prepared to say, but his own opinion was that they had not. There had been a weak management, and he should warn them to be more careful, vigilant, and discriminating in the care of children. As he had said before, they must use more Corn. man sense. If a schoolmaster could not look after the health of the children as well as look after the teaching, the sooner he made way for somebody who would do it the better.— Mr. DARBISHIRE (the late chairman of the Schools Com- mittee) then gave an account of how the " quasi- pauper " inmates came to be eent to the schools. He agreed with Mr. Henley that the itch cases should have been better attended to, as they had seldom been entirely clear of them. He had, however, a very poor opinion of the hospital, and he thought it would be better to bring patients to the workhouse hospital. It was, be said, the wish of the committee that She schools should be kept in first-class order and reputation —Mr. JEANS thought that if patients were brought to the work- house they would frustrate the whole object for which the schools had been built, that was to keep the children iso- lated from the workhouse.—Mr. APPLETON referred to the case of one of the pauper women at the schools, named Parkes, who, be said, had been compelled to come to the workhouse through having fits. She was a respectable woman and a good seamstress, and it had been thought that she would be of more use at the schools than at the work- house.—Mr. JOLLEY thought the mistake the Guardians had made was in having sent paupers to the schools.—Mr. HAR- RISON hoped the Guardians would not hold their bands till a thorough reparation of the defects mentioned by Mr. Hen- ley had been made —Mr. BROWN was not at all surprised to hear the report Mr. Henley had given them. For a long time he had not been satisfied with the management of the schools, and he bad been of opinion that stronger manage- ment was required.—Mr. BLACIIHURST scarcely understood the remarks of Dr. Mackie and Mr. Brown, and thought they were very unfair to Mr. and Mrs Mines. If those gentlemen bad charges against Mr. Mines why had they not brought them openly before the Board Dr. MACKIE and Mr. Bnowar both repudiated having alleged anything against Mr. or Mrs. Minea—The CHAIRMAN said Mr Mines had always en- deavoured to carry out in the best way be could any sug- oreetion on the part of the committee He thought Mr. Henley's remarks rather had reference to the medical treatment of the schools.—Mr. HENLEY said that as regarded the superintendent he could not altogether acquit him of blame for the state of the establishment. They must make the bead of an establishment responsible, or discipline would be at an end—khear, hear)—and he hoped that now Mr. Mines would look after the establishment as a superin- tendent as well as a schoolmaster. Mr. Henley then again impressed upon the Guardians the necessity of removing pau- pers from the schools, and said that all that had been stated Only confirmed his opinion as to the necessity of doing that. He was also of opinion that the staff might be reduced as the work that was to be done did not seem to require the number of persons they had engaged. In answer to the Chairman, Mr. Henley said he did not see the use of the doctor visiting the schools more than once a week in the absence of disease, but they should regulate a matter of this kind by the custonas of private life. If they had no disease they did not want a doctor, but in the case of an es- tablishment of this kind it was beet that visits should be made even when there was no disease, and that every child should be examined as to the absence or otherwise of dis- ease.—Mr. Appttrote said it was only fair to the doctor to mention that they had not had a death for six years at the SClaool9.—The CHAIRMAN said he could assure Mr. Henley that the matters be had brought before the Board should re- eler(' their attention.—The discussion then dropped.

I they were disclosed in favour of the Guardians. (Hear, I hear.) The representatives of the Newton Commissioners preferred to call no witnesses, although they had six In attendance. The costs had since been taxed at one-balf on the amount of costs that was prepared by the registrar of , the court as between party and party. Referring to a ! statement made at the last meeting of the Newton Commis- sioners, he (the Clerk) said the case did not come off on a Itechnical point. They bad been required to meet the case of the opposite side,and their counsel preferred to speak for one hour and forty minutes in opening the case, and not to call a single witness on the merits. Their counsel could therefore not examine, but he (the Clerk) knew Mr. Jeans was prepared with proof had the case been dis- cussed either on its legal points or merits.—Mr. Jima hay. lug briefly referred to the case, Mr. DARBYSTIMB expressed ! the opinion that Mr. Jeans deserved the thanks of the Board 1 for the way in which he had conducted the case.—The : CgAtingarr moved that Mr. Jeans be paid the amount of 1 the taxed costs, and theta vote of thanks be accorded him. ! —This motion was seconded by Mr. BnowN, and supported 1 by Messrs. Bonnell, Appleton, and Harrison, and carried.— Mr. JBLNS, in responding, said he was convinced that the 1 Newton Commissioners never had any claim against them either legally or morally. The letter they produced from Mr. Sutton was simply expressing Mr. Sutton's own indi- -1 , vidual opinion as to a course ot action which the Board , might take, but that letter was never intended to be a con- tract, and it was monstrous ever to bring it forward as such. , —1r133 CLIMIC explained that had they gone into the Case ' on its merits, he should have shown by the correspondence ' and legal business of the very same year in which the let- ter was written, that it was never intended to have such an effect—This concluded the business.

-- The professional element in the North appears likely to maintain its ascendancy over the South if the North and South Colts' match can be accepted as a guide in this direc- tion. Yorkshire supplied the greatest run-getters in the persons of Preston and Nicholson. The former was also successful as a bowler, taking five wickets for twelve runs.

The first of the Lancashire trial matches is now con- cluded, and an estimate can be formed of the talent existing In the northern part of the county. Some fair batsmen were found, but none of such excellence as to make their inclusion in the county team certain. C. Billington and the Rev. Mr. Baines appeared to most advantage in this respect. In G. Bigg a promising bowler was found, as he took six wickets in the first innings for 45 runs. It is disap- pointing to hear that the Barrow public evidenced little in- terest in the match, which was very poerlv attended on both days. The county cannot be said on this occasion to have played its full strength, and it will be noted that Crossland was very little called on, Watson and Barlow doing nearly all that was needed in the bowling department. Robinson confirmed the previous impression that he is in good batting form this season.

At the present time, when nearly everyone is talking of the "money-grabbing " propensities of the Australian team which visited England last summer, it will be interesting to know that although the colonists netted large sums, they were by ne means the only ones who re iped substantial benefits. All their opponents in this country received great help, and none more so than the M.C.C. and Surrey. The annual meeting of the M.C.C. has just been held, and the year's balance sheet showed that the gross receipts were £15,065 Is 3d, as against £ll,OOO 18s 94 obtained by the Surrey Club. These figures tell eloquently of the interest in the national game. So far as the "gate" was concerned, the Oval took over £9.948 against £4,464 at Lord's, but ,he M.C.C. had a subscription list of £8,453 163, which perhaps in a great measure accounts for the difference.

CHERTISAM HILL V. WAIIIIINGTON.—Thie match was played at Cheatham Hill on Saturday, and resulted in a draw. A late start was made owing to heavy rain, and several showers stopped the progress of the game. The home team won the toss, and commenced with Harper and Beesten to the bowling of the brothers Lawton. Beeston gave an easy chance to Fairclough, and gave way to Heap. The t.atsmen played steadily, and the score rose to 52. At this point Armstrong Smartly removed the bails, and Harper was out for 30. Bleakley came next, and commenced with a few fluky hits, but settled down and bit heavily. Denton secured Heap at slip, left hand high up, and Morgan came in. A heavy shower came on, and bowling was difficult. Morgan contributed singles, and in trying to run a second run from a long hit to the on was run out by a smart re- turn by Clarke. Up to this time, Jolley, Denton. and the Lawtons had bowled, of whom Jolley had been the most successful. J. C. Lawton changed ends and runs came slowly. At 97 Bleakley hit up to cover point and was accepted ; Holt was bowled ; and two runs later Perrin was sent back by a bailer. Wallington was put on, and bowled two maidens to commence with. Swallow let out to leg, and hit him over the boundary for six, but was neatly taken by Denton next ball. Both Barnes and Firth had near escapes of run out, and soon after were secured by Hind and Kidmain respectively. J. C. Lawton obtained five wickets for 33 runs, and Wallington two for 17. Arm- strong was very smart behind the wickets, no byes being registered. Warrington commenced with Fairclough and Wallington, the Cheetham pros. bowling Fairclough cat twice for twos, and drove hard for four from Barnes' first over. Wallington was taken by a yorker, and Fairclough was caught from a high hit over the bowler. Harper from mid-cn ran round and secured an excellent catch. Clarke and Denton were now together, but rain interfering the players ran to shelter. Clarke cut Firth for four, and bit him to leg for a similar number, while Denton cut Barnes beautifully twice to the boundary. Clarke gave way to C. G. Lawton, and now was seen the best cricket of the after- noon. Both batsmen hit freely at loose bowling, but in defence they were very strong. Swallow, Heap, and Perrin were tried, but all to no purpose. Barnes and Firth were again put on, but at time the batsmen were still together. Denton's defensive play was much admired, while Lawton played freely in a taking style. OHEHTFIAM HILL.
