DYNAMITE 14-APIASIO NS. TRIALS OF PRISONERS. At Salisbury, on ISlondly, Richard Holloway and William Clarke were charged with participation in various explo- &MlS. Mr. C. Matthews, who represented the Treasury, stated that against Holloway they had evidenc3 that he had been connected with six successful explosions, or with the manufacture of explosives for that purpose, and to the majority of these be had confessed. The explosions were at Salisbury, on the Herbert Statue and council chamber at Warminster Town Hall, and three at Andover. Holloway had obtained the sabstances to make the explosives from a London chemist, and had induced Clarke to use them. Wit- nesses, including a servant girl who formerly lived at tho house of Holloway's mother, were called to prove the pos- session by Holloway of tins, piping. and wick discovered at the scenes of the eutrages. Both prisoners were committed for trial.

The trial of Burton and Cunningham for treason-felony and minor offences connected with dynamite explosions at Westminster, the Tower, and other parts of Londou, was' commenced at the Central Court, London, on Monday, be- fore Mr. Justice Hawkins. The prisoners pleaded not guilty.—The Attorney-General said the charge of treason- felony fell little short of high treason, except that it re- moved it from the category of capital crimes. He narrated the circumstances of the arrival in London of both pri- soner,, and traced their movements and communications with each other.—Mr. Hart, station master at Paddington, and other witnesses, gave evidence of finding in the cloak- room, just after the Victoria Station explosion, 45 cakes of dynamite in a portmanteau and a detonator with a pistol at-, tached.—Other witnesses described the clockwork and dyn- amite discovered at Charing Cross Station and similar dis- coveries at other railway stations.—Robert Thomas, licensed porter, Southampton. proved seeing Burton land at South- ampten. Witness accompanied him to buying two bags, one of which was that found at Charing Cross.— Mr. Bennett, who sold the bag produced, identified it, and also Burton, who wore a coat • with patu- liar buttons, which was found packed in the bag with the dynamite.—The case was adjourned.—On Tuesday the Attorney-General said he understood from Mr. Little that he had been unable to see the prisoner Burton for con- sultation except in the presence of a warder. He thought there could be no objection to the relaxation of the general rule —His Lordship said that the application must ito made to the Home Secretary. It was necessary that there should be very stringent rules.—William Wall was then called, and spoke to Burton having called at his shop at Southampton to have the portmanteau which he bought at another shop repaired. The portmanteau was the one found at Charing I Cross Station.—Kate Biddleconabe spoke to the arrival of Burton and two other men at Day's Hotel, Southampton, on February 20th, 1834.—William Taylor (tailor) proved that trousers in Burton's possession were of the same serge as a pair found in the portmanteau deposited at Charing Cross Station.—Henry Weeks, police officer, New York, stated that be was employed to watch the arrival of the French ship Laurent, which reached New York from Havre on the 131 of March last year. The prisoner Burton arrived be' that vessel.—Robert Levy (a boy) and P.C. King spoke to finding a bag containing dynamite at the foot of the Nelson column on May 30th last year.—Cross-examined, King stated that he saw nothing of the prisoners in the vicinity on that occasion.—Evidence having been given as to the explosion, Mr. Little submitted that the evidence as to the explosion last year was not proof of a conspiracy on the prisoners' part.—Mrs. Elliott, of Limehouse, spoke to Bur- ton having lodged ot her house from May 28th till Septem- ber. He then left and returned again at Christmas.—Two witnesses deposed to Burton having been employed as a joiner at Limehouse from May till September, and to his possession of a brown American box.—Evidence was next given as to the arrival of Cunningham at Liverpool in the Adriatic from New York on the 20th December. He had an American trunk similar to that produced. He left for London and arrived at Broad-street Station on December 24th, tak- ing the box with him. He lodged in Mitre-square from December 26th to January 10th.—P.S Crawford believed he saw Cunningham, Burton, and another alight from the train at Gower-street, but he would not swear to Burton.— P.C. Roper watched Burton leave Mitre-square on Janu- ary 10th and proceed to Aldgate Station. Afterwards he met Barton and Cunningham coming together from White- chapel. On Wednesday a statement made 43, Burton at Row- street was read, in which the prisoner said he had never met Cunningham until he saw him in the dock at Bow- street. Several witnesses, including the landladies with whom Burton and Cunningham lodged in the East End, described the movements of the prisoners and the removal of trunks, Ac., at different dates. Others proved that Cun- ningham was in the Banqueting Hall of the Tower just before the explosion ad was stopped and questioned at the gate, where he was arrested. The case was again ad- journed. On Thursday, Inspector JdrVill deposed to his interroga- tion of Cunningham at the Tower after the explosion and to finding a detonator in his box. He traced the American trunk to Burton's lodgings. Sergeant Cole, who was in- jured in the Westminster Hall,described the sin and ap- pearance of the package of explosives found there. Col. Majendie said atlas powder was of no commercial use in this country, and could not be imported without license ; neither could detonators. He described the means employed to cause the various explosions. The trial was again ad- journed.
TIIE LIBERATDN SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the above society was held on Wednesday evening at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, under the presidency of the Hon. E. Lyulph Stanley, M.P. ; and amongst those present were Sir R. A. Cunliffe, Bart., M.P., Mr. Ittingworth, M.P., and the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon. The Chairman, ia opening the proceedings, said the large gathering which hesaw before him was a practical proof of the interest taken in the work of the Liberation Society, and he thought the present was more than a special occa- sion, considering their close proximity to a general election and to the admission to political power of a large number of persons belonging to a class hitherto excluded. At the present moment the consideration of foreign questions thrust domestic matters out of sight, especially the all- important problem of religious equality. (Hear, hear.) Even among home questions he was not prepared to say that the final establishment of complete religious equality was entitled to the first place in the Parliament that would as- semble next year. Local self-government, decentralisation, the efficiency of the parliamentary machine, the housing and the social welfare of the poor, and the reform in the land question, and many other questions, would jostle for precedence with the principle which they ad. vocated. The Liberation Society did not wish to dictate to the Liberal party the precise order in which the questions should be taken, but never- theless they believed that the impartiality of the State was absolutely necessary for perfect religious equality. That was the only principle compatible with justice, and he be- lieved that if the principle were fairly applied it would raise the tone of political life, that it would be in harmony with religious truth, and would tend to the welfare and pro. gene of religions life in this country. (Cheers.) They therefore usged upon all members of the Liberation Society, and upon all sympathisers with its efforts, the necessity of impressing upon the political organisation with which they might be associated the importance of giving due promi- nence to their aspirations. (Cheers) Great activity of late had undoubtedly been shown by the Church of Eng- land, which they rejoiced at. At the same time they were of opinion that this awakering was mainly due to the large infusion of the principles of their society. (Cheers.) While most willing and ready to recognise the efforts which had keen made in the warfare against vice, at the !same time they were of opinion that the gain by public endowment was more than countsrbalanced by the evil of the alliance with the State. Hisestablishment in the colonies had worked satisfactorily, and in neither the colonies nor in Ireland would the disestablished churches like to co back to the days of pampered bondage. They looked forward to the time when the same thing would follow in this country, and when they would find every one en a footing of social religious equality. They would then ens a growth of national sympathy and of freer communication of philan- thropic effort, which would multiply the power of this nation for its welfare and prosperity. (Cheers.) The Rev. A. Mackennal said they had met to consider a question of vital national importance without any sectarian bias, the main object they had in view being to bring about a liberation of religion from State patronage and center)), and no to establish religious rqnality.—After a few observa- tions from Sir R. Cunliffe, the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon, in a characteristic speech, denounced the patronage by the State of one religious community over another, and said that if one sect was to be choeen out and favoured by the State, it

did not matter how good it was, it:was an injautice to all the other churches, and an injustice to those who belonged to any church at all. (Hear, bear.) He was certain that there was scarcely a man living who would have the audacity to propose at the present moment, if then were not at the present moment one already established, to set one up. (Hear, hear.) They believed that the very establia,h- ment of a church by the State tended to the concealment of men's convictions—(hear, hear,)—and thought that the dif- fering parties in the Church would not keep together but for the State endowment. They felt certain that tl e truth would speak out more ,alainly and would have a greater power if it were not rendered dumb by the posq.ion of its advocates. Religion and not polite had brought him to the meeting, for, with regard to politics, it seemed to him that each succeeding party spent more money than its predecessor, and that neither party was able 10 see the vir- tues of the other because it was so engrossed with its Own. (Cheers.) In conclusion, he thought that a church which numbered amongst its adherents the wealthiest of the weal- thy, and almost all the peers of the realm, ought to be self- supporting and ought to be independent of the State subsidy. The Rev. A. Oliver (Glasgow), Mr. Illingworth, M P , and others addressed the meeting, which terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

The annual meeting of the;:council of the society was held in the afternoon at the Cannon-street Hotel. Mr. H. R. Ellington presided. The secretary (gr. Robjahris) read the report, which referred to the progress the disestablish- ment question had made in England, Scotland, and Wales. The committee also appealed to the society's friends for funds to circulate leaflets addressed to new electors in order to gain adherents to the principles of the society. The treasurer's financial statement showed that the receipts had been £9,416, and the payments £B,67o.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, called attention to the fact that the present circumstance in which the country was placed called for more than usual care aud exertion on the part of the society in promoting the objects they had in I I view. The Church party were beginning to awaken to the I seriousness of the position which they occupied. It was said that they were opposed to the Church. but that was not true. They were simply op- posed to it as a State institution. They felt that religion was damaged by being overridden by the State.—Mr.Wood- all, M.P., seconded the motion, and in alluding to the Burials 15:11 said it had been stated that the adoptio n of the measure would lead to scandals and irreverence in the churchyard, but there was no instance of scandal or irrev- erence on record. The Government Cemetery Bill, he said, would have the effect of removing the invidious dis- tinction between consecrated and unconsecrated ground. He also added that the outlook was satisfactory, and seemed to point to the ultimate achievement of the great principle of religious equality—Mr. H. Lee, M.P.,supported the motion, and it was carried—Resolutions were adopted in support of disestablishment in Scotland and Wales, and in favour of amending.the laws which regulated the pros ision and man- agement of parochial burial places.—The concluding resolu- tien was in favour of the abolition of oaths. .

div.p: EARLESTOWN.

• -• • IMPORTANT PROPERTY SALE.-000 of the most impor- tant sales of property at Eeriest° wn within recent years took place at the Wellington Hotel, Earle-street, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. William Mills, auctioneer, Legh-street, put " under the hammer 'several lots of leasehold property situate at Earlestown and Newton. There was a very large attendance, among the gentlemen presmt being Messrs. It Kirkconnel (solicitor, Warrington), F. Harwood, V. Hall, D. Barcroft, J. Gooding, Chandley, Ormond, Adams, Pim- blett, ckc. The bidding on the whole was very spirited, and several of the lots induced a lively competition. LII3ERAL EXECUTIVE FOR NEWTON DITISION.—A well attended meeting of the Executive Committee of the Liberal Three Hundred for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire was held at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, Fairclough-street, on Monday evening. The chair ' Was occupied by Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P. (Haydock), and there were also present Messrs. R. Pilkington (Rainford), A. C. McCorquodale, J.P. (Newton), W. Mitchell (Gol- borne), Rawlins. and Maitland (Rainhill), Sac. The pro- ceedings were principally of a business character, including the consideration of arrangements for future meetings. Sub- committees were appointed to arrange lectures, meetings, rkc., throughout the division, and also to take charge of registration matters. Mr. Thomas Howard (secretary) reported that he had visited the oublistricta of the division, and seen that represectatives to the General Council were daily appointed according to the population. This was the only business of public interest. Irinnwswlcx WESLEY AN SUNDAY SCECOOL.—Tho anni- versary sermons in connection with the Brunswick Wes. leyan Sunday and Day Schools were held in the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Cross-lane, Earlestown, on Sunday, and were of a very successful character. In the morning and evening the preacher was the Rev. John Pullitt, of Sum- merseat, whose earnest addresses were attentively listened to. In the afternoon a service of song entitled " The Corn- ing of Emmanuel" was given by the chapel choir and a number of the school children. The chapel was crowded to its utmost capacity. The choir was under the leadership of Mr. Hugh Parr, and Miss E. L. Gre3nall presided at the pianoforte. The service was of an interesting character. The solo parts were sung by Miss C. Roberts, Miss Swann, Miss Sydes, Mr. Swann, Mr. Gilmour, Mr. Gib. son, and Mr. Atkinson. A quartette by Miss Wal- ton, Miss Jones, Mr. Gibson, and Mr. Atkinson was nicely given ; and Miss Swann and Miss Sydas well rendered a duet. At the close of the three services a col- lection in aid of the school funds was made, the aggregate amounting to over £413. EXTRAORDINARY " TRAGEDY " AT WARGRAVB.—A " tragedy " of an extraordinary character, and one resulting in the loss of over a dozen lives has this week been perpe- trated at a spot within one hundred miles from Wargrave Church. The "shocking occurrence" haa naturally excited a great deal of talk and comment in the neighbourhood, and one of the parties concerned has since been looked upon as quite a " heroirie." On Monday morning the discovery was made that a certaia "dwelling" had been entered by same stealthy "robber," and evidently regardless of either age or sex the intruder had slaughtered all the inmates, to the number of about a dozen. On the sad discovery being made there were many vows of vengeance, and the life of the reckless rascal was eagerly sought. An alarm was given, and the news of the affair quickly spread. After some hesitation a young lady residing in the district ventured to enter the dwelling in which the tragedy had been committed, ant, if poseible, secure the " desperado " before he could escape. To the astonishment of the by- standers she carried out her designs, and after a short scuffle she made her appearance, grasping by the neck the "mur- derer," of whose guilt there were many evidences. The "slayer of the innocents" did not long survive his " vic- tims," for he shortly afterwards met his death in attempting to swim with a brick tied to his neck. The moral of the story of the "catastrophe" is "Do not have pigeon-cotes where cats, and especially those of the Thomas persuasion, can enter without observation and in the easiest poasible manner."

THE ADVENTIIILEB OF A Goax.—Before Messrs. Geo. McCorquodale, It. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie C. Pilkington, and W F. Gooch, at the Newton Town Hal; on Saturday, Patrick Mahoney, of Market-street, Earlestown' was sum- moned for allowing his goat to stray on the highway on the let inst.—The defendant's son appeared for his father.- 13. C. Hunt stated that at six o'clock on the night of Friday, the date named, he was on duty in Market street when he saw the defendant's goat coming out of Dr. Handyside's garden. He drove it home, and told the defendant he would be reported for allowing h's goat to stray. The police had had frequent complaints about the goat destroyiag the plants and flowers in the garden.—The defendant's son : Why does Dr. Handyside get you to do his dirty work ? The Clerk said the defendant must not ask such questions. —The defendant's son stated that they had had the goat about 18 months, and when it had been tied to a post on a vacant piece of land lads cut the rope and the goat ran away. The lads had taken the rope several times.—The Bench expressed the opinion that the case had better be ad- journed so that the defendant himself could attend.—The defendant's son: My father cannot speak on it as wal as I can, for he is not at home. I have taken the goat out many a time, and it has come home with the rope cut.—The Chairman: If you had a chain the boys could not cut it. —The defendant'a son : No, air, but they might loosen the chain.—The Chairman (after consultation with the other magistrates) : The Bench are quite willing to let your father off on the payment of cost...—The defendant'a son : How much is it a—Superintendent Jackson pointed out that the defendant was fined Is and costs on the 13th February last for a similar offence; and .the Chairman remarked, amid some amusement : You must pay a fine of 23 GI and costs.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S SALE OF WORK.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S SALE OF WORK.

On Tuesday afternoon a sale of work was opened by Miss Shakerley, Belmont Hall, Northwicb, in St. Paul's School- room, Warrington in aid of the mission woman fund. There was a large and fashionable attendance, amongst those present being the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Harrison), Lady and Misses Greenell, Mr. G. Greenall, Mrs. Seamont, Mrs. Quekett, the Rev. S. and Mrs. and Miss Wil- kinson, Colonel, Mrs., and Miss Thackwell, the Rev. St. A. Duke, Rev. Canon and Mrs. Dodd, Mrs. R. Davies, Mrs. T. Morris, Mrs. and Mies D. W. Flimsy, Misses White, Mr. V. Davies, Mrs. Wilcock, Rev. W. H. and Mrs. Williams (Padgate), Mrs. J. White, Mrs. T. H. Lyon, Mrs. and Miss Buckton, Mr. Jolley, Mrs. J. Gibson, and numerous others. The stalls, which were replete with elegant and valuable articles, were presided over by Mrs. and Miss Wilkinson, Miss Chorley, Miss Brundrett, Mrs. Greening, Misses Green- ing, Misses Geddes, Miss Craik, Miss Lawless, Miss Thacke well, Miss Westwell, Misses Fraser, Mrs. Oyley, Miss Braide, Mrs. Constant, Mrs. Lawton, Mies Bolton, Miss Ashurst, Miss Townsend, Miss Clive, Mrs. E. Woods, Mrs. Jolley, Miss Pendlobury, arc. A good assortment of beautie ful and valuable dowers had been contributed by Mrs. Davies (Birchdale), Mrs. Nicholson (Thelwall Hall), Mrs. Stanton, and Mrs. Cotton.—The Rev. S. Wilkinson, in introducing Miss Shakerley, said he hltcl a very light and pleasant duty to perform, mid that was to introduce Miss Shakerley, to whom they offered their siocere thanks for coming so long a distance to opea that sale of work. Their thanks were also due to those kind ladies who had bees the means of getting together the articles they saw on the stalls. He could testify from personal experience what a great amount of liberal efforts the ladies had undertaken. Week after week a party of ladies had assembled at the vicarage to work for that sale, and many besides those connected with their own parish had also helped them. That afternoon they returned thanks to one and all of those who had helped them so kindly in their work.—Miss Shakerley said she felt very much the honour of the Invitation to open that sale of work, which had been given to her by her friend Mrs. Wil- kinson. She bad the more pleasure in doing so because she felt sure of the sympathy other friends and neighbours with the good cause for which that yearly effort was made. It appeared to her that the only method that remained to them for the expression of their opinions was in the per- formance of kind and liberal deeds. With regard to the sale she had no doubt that the result of it would be to lighten a burden which they knew could hardly be borne by one per- son or even with the assistance of the kindly helpers who had already done so much. As she felt sure that the ladies were ready to sell and the ladies and gentlemen anxious to buy, and as she knew very well that on an occasion of that sort time might be very much better spent than in listening to any remarks that might be made, she should be sorry to detain them -any longer, and it became her duty and pleasure to declare the sale open. (Applause.)—The eale wee then proceeded with. In the course of the afternoon and evening songs were sung by Mies Whitley, Miss Brandrett, and Messrs. Parkinson, Sherlock, Reddish, Rad Guise. Mr. Lythgoe presided at the piano. In the evening a variety entertainment of an enjoyable character was given by Pro- lessor Frakell and his daughter. There was a good attend- ance throughout, and the sales amounted to £7B.

div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Alford' Chambers, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. E. Carey presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, J. Houghton; H. Gaekell, J. Taylor, F. Hayes, F. H. Pack- buyst, D. Wright, B. Dutton, B. Brown, T. Handley. W. T. Ilusband, J. T. Allen (clerk), J. Carr (engineer), T. Higgin- iOn (surveyor. • -

div.head: TUB SHIP CINAL.
div.p: TUB SHIP CINAL.

Dr. O'Keeffe said the deputation formed to deal with the Manchester Ship Canal business, on behalf of Widnes, hati :really got all the Board required. The interest of Widnes had been by no means overlooked, and the deputation had been of service to the manufacturers, and he hoped to the township at large. The deputation had not only secured protection for the outlets of their sewers, and the prevention of their silting up at Hutchinson's Dock, and at the Old Dock; but if in any instance vessels could not come up the river, the Canal Company would tow thern up the canal free of charge, an arbitrator being appointed if required.

THE NEW PUBLIC OFFICES. The Clerk stated that the Local Government Board had forwarded four copies of a provisional order partially repeal- ing the Improvement Act, 1867, and the Local Beard Act, 1875. It would shortly be submitted to Parliamentior con- firmation. This is in reference to the new public offices, and the power to borrow money.

div.head: – GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: - GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The Engineer reported- to the Gas Committee that the working of the Volunteer Fire Brigade had net proved sat- isfactory in consequence of members failing to turn up at drill, and he asked that the system and form of rules should be reconsidered. Ile also stated :—" Seeing the continued depressed state of the sulphate of ammonia market and the consequent low price of ammoniacal liquor, he would re- commend that a plant be erected at the gas works for work- ing their own liquor ioto sulphate, which would always give the 'bard the advantage of manufacturing profits." The mean rainfall fur the month bad been 1.65 inches. The it- lutninatiag power of the as had averaged 1712 candles. It was recommended that ti e tender of Hathorn, Davey and Co of £2lO to supply, tix, and set to work; their patent differential valve ge a to the Netherley engine "James Cross," be accepted; an allowance of £lO to be made for the old gearing. Ipstructions were given to amerd the rules, and the considara,ion of the sulphate of ammonia plant. The minutes were ad,rtA on the motion of Mr. Gaskell. aeconded by Mr. Wright. THE STOPPAOE OF A YoorpaTa DEACON•ROAD IMPROVEMENT. The Highway Committee had received a letter from the London and North-Western B. al way denying liability with regard to the Bridle-road and footpath t) Ditton, and stating that the Board could take any course they thought fit. Sub- sequently counsel's opinion was obtained on the subject, and Messrs. Oppenheim and Malkin, solicitors, were instructed to write the S. /cc M. RN, Cs. and other parties concerned in the stoppage of the footway.—The plans of 18 houses in Chester-street, for Mr. 0. G. Pritchard, were approved.— a deputation consisting of Mews. Carey, Taylor, and Dut- ton was appointed to wait upon Messrs. Bolton and Sons with regard to the closing of West Bank-street.—The Chairman moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded the adop- tion of the minutes.—Mr. Brown said he saw from the sur- veyor's report Deacon-road was being repaired at the pre- sent time. Near the quarry the footpath was only 21t. 601. wide, and it appeared to him that this width shoald be in- creased whilst the repairs were being carried out, so that passengers could pass each other, which they could not do now. He also desired the committee to take into consider- ation the necessity of putting another lamp or two in the road. It was the darkest passage in the township from its natural position and formation and the fewness of the lamps there.—The Chairman said the pathway was certainly very narrow at the quarry, but the Surveyor had explained to him that it was made I. line with the pathway further down the road, and to widen it would not be any public con- venience as it would °lily make the road still narrower than it was, and as there was no expense connected with the repairs to the pathway as it was now, it was thought better to leave it at its present width. He acknowledged that Deacon-road was badly l.ghted, and he promised the sub- ject should have :he Attention of the committee when the dark nights approached. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

The Medical Officer reported to the Health Committee that durin;,, the month of April there were 95 births amd 45 deaths, beirg at the rate of 44.22 end 20 per 1,000 per annum. Thirteen deaths occurred amongst children under one year There were no delthe from zymotic disease. The Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for the month were £29 13s 4d, being an increase of £2 914 d as compared with April, IsB4.—Dr. O'Reeffe in moving the adoption of the minutes, said during the time the deputticn reSpecting the Ship Canal was in London, he and the clerk to the Board waited upon Mr. Rowcliffe, solicitor to the Legh estate, with reference to the infectious diseases hospital Ihey represented to him the Board's case' and be re- ceived them in a very favourable way, so that he (the doctor) thought the cost of building the wall would be considerably diminished. Is fact that instead of costing £l,OOO it would only cost from £2OO to £3oo.—Mr. Brown seconded the motion which was passed. FININ CE.

The Finance Committee recommended that the following accounts be paid :—Gas, £478 191 3d • water, £123 18s 1d •, highway, £543 53 I/ ; health, £32 19s 7d ; hospital £8 15s ; and finance, £1 148 2s 3d. The minutes were passed oa the motion of Mr. Hayes, seconded by Mr. Dutton. TEE RATE. . A rate of Is in the £ fur the present half year was sealed and signed RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB ANNUAL DINNER. The annual dinner in connection with the Runcorn Foot- ball Club took place on Thursday evening in a marquee erected on ground adjoining Bridge-street Cocoa Rooms. Mr. A. Rigby was the caterer, and the repast he had pre- pared gave every satiefaction. Mr. T. Jones, of the Barley. mow Hotel, Church-street, provided the refreshments. The after proceedings were presided over by Mr. J. R. Frith, Mr. S. Orme being in the vice-chair. Amongst those present were Dr. Mangan, Messrs. F. J. Parry, H. Hughes, R. Gorst, F. Joule, A. E. Hawkins, T. donee, T. E. Booth, C. Dalton, W. Carroll, W. Crosby, W. B. Frith, J. B. Clallte, J• Graham, F. Timmins, H. Booth, W. Wright, W. B. Erimelow, J. Clarke, C. Pownall, and J. E. Longshaw (sec- aetary).—The Chairman gave "The Queen and Royal Family" and tha Vjce-chairman "The army, navy, and volunteers" and both toasts were duly honoured. Mr. F. J. Parry proposed" Success to the Ytuncorn Football Club" and in doing so said the club had had a very successful season during the past winter, and he hoped with all his heart they would have a more success- ful season during the coming winter. (Applause.) He understood that matches bad been arranged with Birkenhead Park, New Brighton, Walton, Liverpool .Old Boys, Wigan' end several other good clubs, and he personally wished that they might beat then all. (Ap- plause.) He had the pleasure last season of acting as referee at Runcorn on several occasions, and one match he thought they deserved great credit indeed for winning, and that was the match against the Liverpool Gymnasium. (Hear, hear, and applause.) His reason for that assertion W%5 that the Gymnasium had the assistance of three of the best players of West Chesil,. 0. viz, Messrs. Black, Jackson, and Rivil ; and although be was acting as referee, which duty he always endeavoured to perform fairly, he was delighted that they were the victors. In his opinion their captain got one of the finest tries on that occasion that he had seen this year. (Applause.) lie noticed that the club had had the good sense te reelect Mr. Hughes captain for the ensuing year—(hear, hear, and applause)—and he hoped that the majority of the best players, including Speakman, Andrews, Clarke, and othera of the first team would be seen in the van when they again set the ball rolling. (Applause.) The toast VMS enthusias- tically drunk. The president, in responding, said he had great pleasure in meeting them again that evening, and to be able to congratulate them upon a suc- cessful season. They were to meet better clubs next year, and it behoved the captains and the subalterns to put their shoulders to the wheel, so that in the coming season they might surpass the glory of the omit. (Hear, hear.) He referred to tee importance of obeying their captain. He was sure the players might rely upon their captain in every sense of the word, for he (the president) had not seen a more gentlemanly captain anywhere. (Applause.) He was fair, and always ready if there was a doubt to give way— (hear, hear)—and that was not often the case with football captains. (Hear, hear.) Ihe club had only to be loyal and judicious to become one of the finest clubs in the county —(applause)—and he hoped the successes of the past would be an incentive for the future, awl that after meeting some of the first clubs they would bring home a trophy worthy of their deeds. (Applluse.)—Mr. H. Wright proposed the health of the president and vice-presidents in a suitable mariner—The toast having been drunk, the President re- plied, expressing his admiration and appreciation of ath- letic exercises. He earnestly hoped the cricket club would be supported by the menibers of the football club, and al- luded to the formation of a rounders club in connection with the Y.M.C.A., which he trusted would be successful. —Mr. S. Orme also acknowledged the toast—Dr. Mangan gave the sentiment Our captains." After speaking of Mr. H. Hughes in complimentary terms, Dr. Mangan ea- Premed his adaniratioa of the play of the second team, which he believed was an organieation of sple.ndid promise. (Applause) Mr. Clarke excellently Captained the team. Tne, toast was honoured with great cordiality—Mr. Hughes and Mr. J. B. Clarke ably re- sponded.—The President neat gave " The secretary (Mr. Longshaw), the truants,* (sir. Johnsen), and committee," referring especially to time energetic and stele manner in which Mr. Dongshaw bad devoted himself to his duties.— Mr. Longshaw replied in a few choice words, and Mr. T. E. Booth acknowledged the honour on behalf of the committee. —Mr. H. Hughes proposed success to the "West Lanca- shire and Border Towns Football Union." He said this Union was formed because it was believed that the Asso- ciation game Was driving the Rugby game away altogether, but the matches played at Runcorn and at Wigan under the auspices of the Union had shown that fear to have no foundation, and a flourishing season neat winter was antici- pated. (applaueea—Mr. Parry, in responding, said he should always have great admiration for the Runcorn Club, becau,, theirs was the first team to come forward to play the inaugural match for the Union, the result being that woe addel to the funds.,, (Applause.)—The toast " Toe Visitors" was proposed by Mr. W. Wright, and responded to by Mr. W. Crosby; "The town and trade of Runcorn" by the vice-chairman, and responded to by Mr. W. Carroll ; the list concluding with the "Press," proposed by the chairman, and acknowleaged by Mr. Whalley, of this journal. During the evening the proceedings were ren-
dered more pleasant by songs given by Messrs. C. Pownall, F. Joule, S. Orme, and W. Wright, Mr. itavenscroft presid- ing at the piano. Mr. C. fackson gave a recitation.
DEATII AND FUNERAL OF THE VICAR
OF HELSBY.

Amid every sign of general sorrow, the remains of the lat‘Rev. John D &yid Bayard, 8.A., vicar of Helsby, near Frodsham, were laid to rest on Wednesday. The death of the rev. gentleman took place late on Friday night week under very sad and sudden circumstances. For several yeare Mr. Bayard had been in delicate health, and for some time had performed his multifarious parochial duties under great physical suffering and weakness. Even on the day of his death he was going about as usual, and paid several visits to his parishioners. About seven o'clock he was seized with a sudden illness; and, suffering much pain, he passed into a state of unconsciousness. Dr. Robson, of Frodsbam, was sent for, and pronounced that the patient was suffering from apoplexy. Every- thing poesible was done for the suffaer, but after lingering until ten o'clock, he closed his eyes in death. Mr. Bayard was born in 1845, and belonged to the Princi- pality. He was educated at St. David's College, Lampeter, where he passed high in claesics and literature. He was ordained deacon in 1869, and priest in the following year by the Bishop of Llandaff. For some time he was curate-in- charge of Greenfield, near Flint, where he was noted as an energetic and painstaking pastor. In 1876 he accepted the living of St. Paul's, Helaby, which was only set apart in that year as a separate parish. He was, therefore, the first vicar of Helsby, and naturally found wide scope for his energies. At the t'me of his coming to Helsby there was no Sunday school connected with the church, and recognihing the value of such an institution, and the pressing need of increasing facilities for giving religious instruction he earn- estly set about the establishment of a school. The vicar was aided by several zealous adherents to the church, and soon a prosperous school was formed, at which there is now an average attendance of 130. By his exertions and influ- ence, the day school was remodelled and passed under the care of the Government, and now has an average attendance of 150 scholars. During the early years of his incumbency, the present heniseme residence, adjoining the church, was built by public subscription, while the various institutions of the church have been substantially advanced. At the funeral the chief mourners were Mrs. Ilivard, Master William Bayard (sop), Misses Blanche, Mary and Annie Bayard (daughters), Mr. Bayard. the deceased's father, and two brothers, who came from a distance. The scholars be- longing to the schools were also in the procession, and many of them carried flowets of bright bloom, which they pieced on the coffin. The children were under the charge of Mr. Hill, schoolmaster,and while in the church they sang the hymn commencing "A few more years shall roll." 'The building was completely crowded with parishioners, and amongst those present were Mr. and Mrs. James Reynolds, Mr. and Mrs. G. L. Davies, Mr. and Mrs. Aman, Mr. and Mrs. Boulderston' Mr. and Mrs. Serif, Mr. F. A. Wright, and Mrs. Sarrett. The service was conducted by the Rev. Canon Dpperton, vicar of Inca, the lesson being read by the Rev. Canon Greenall, of Grappenhall. The other clergy present were the Revs. E. P. Alexander, vicar of Alvanley ; 11. R. Wbytehead, vicar of Norley ; E. A. Bagot, curate-In-charge of Aatou ; W. S. Hoole, Thornton; A. Grier, Kingsley; and R. M. P. Butler, curate of Frodsham. On being lowered into the grave many floral tributes were placed on the coffin until it appeared to be one mass of wreathe, crosses, and bunches of flowers. Amongst the wreaths placed on the grave was one from the choir of the church. A beautiful cross of roses

made by Mrs. Reynolds and Mrs. Alexander, was placed on the grave by Master Willie llavard. Before the last point was reached in the solemn ceremony, the scholars, assisted by the chpir, sang the hymn commencing "Brief life is here our portion." The living of Helabv is in the presentation of Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., of Foxhill, and is valued at £l6O per annum.

div.head: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

The head-master, Mr. W. A. Watts, M.A., has just sub- mitted kis report for the year ended Christmas, 1884, to the governors. After referring to the opening of the new build- ine.e he sees :—" The first term, ending April 10th, 1884, we had 23 boys; the second term, ending July 25th, the same number, having lost one and gained oae ; the third term, ending December 13th, 1884, the number was 26. The amount received in fees for the term ending December 22nd, 1883, was £l6; the annual fee, which was origin- ally fixed at £lO per boy, having been reduced to £B, with a reduction in the case of brothers, and the alteration having been made retrospective; so that although £2O was actually paid in, £4 was allowed on the ensuing term's fees to those who had paid an the higher scale. The amount of fees for the Easter term, 1884, was £59 15s 61; for the summer term, £6O 1334 d ; and for the Chrismas term, £63 69 Bd. In pursuance of a resolution of the Governors, an examina- tion was held at the school on Saturday, September 13th, of the candidates for two free scholarships. Eleven candi- dates presented themselves, three of whom came from Simm's Cross Board School, two from West Bank Beard School, five from Widnes. National School, and one from Penketh Wesleyan School. Several of the candidates dis- tinguished themselves, and had the number of scholarships to be awarded been greater, I should have been glad to have accepted four. The highest place was taken by Charles A. Bate, of Simm's Cross Board School, who obtained 781 marks out of 1,000; the second was George H. Sherratt, of West Bank Board School, who obtabsed 732 marks. These two received scholarships, their parents hav- ing duly complied with the necessary formalities." In the early part of December two bays .were presented at the College of Preceptors' examinations, and both passed creditably. T. Knowles was placed in the Ist division of the second class, having passed in English, Latin, arith- metic, Euclid, algebra, chemistry. and book-keeping, his standing being 53rd out of the 608 who passed in that class, in which 1,376 were examined. L. H. Linnell was placed 19th in the first division of third class, out of 1,728 who passed in that class, in which 1,884 were presented. Linnell received special distinction in chemistry, and passed ' in English, Latin, arithmetic, Euclid, and book-keeping. Next Christmas some 20 boys or so ought to be ready for such an examination as that of the College of Preceptors ; and as the scheme requires us to have the school examined each year by independent extminers, I would recom- mend the governors to take the necessary steps to con- stitute the school a centre of examinations for the Col- lege of Preceptors, and to have our own examination every Christmas. We could then present the majority of the school each year, thus securing a satisfactory indepen- dent test of the progrees of the classes. There would be payable also a small fee of ten shillings by each candidate, to which I hope the great majority of the parents, consider- ing the character of the examination, and the attendant ad- vantages, would not object. The nearest centre at present is Liverpool, and the difficulty and expense of sending can- didates there would prevent any number of our boys from taking advantage of that centre. Not only would this diffi- culty be overcome by our having our own centre, but no doubt other candidates would be sent to this school to be examined, and so cause ours to be looked upon as a central institution for the district, which could not fail to be an advantage to the school." Reference was then made to the Prize distribution, a report of which has appeared in The Examiner, and Mr. Watts concludes by suggesting that as the school year ends at Christmas the scholarships should date from January instead of September. This alteration would he approved by the masters of the elementary schools, to whom the September examination appeared inconvenient In consequence of that being the usual peried for inspection of their schools.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The King of the Belgians has addressed a cordial invita- tion, through Monsieur Is Prince de Caraman, Minister of Foreign Affairs, to Mr. Adamson, the chairman of the pro- visional committee, asking himself and his colleagues to attend the forthcomir'e, congress at Brussels on Inland Navigation, on the 24th May. The plans to be discussed at the congress embrace the suggested construction of a ship canal for vessels of a large draught up to Brussels and the development on an extensive scale of waterways through- out Belgium. We understand that the Ship Canal Committee have accepted the invitation of the King of the Belgians, and all arrangements will be made bs the Belgian Government for the convenience of the deputation in Brussels. Mr. Adamson has also received an autograph letter from the Italian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Signor Mancini, in which his excellency states: I received through our con- sulate a copy of the plans and sections of the works to be executed for the construction of the proposed Manchester Ship Canal, which copy the committee over which you preside are pleased to offer for the acceptance of his Majesty's government. I hasten to express to your good- self and the committee our sincere thanks for your testi- mony of regard for our country in presenting us with so valuable a work. I have transferred the same to my honoured colleague of Public Works, to be kept safely in the archives of that department for inspection by all those who mike these subjects their special study in Italy, and desire to be- come fully acquainted with the great work to be accom- plished in your important commercial centre. The Mersey Docks and Harbour Board on Thursday adopted a report of the Parliamentary Committ3e of that body, in reference to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. The report that the strength of the case of the petitioners against the bill was seriously prejudiced by the course adopted, contrary to their desire, by the House of Lords' Committee at the outset of the case, in dividing the engineering from the commercial case, and in hearing and deci ling the former before the latter was entered upon. The whole case against the bill ought to have been heard before a decision on any part of it was arrived at. Considering that the eminent engineers consulted on behalf of the Board were strongly of opinion that the works proposed by the bill involved serious danger to the estuary and the bar, and incidentally to the Board's docks; and that OR the other hand it could be shown that the scheme if carried out, would not accom- plish any commercial results at all justifying the incurring of those grave ritske, the Parliamentary Committee proposed that the oppositiOn of the Board to the bill in all respects should be continued before the Select Committee of the Rouse of Commons.

A large meeting to protest against increased duties on "the drink of the people" was held in Trafalgar equare. London, on Wednesday evening. The dimensions of the gathering gave the police some trouble, and there arc said to have been several conflicts in which sticks and stones were—used, but no serious disturbance of the peace oc- curred.

ACCIDENT ON THE Hann.—Early on Thursday morn. ing sounds were heard proceeding from the " keel ' which capsized in the Humbnr on Wednesday, and as it was be- lieved that some of the five persons on board might be still alive, the vessel was towed ashore and enteted. Mrs. Snow- den, wife of the captain, and one child were found in the cabin, baying wonderfully survived a 17 hours' imprison- ment in the overturned craft. The dead bpdies of the captain and two other of his children were entangled in the rigging.

div.head: . THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1885. OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: . THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1885. OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THVESDAY.

This has bean for the Prime Minister a week that would try the strength, physical and mental, of a much younger man than Mr. Gladstone. Twice the patriotic. Opposition have had a life-and-death struggle with the Ministry. Had they woo, and in respect of one or two critical divisions they had some reasonable expectation of triumph, Mr. ' Gladstone and his colleagues would have been displaced, and Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill would have reigned in their stead. The first fall was tried on Monday when, on the Consolidated Fund Bill, the new Par- liamentary form of the Vote of Credit, Lord George Ham- ilton brought forward what was called a vote of censure. The very form in which this motion was presented spoke eloquently of the divided state of the party who are ready to govern the Empire and in the meantime cannot control their own private affairs. Lord Randolph Churchill, who at least rises above the pettiness of half measures, was pre- pared to submit a good old-fashioned vote of censure, based upon his views of the conduct of the Government as ex- pressed in many speeches. But the wise men on the front bench protested that if that were done it would drive off some hesitating friends of the Government. If they made their net big and loose enough they might catch some votes from the other side. So without expressing any opinion of the conduct of the Government, and whilst eagerly de- claring their readiness to vote supplies, they demanded fur- ther information as to the policy of the Government both in India and the Soudan.

This demand was fully met. The Liberals heard with satisfaction that the Soudan book, with its many blood- stained pages was about to be finally closed. Not less joy was manifested at the information that the Afghan Bound ary had been substantially settled, and that it was satisfac- tory not only to her Majesty's Government, but to Lord Dufferin and the Council of India. After this there was nothing to be said except te congratulate the Government upon having come to a wise determination in the Soudan, and upon having achieved a great triumph in Afghanistan. That is the ordinary, business, common-sense view of the situation. But the Opposition were prepared with their speeches. They had whipped tip their forces ; they had still some hope of snatching a few votes from the Liberal side, and the fact that their demand had been complied with and the information they sought fully placed at their disposal made no difference. They went on just the same as if the Government had stubbornly remained silent. It was the same in respect ef the debate on local taxation, which took place on Tuesday. The Conservatives in their resolution de- manded relief of local taxation in connection with the charges under the Registration Acts. Mr. Gladstone met their demand by doubling the grant already offered to Eng- land, and adding fifty per cent to that allotted to Ireland. But the debate went on just as if he bad turned his back upon them, and, to the ultimate chagrin of the Conserva- tives, a division was taken showing for the Government a majority, unexpectedly large on this question, of 22. In both these debates Mr. Gladstone took a leading part. He made two speeches in Momlay's debate, one at the beginning and onset the end. It was half-past one in the morning when he rose to wind up the debate. This is a sours, of procedure entirely foreign to Mr. Gladstone's modern habits. He is always more anxious to elicit the opin- ion of the country papers than of those published in London. He recognises the difficulty of reporting for the country papers a speech delivered by him at any time after din- ner. It will, accordingly, be noticed on review of his speeches during the present Parliament that nearly all the important ones have been delivered before eight o'clock, thus providing full opportunity for them to reach the country. He had, however, no option in the debate on Lord George Hamilton's amendment. He was bound to speak, and opportunity did not present itself till long past pia- ; night. This is the mote to be regretted since the speeds wee a most striking one. Its force was felt and attempted to be met by familiar tactics on the part of the Conservatives. They interrupted him at nearly every sentence, and were only too successful in exciting his irritability. But they could not disturb the forward march of his argument. He showed in pitilessly clear language how the Conservative party had approved the action of the Government as long as it tended in the direction of war. The moment peace bscarne possible they separated. I met at dinner the other night M. Lessor, of whom so much has been heard during the last few weeks in connec- tion with the quarrel with Russia. One would imagine as the result of much talk about the Russians, that he would turn out to be an elderlydiplomatist, with wrinkled brow and cautious ways ef speech. I was astonished to find a young man of some thirty-five or thirty-six, with simple unaffec- ted manner, light-hearted, and as merry as if he were not the depository of imperial secrets. I happened to sit next to him at dinner, and subsequently had a long conversation. He impressed me as being a man of singular ability, whose frank, almost boyish manner conceals profound purposes. He does not speak English, a drawback he is laboriously endeavouring to overcome. Like most Rassians he speaks French as well or at least as fluently as his native tongue. He spoke of his mission in England with curiousfranknees, discussing the position of the two countries as if he were a disinterested looker-on. One thing that struck me more than once in listening to his plea for the perfect innocency of Russian intention was that he was reciting an article from the Pall Mall Gazette. The identity of thought and even ; the similarity of argument were curious and significant. Mr. Watts, R.A., is, in a certain sense, one of the most remarkable painters of the day. He has now been before the public for nearly half a century, his first picture being exhibited in the Academy when he was only seventeen. He has just received from America a letter he mach prizes. Last year he took a characteristic step. He lent for exhibition in America some of his finest pictures, not asking or receiv- ing a penny for the loan. They were housed in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, where they have attracted so much attention that the President has written to Mr. Watts asking him to extend the period of the loan till October. Mr. Watts has consented, and in private con- versation expressed himself as much flattered by this re• queet as if it had enclosed a cheque for £.e5,000 for the loan of the pictures.

We have not heard anything lately of the dynami- ards, except ia connection with the trials sow going forward. But the Roused Commons, when it finds time to deal with the Civil Service Esti- mates, will be unpleasantly reminded of the exis- tence of the plot. They will be asked to vote not less than £38,000 simply on account of the expenses of police en- gaged in special duties in connection with the dynamite outrages. This sum is nearly equal to the amount the Government have consented to contribute from the imperial revenues in aid ef the charges under the Registration Act, upon which the fate of the Ministry turned on Tuesday night. Of course this £38,000 does not cover the full cost annually Incurred in endeavouring to combat the machina- tions of these nameless scoundrels, not to mention the money damage from time to time accomplished. But as far as it goes It marks an enormous increase. Last year £12,000 sufficed to cover the charges on account of special police. A terrible cloud overshadows what should be the bright day of the Princess Beatrice's wedding. "'he Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, uncle of the bride, has lifted up his voice against the wedding on the ground that the alliance is not one equal to the expectations or the position of the daughter of the Queen of England. That, it is understood, is an opinion in which the Duke finds agreement with the Prince of Wales. Indeed, it may be said that the opinion is general throughout London. At one time there was a report current, and it certainly is not essentially improbable, that Princess Beatrice was likely to be married to the Prince Imperial. That would have been a highly popular marriage, even if there were no prospect of the Prince ever coming to the throne his father lost. But little is known about the acting bridegroom, except that he is another German princeling for whom the British taxpayer provides house and board for lire. Two or three months ago the speculation was hazarded by some accustomed to take forward views in political affairs, that not more than half of the members of the pre- sent Parliament will be found seated in the reformed House. The guess seemed somewhat bold when first put forward, but on a study of the lists of candidates now being prepared, it will be seen to ba well within the mark. The blanka in the lists are being rapidly filled up, and, as things appear at present, it would be no great matter for surprise if not half of the present members were found to be seeking re-electiononuch less securing it. Many of the new constituencies demand new men, and, as a good num- ber of the older amoeg the county members do not care to fate the turmoil of a contest under the fresh conditions, while several of the small town representatives are so un- distinguished that the created censtituencies are not likely to be tempted to secure them, it will be found that the com- ing Parliament will have an unusually large proportion of members whose faces are as yet unknown to the habitues of Westminster.

By common consent, even of those whom fate has forced to be his opponents, Sir Richard Cross is considered a "well-meaning man," and no one doubts that his recent exhortation to the inhabitants of London to choose only men that are upright, honest, and good to represent them at the coming vestry elections was framed with the best inten- tions. The puzzle under present conditions is to know how to select the upright, the honest, and the good candidates from the house-farmers and property-jobbers who at present hold high revel upon more than one London vestry. The fact is, as Sir Millard is doubtless beginning to be dimly aware, the existing system Offers a premium upon corrup- tion, and, until Municipal Reform is obtained, a7purification of the personnel of the vestries is almost beyond hope. Were there created a definite body, chosen by open election, and its members known to the local world, Sir Richard would not again have reason to exhort.

So far as the second of the objects aimed at by the Irish, Viz, separation, I will not now prophecy as to the result, but proceed to ask the question—Why do you want separa- tion, or for what reason should you coquet with the Tories? Have not English and Irish Tories done their best to frus- trate the labours of Mr. Gladstone during the present ses- sion in his efforts to deal out even banded justice to Irish- men? Has it not been in consequence of the help received from Irish members that the Tories have made the attempt to saddle upon borough ratepayers the taxes naturally be- longing to county landowners ? Look to it, Irishmen; your leader in Parliament are betraying you. I have no doubt some of you read the famous Beaconsfield manifesto, issued through the Duke of Marlborough to the nation, dated March Bth, 1830. In it the late Earl of Beaconsfield compared the action of the Irish party to "pestilence and famine," and called upon "men of light and leading " to resist all the Irish efforts made towards disintegration. In ne portion of this famous literary achievement is there a word of redress for Irish grievances, but the hint is strongly thrown out that the iron glove most still enclose the velvet hand. The English people in large majorities declared in favour of throwing the iron glove on one side. Mr. Glad- stone and his Cabinet stated from their places in Parliament their cordial acceptance of this policy; yet bow was it met by the Irish Why, sir, by the basest ingratitude, and to the complete and utter disappointment of the Radical party, a Coercion Bill was brought in. Even then Mr. Bradlaugh, in the absence of Mr. Parnell, moved its rejection, but all to no purpose. The Irish were coercing the English, and it was a qaestion on which side lay the power. Measures for the redress of Irish grievances were brought in, only to be rejected or so mauled and twisted about by the House of Lords that the parent scarcely knew his own child. In 1882, when the Land Courts got to work, outrages at once began to decline, and before the Crimes Act was passed they had diminished from 495 in January to 284 in June. Ip fact, it is is certain no Crimes Act would have been passed but for the woeful Place dx Park tragedy. It is in consequence of the humane and altogether beneficial measures passed by the present Liberal Government that the Tory Daily Telegraph of May 7th, 1885, is forced to make the following confession as to the present state of Ireland. The "courageous pro- gress of the Prince and Princess of Wales has revealed to all the existence of a loyal community full of happy pro- mise for the future. We have already observed that the present aspect of the island displays a gradual but un- doubted return towards orderly life. There is clear and welcome imprevement." After Tory evidence of this kind, in confirmation of the improved state of Ireland, surely Irishmen will see the great necessity for re-considering their . decision as to agitating for separation. Good and useful work would be to put plain and truthful statements before [ the English people, respecting Dublin Castle officialism, to enlist their sympathy and gain their influence to ward eff for the future all Coercion Bills. This being accomplished, Home Rule, in the same sense that English people mean when speaking of County Government, may become within measureable distance, and peace once more dawn upon poor Ireland. May 12th, 1885.

div.head: Kettral to tile editor.
div.p: Kettral to tile editor.
LONGFORD DEPO r.

Sir,—There is a letter in your issue of last Saturday signed "Pedestrian," in which he refers ts what he calls a "mountain of filth "at Longford depot. I shall be glad if he will point out where it is to be found, as I wish to see it. —Yours respectfully,

div.head: "MANY HAPPY RETURNS OF THE DAY."
div.p: "MANY HAPPY RETURNS OF THE DAY."

Sir,—My old friend, 'my uncle," Sir Gilbert, celebrated his 79th birthday last Monday. I think my friends in Sankey-street were very much remiss, inasmuch as they did nothing whatever to celebrate the event. They might at least have got up a workingmen's dinner to Sir Gilbert, and it would have given them a chance to again distribute a few hundred gallons of soup and a quantity of plum pudding which was not "left" therefrom. Wishing my old friend all happiness and comfort ia his declining years, in which I am sure all your readers will join, I am, yours, Ice., MAJOR.

div.head: PROPOSED INTERCEPTING DEPOT.
div.p: PROPOSED INTERCEPTING DEPOT.

Sir,—Referring to your report in last Saturday's paper of the Town Council's proceedings in connection with the above scheme, it may be well that your readers should be informed that the Sanitary Committee's agreement with Mr. W. J. Legh for lani near 0 rford•lane will not pass un- challenged, as it has roused a very strong feeling against it. The Local Government Board has already been communi- cated with, and a memorial asking them not to sanction the purchase of such land for an intercepting depot is in course of signature, and will shortly be forwarded to the Local Governmsct Board.—Yours, dec., May 15th, 1885. SANITAS.

div.head: TEIE VICAR OF KINGSLEY.
div.p: TEIE VICAR OF KINGSLEY.

Sir,—l was glad to see in your last issue a letter signed " A Parishioner," who refers to what he appropriately terms "clerical intolerance," in speaking of the action of the Vicar of Kingsley on the subject of graves. In saying I was glad to see the letter, I do not mean that what is dealt within it gave ma pleasure, but it is certainly a plea- snre to find that one of the parishioners has courage to ex- pose such gross intolerance on the part even of a vicar. A vicar may not be as other men are, but it would be well if some of the "cloth " would remember that while they, or many of them, revel luxuriously in fat livings, exacting , the full extent of their power, the age is progressing, and the working-man can now think and act for himself. The work of the Liberation Society may be slow, but it is sure, and the constantly recurring instinces of clerical intolerance must be ventilated before the public, continually and per- sistently. Then, perhaps, the werk of the society will not Only be sure, but speedy. Disestablishrnent will follow, and autocratic clergymen will have to pay more attention to the wishes of their parishioners, or seek employment elsewhere. —Yours, ctc.,
NOT A PARISHIONER.
THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

Sir,—The good tempered and moderate tone of " Chair- man's " letter in your issue of Saturday last, commends it to the careful and well-deserved consideration of all sincere and earnest Liberals. If the same courteous and loyal spirit characterised the speeches delivered on Sunday afternoons in Orford-street a little oftener, the Irish cause world bene- fit thereby, end there would be little risk of straining the relations which have existed so amicably for many years past in Warrington between the English and Irish sections of our community. I would venture to say to "Chairman " that such Irishmen as fancy "that certain member's of the Liberal party in Warrington are more opposed to their or- ganisation than any of the opposite party." are completely mistaken, and have no ground for such a suspicion. One thing is quite certain, that is, no Tory looks with friendli- ness upon any Irish movement, except so far as he may recognise in it an element of difficulty and trouble to the Liberal party. I have an intimate acquaintance with many Liberals in Warrington, and I am free to say that almost without exception there is no body of men in any town jn England who are more thoroughly in earnest in desiring to assist at the further emancipation of the Irish people from the evil of castle misgovernment and landlord tyranny. At the same time I would enter my warm protest against the insolent and uncalled for attack made by Mr. Biggtr upon our respected member. Mr. McMinnies's political and personal consistency shou'd have saved hies from the malice of one so completely beneath him in every respect, and so absolutely a stranger to him. I know sufficient of the Irishmen of Warrington to believe that they remember with pleasure and gratitude the devoted services covering the larger portion of a life now well extended, which Mr. McMinnies has rendered ungrudgingly to them and to their country's cause. One word more and I have done. Whatever the Tory party may be disposed to offer in exchange for the Irish vote, will be done as a question merely of party expediency, and at the sacrifice of principle. On the other hand, the men of the Liberal party will, as a matter of justice and righteousness, spend their strength in so assimilating the laws and privileges of the English and Irish races, that in the course of a few years there will re- main no vestige of wrong-doing except such as is left to us as a memory of the wickedness of a bygone age.—Yours, FIDES.

Sir,—please allow me a little space for further remarks anent the recent meeting of the Warrington branch of the Irish National League. I am anxious that the Irish portion of our fellow townsmen should not suppose that the Liberal party are opposed to agitation carried on in a con- stitutional manner, for the purpose of remedying grievances, or that of making life worth living in Ireland. What is ob- jectionable, nay detestable, is that under the cloak of lawful agitation the leaders of the Irish party think they are gul- ling the English people. It is lawful upon the public plat- form to "impeach the House of Brunswick," to place in contraat different modes of government, to urge the estab- lishment of a Republican form of government in preference to our present monarchical and cumbersome system ; bat it Is not in accordance with constitutional government, or with the laws that govern and preserve the human family, to hatch and plot schemes having for their object the dee- truction of human life and property. . .

_ I am proud to say that the Radical party of England to- day recognise the power and benefits of freedom of speech, and, while labouring for a free platform, hate and detest all ambiguity of language, it being calculated in the end to bring only defeat and disappointment to all concerned. I do not purpose to take much notice of "Chairman's " letter ; it is so worded that it deftly leaves out all that con- cerns the public. The writer must have had his tongue in his cheek, and been chuckling at his cuteness at so diplo- matic a style of evading the point at issue. I am charged with ascribing certain words to Mr. Biggar which he never said. Well, when I wrote my letter I had not the benefit of having a report of his speech, and so had to treat to memory, yet I find from the report in the Examiner that I was strictly correct. These are Mr. Big- gar's words :—" The opinion had been proved Lobe correct, by the result of a recent election that a very great number of the non-Catholic population Of Ireland, who had hitherto abstained from supporting the Irish Parliamentary party, would in the future give their aid to it." Now, I grant there is no mention of the word disunion here ; but I had the benefit of listening to another speech made by a Mr. Cox, and I must assert that under no other government would such a wild maniacal speech have been tolerated. Diannion and separation were the objects distinctly urged, and at each treasonable point a gleam of satisfaction spread over the countenance of that amiable and amorous hose purchaser. Mr. Biggar. Igo further than thief and dis- tinctly charge the organisers with descending to a base and dishonest piece of fraudulent work in daring, to announce to the audience that the Catholic clergy of Warrington were in sympathy with the movement. Contradictions to this have appeared from the clergy, bus what would open the eyes of poor Irishmen would be a full and ample statement of what passeed at the knife and fork tee at re certain hotel the earns Sunday evening. Efforts may be made to remove obnoxious clergymen, but if they have one duty more than an other, it is that of so guiding their flocks that happiness and not misery shall be the result of such guidance. Doing this, they need not fear "the three tailors of Tooley-street.!' The objects of the meeting were twofold. First, to so organise that when the leaders in London decided to send down a manifesto the Irish voters in Warrington; and I may say the same tactics are being pursued all over the king- dom, should be under the control of local leaders, and thus be able to go, in the words of the chairman, " blindfold to the polling booth." Second, when so organised, to place Mr. Parnell in a position where he may "deliberately take off his coat for the sole purpose of cutting the links that unite the kingdom." Now the first of these objects I pro- test against for this reason—lrishmen living in Warrington, and receiving all the benefits of citizenship, have no right to so direct their poiitical influence in favour of so-called Irish rights as to prejudice and injure Englishmen's politi- cal power; nave no right, in fact, to attempt to stultify my. vote at the polling booth. If they want to specially and solely vote for Ireland, let them go to Ireland to do it. I earnestly advise them to make such decent use of the public platform and the public press as will bring the Eng- lish voter to see the great necessity there is for immediate and drastic reform in all that relates to Irish government. Do they want to know' what prevents Englishmen from giving enthusiastic support to their movement? Well, I will tell them. First, we refuse to have the kingdom cut up; we refuse to see the Irish people become the tools of ambitious charlatans, and the prey of rival kingdoms. We remember that the intended murder of Mr. Blake, at Loughrea, was so well known generally that people went to the windows at the end of the town to see it committed. He was murdered at noon, about half a mile outside the town, on a feast day, the road being well dotted with people coming to chapels. In cold bloodedness and daring this crime was unsurpassed, yet to this day no trustworthy in- formation has been received with reference to the assassins. We cannot forget the apathetic attitude assumed by the Irish party at the Phoenix Park tragedy three years ago, nor yet the jubilant anniversary just held in New York over the event. Mr. Redmond, M.P., speaking at Kilmallock, on the 12th of April, said "Ha was sorry that, instead of being held there, that meeting was not assembled on the borders of Afghanistan, for he believed that if the cheer they had just given cool& reach the Russian Bear it would wake up that old animal to set about that clawing which he hoped to God he was soon going to give to the British Lion." (Loud and prolonged cheers.) [A voice: "Three cheers for the Matadi," (Cheers.)) Now I ask the Irish party in War- rington to carefully analyse these words. Here you have a member of the British Parliament openly wishing success to a British enemy, openly showing that Irish leaders think that England's distress may lead to Irish success. Is it to support this that they would follow Mr. Loughlan blind- fold to the polling booth? I give them credit for more sense.
