div.head: CLIFFORD DIX.
div.p: CLIFFORD DIX.
LATEST NEWS.

the American, won lawn-tennis championship at Hampton Court on Friday. A Cabinet Council was held at two o'clock on Friday afternoon at the Premier's residence. It is rumoured that the Crimes Act as re-enacted will be in the form of a vary mild peace preserration act. The Lancet, in view of the sudden illness of Lord Dor- mer, once more advocates the conferment of medical peer- ages. The strike in the China trade in South Stafford and East Worcester terminated on Friday by the submission of the majority of the workmen. A Central News telegram, dated Berlin, Friday afternoon, says : The Reichstag, at its sitting to-day passed the new Commercial Treaty with Spain without diffi- culty.
It is stated that Lard Randolph Churchill has definitely decided to contest the Central Division of Birmingham, and has csmmunicated his decision to the local com- mittee.
A London correspondent • telegraphs that Mr Finn J. Fargus, author of 'Called Back," &c., better known by the nom de plume of Hugh Conway, died yesterday morning at Monte Carlo.

On Friday Alfred Henry Parker was charged before the South Shields magistrates with wounding Christopher Barnes on the high seas on the 16th April. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Durham Sessions. _ _

Ssamos Kumla ACCIDENT.-- At noon on Friday a mineral train left the metals near Possie Station, on the North British Railway, and completely blocked both the up and down lines. Five brakesmen were injared. . . _

The Irish party kopt the House going until half-past two on Friday morning in the hope that they would embarass the Government by obstructing the Registration Bill. They were, however, defeated, and the Bill passed the third reading. Tam CONGREGATIONAL UNtox.—The Congregational Union met again on Friday. A letter was read from the president-elect, excusing his absence on account of illness, but thanking them for the honour done him. Attemp's will be made to open the Memorial Hall Library to Congrega- tionalists generally, and it was announced .£4OO had been subscribed for the purchase money of the Davies Library, £6OO.

FUNERAL OF Sru WATET/4 WYN/C—The funeral of the late Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, Bart, M.P., took place at Llangedwy on Friday. The procassion left Wynnstay promptly at six o'clock. The remains were deposited in a hearse, which was completely covered with wreaths and floral tributes sent from all parts of the country. The re- mains were conveyed to Llangedwyn by road, accompanied only by Lady Williams Wynn, Sir Granville Wynn, and Miss Cocks, In a brougham. The line of route was thronged with sympathisers. The remains were laid in the grave, and the coffin decked with flowers. THE DISPUTES IN THE COAL TRADE.—The Executive Committee of the Durham Miners' Association on Friday forwarded £lOO to Mr. Benjamin Pickard, of Wakefield, on behalf of the men on strike at Denby Main Colliery, West Yorkshire. The same committee also gave £5 on behalf of the men on strike at Manvers Main, South Yorkshire. The miners employed at Shireoaks, Kiveton Park, and Wales- wood Collieries haveall returned to work at the 10 per cent. reduction. There are now no colliers out on strike south of Sheffield, and indications of the end of the dispute are ap- parent. The strike has lasted five weeks.
COLLISION BETWEEN_ STEAMERS -TEN MEN
MISSING.

The C.)wes correspondent of the Press Association tele- graphs :—The German steamer Messina came into collision with the British steamer Numida, of London, off Dar- leston Head, during Thursday night. Ten hands of the former vessel are missing. The Numida bad her bow stove in.

div.head: DYNAMITE EXPLOSIONS.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE EXPLOSIONS.

The trial of the prisoners Cunningham and Burton, for treason felony connected with dynamite explosions in Lon- don, was continued on Friday at the Central Criminal Court. The case for the prosecution having been concluded, Cunningham's counsel called two witnesses to prove that on the night of the Gower-street underground-railway explos- ion Cunningham was at his lodgings. Barton obtained per. mission to make a statement, which lasted an hour, as to hia visit to England. He etated that he was innocent, and that be came here for the benefit of his health. Burton's counsel addressed the jury on his behalf, and submitted that there was no evidence of conspiracy on his part with Can- ningham or anyone also. The farther hearing of the case was adjourned till next day.

div.head: REVOLT IN KASHG&R.
div.p: A REVOLT IN KASHG&R.

The Central News correspendent at Bt. Petersburg telegraphed (via Grimbinnen) on Thursday night :—A telegram from Teheran states that the Mussulinans of Kash. gar have risen in insurrection, ag 'inn the Chinese, and have driven the Mandarins out of the principal towns. Their leader, who is a son of Yakeob Bey, has invoked the protection of Russia. He asked for a Russian occupation of the province, and the supply of arms and ammunition. This news has created a considerable sensation. THE WITHDRAWAL FROM [WARM.

StrAWIM, Fnmay--Orders have been issued for the withdrawal of the Guards, the Royal Horse Artillery, and the British Cavalry. The Grenadiers and Scots Guards will leave in the troopship Jumna to-morrow. General &reeves will remain here to superintend the final arrange- ments. General Graham and staff will sail int he trans- port Deccan. Generals M'Noil, Fremantle, and Ewart will follow shortly afterwards. The permanent garrison will consist of one battalion of British Infantry,a battery of Artil- lery, a company of Sappers' the Native Infantry, and the Native Camel Corps, under the command of General Hud son. The Australian contingent will leave in the transport Arab. The following officers will accompany General Gra- ham: Majors Collen and Grover, Lieutenants Stopford, Andersen, and Lindsay.

div.head: ENGLAND AND RUSSIA..
div.p: ENGLAND AND RUSSIA..
REPORTED HITCH IN THE NEGOTIATIONS.

Paws, FRIDAY 10 A.M.—The St. Petersburg correspon- dent of the Debats telegraphs that Rusria has entirely re- jected the agreement arrived at in London. Russia demands the right to have an acknowledged representative at Cabul. French diplomatists express the opinion that this demand Is more serious than any question arising out of the fron- tier.

The Press Association understands that the present state of the negotiations upon the Russo-Afghan frontier is as follows :—The British Government' have received notifica- tion that certain matters of the arrangement made by Earl Granville, Earl Kimberley, M. de Steal, and M. Leasar will require fuller explanation before they can receive the rati- fication of the Russian Government. The points indicated are not of such a vital nature as to lead to a disruption of the whole arrangement, and will, it is strongly believed, be satisfactorily settled at the further pourparias to take place between Earl Granville, Earl Kimberley. M. de Staal, and M.. Leant..

The Pall Mall Gazette says there is rno truth in the statement published by the Standard that the Russian Government is raising difficulties about the settlement of the frontier, and the Daily News is also misinformed when it states that despatches have arrived accepting the proposed agreenient. Only one or two points of detail respecting the frontier delimitation remain open, and ho serious hitch Is possible. The definite couclustou may ba delayed a few days.

DISCONTENT OF THE SARIKS. A Central News telegram, dated St. Petersburg (via Gum-. binnen), Thursday night, states :—A private report from General Komaroff, received by M. de Giers, states that the Sariks protest strongly against the delimitation of the fron- tier proposed by M. Lesser as altogether unacceptable. The Suits declare that by this arrangement all the best pasture lands would be made over to the Afghans. A council of wars has been held to consider these protests, and upon inves- tigation it was evident that the representations of the Sariks were well founded, and further negotiations on the subject between the powers interested are therefore imperatively necessary. lam able to assert that the official proposal for arbitration has been transmitted to the King of Den- mark.

CABINET MEETING. All the Ministers attended the Cabinet Council which met at two o'clock on Friday afternoon. The delibera- tions, which, it is understood, were almost confined to the Afghan frontier question, lasted until a quarter past four. Previous to the meeting of the Cabinet, M. Lesser visited the Foreign Office, and remained in consultation with the Under Secretaries for some time. Mr. Condie Stephen was also in attendance. It is stated, on authority, that DO hitch, properly so called, has occurred in the negotiations with the Russian Government. Communications on matters of detail are still being exchanged, but the basis of the pro- posed frontier settlement as arranged last week will, there is every reason to believe, receive in due course the approval if the Russian Government.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at 4 o'clock.

MISCELLANEOUS..—The Duke of Argyll gave notice toe move the rejection of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill on th second reading. The Secretary for Scotland Bill was read a first time. The Lord Chancellor gave notice to read the English and Scotch Registrations Bills the second time on Monday, and it was arranged to sit on Thursday to pass bills, the House then to adjourn for the holidays. Earl Granville moved, and the Marquis of Salisbury seconded an address to the Throne in reply to the message ou making provision for the Princess Beatrice on her mar- riage. The address was voted.—Lord IVEmyss called atten- tion to deficienc es in the organisation and equipment of the auxiliary forces. The militia were inefficient, badly officered and equipped, whilst the state of the volunteers demanded careful consideration.—The DUBE of CAMBRIDGE said the whole question resolved itself into one of money. —Earl Wemyss's motion was lost, on a division, ny 23 votes to 20.—The Parliamentary Elections Redistribution Bill was formally read a second time.—On the motion of Earl KIMBERLEY, it was arranged that the principle of the Bill should be discussed on its ccmmittee stages. Earl Eimaberley stated that for the purposes of registration it was desirable that the bill should pass into law as soon as possible. After discussion the committee's stage was fixed for Monday, June Bth. The House adjourned at five minutes past eight. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

- The House met at four o'clock. THE GRANT TO PRINCESS BEATRICE.—Mr. C. LEWIS gave notice that in Committee on the Princess Beatrice Annuity Bill he should move an instruction to the Corn- mittee to insert a clause suspending this and all similar an- nuities where the husband has a seat in Parliament.

ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.—Lord FITZMIIIRICE:WPiying to Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, said no answer had yet been re- ceived from the Czar as to the line of frontier of Afghanis- tan approved by Earls Granville and Kimberley, Baron de Steal, and M. Lessar.—Mr. GLADSTONB, replying to Sir S. Northcote, said the negotiations with Russia were not yet concluded. They were awaiting communications respecting one part of the frontier, and some few days might elapse before the negotiations were concluded. The papers laid on the table would break off at the Penjdeh incident. Later on Mr. Gladstone, in reply to a question, said he knew nothiug of a Russian demand to have a representative at Cabot.

TEE COURSE OP BUSINESS.—Mr. GLADSTONE said during the present session the Government proposed to proceed with the Crofters' Bill, the Secretary for Scotland Bill, and a Bill for Intermediate Education in Wales. As regarded Ireland, it was intended to embody various provisions of the Crimes Act, found valuable and equitable, into a bill, and to ask the House to pass that measure into law. He regretted they could not proceed with the measure for local government for Ireland and the Lend Purchase Bill this session.

SUPPLY.—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply Sir W. LUBBOCK drew attention to the state of forestry in this country, and moved for a Select Committee to consider whether by the establishment of a Forest School, or other- wise, our woodlands could be rendered chore remunerative.— Dr. LYONS seconded the motion and Sir H. MAXWELL sup- ported it.—Mr. GLADSTONE approved of the appoinment of a Select Committee, and thought good would come of it, but he reserved perfect freedom of opinion in regard to the establishment of forestry schools.—The motion was agreed to.—Mr. KENNY called attention to the conviction of the Brothers DolahuLty. The House was counted out and adjourned at five minutes past seven.

WEDNESDAY MIDEIGHT.—The Reichstag at this refines sitting passed the third readiog of the Castoms Tariff Bill substantially in the form agreed to on tke second reading. The duty on cattle imported for agricultural pur- poses was fixed at 20 marks for oxen from 21 to 5 years, and at 30 marks for more mature oxen and fat cattle. SOFIA, WEIDNESDAY.—The trial of the persons implicated in the outrage committed on the sth inst. upon the gover- ness and lady's maid, in the service of Mr. Laseelles, the British diplomatic agent, took place to-day, with closed doors. All the accused were found guilty. Two of them were sentonced to twelve years, and the others to seven and six years penal servitude reqpectively, with the loss of their civil right:. The remaining prisoner, beiug under age, was condemned to ten years imprisbnment with- out bard labour. Mr. Lascelles was present during the Proceedings.
